Step four: the driver photos attached to incident reports are unstructured images, so they go to object storage and a separate step extracts their metadata.

Common mistake: treating variety as only a file-format question. A CSV can be messy if its columns change between exports, and a JSON file can be effectively structured if every record has the same fields.

Consequence: if a team builds a nightly batch for data that dispatchers must act on within seconds, they will see stale positions. A pipeline that ignores schema changes will also fail quietly when a new field appears, so the design must account for all three dimensions together.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain has 300 ovens, and each oven sends a temperature reading every second as a small JSON object. Step one: 300 ovens at one reading per second is about 26 million records a day, a high volume. Step two: the readings arrive all day without a break, so the velocity is continuous and a streaming path is needed rather than an overnight load. Step three is not finished yet. A firmware update renamed the temperature field from "temp_c" in older readings to "temperature" in newer ones, so the records no longer share a single field name. Which statement completes step three?
choices: Treat the data as structured, because JSON always has a fixed schema, so the renamed field needs no change in the pipeline.
Hold the readings for a nightly batch, so that any schema change shows up in the morning before it can cause a failure.
Convert every reading to a CSV file so that the column names become fixed and the renamed field stops being a problem.
Normalise both field names into one agreed field during ingestion, because the labels differ between records and a query needs one consistent field.
questions.why: Because the semi-structured records carry labels that differ between versions, the pipeline has to map both names to one field during ingestion so downstream queries see a consistent schema.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm stores scanned proof-of-delivery forms as image files. A query engine cannot read any fields from them directly. Which data category best describes these forms?
choices: Structured, because the images can be stored in a relational table
Structured, because every form uses the same layout on the page
Semi-structured, because the forms carry labels in their file names
Unstructured, because the content has no predefined fields that a query engine can read directly
questions.why: Image files have no predefined fields a query engine can read, which is the defining trait of unstructured data, and a shared page layout does not make them structured.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain keeps a room-booking table with fixed named columns and known types. About 5,000 new bookings arrive per hour. Which description best fits this data's velocity?
choices: Zero velocity, because a table at rest has no arrival rate to measure
Moderate velocity, a steady hourly rate that a scheduled batch load can usually keep up with
Very high velocity, because any rate above one record per minute requires a streaming pipeline
High velocity, because the table has many columns that must each be loaded
questions.why: Velocity is the rate at which new data arrives and how soon it must be usable, and 5,000 bookings per hour with no sub-minute need fits a scheduled batch; column count does not measure velocity.

questions.prompt: A team receives CSV exports from a parts supplier, and the supplier sometimes adds or renames columns between exports. Which explanation correctly identifies the mistake in assuming the file format alone settles the variety question?
choices: Variety is determined by the file extension, so renamed columns are a separate concern
The format is only part of the picture, because a CSV whose columns change between exports can be as messy as any other source, so the schema behaviour decides how the data must be handled
A CSV is always unstructured because it is plain text with no types
CSV is always structured, so column changes cannot affect the pipeline
questions.why: Variety depends on how consistent the fields and shapes are over time, not only on the file format, so a CSV with shifting columns needs the same schema-change handling as other messy sources.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how volume, velocity, and variety, plus the structured versus unstructured distinction, should change the design of an ingestion pipeline, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Volume tells you how much capacity and storage to plan for, and velocity tells you whether a nightly batch is acceptable or whether records must be processed as they arrive. Variety tells you how much parsing and validation the pipeline needs. Structured data with a fixed schema can be loaded and queried directly, while semi-structured data needs field handling and schema-change checks, and unstructured data needs an extraction step before it becomes queryable. The tradeoff is that a streaming design handles velocity well but costs more to run and is harder to debug than a batch job, so for data that only needs to be fresh once a day, choosing streaming adds complexity without benefit. I would size the decision on the requirement's latency, not on how exciting the technology is.
rubricPoints: Defines volume, velocity, and variety in plain terms
Explains how velocity pushes the design toward batch or streaming
Distinguishes structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data and their handling needs
Names a concrete tradeoff, such as cost or complexity of streaming versus batch

suggested.rationale: The core skill is classifying a source and justifying the design in words, which a teammate-style explanation tests directly.

lessons.plain: A large language model, or LLM, is a program trained on huge amounts of text that can read messy written input and produce useful output such as a summary, a label, or a cleaned-up field. Inside a data pipeline, you can call one of these models the same way you call any other transformation step: send it a record, get a result back, and store that result. It is powerful for text that fixed rules struggle with, like free-form support notes. But it is slower, costs money per request, and can give a different answer on a second try, so the surrounding pipeline has to check what it produces.
lessons.guessPrompt: A pipeline receives 2 million free-text customer reviews every night and must tag each one as positive, negative, or neutral. Would you write a rule for each word, or send each review to a language model? What would worry you about each choice?
lessons.teach:
A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on very large text collections to predict and generate language. In a data pipeline it acts as a transformation step: text goes in, and structured or unstructured text comes out. Managed services let you call hosted models through an API instead of running them yourself. The call is a network request containing a prompt, which is the instructions and the input together, and the response is generated text.

Why it works: the model handles meaning that fixed rules cannot. A rule that searches for the word 'late' misses the sentence 'the van turned up after lunch'. A model reads the whole sentence, so it is useful for classifying, extracting fields, summarizing, or normalizing messy text.

Worked example. A nightly job receives 10,000 support emails as raw text. Step 1: the pipeline reads a batch of records from storage. Step 2: for each email, it builds a prompt asking for exactly one category from a fixed list (billing, delivery, damage, other) and a JSON object containing that category. Step 3: it sends the request and parses the JSON response. Step 4: it checks that the category is in the allowed list; if not, it marks the record for review instead of storing a guess. Step 5: it writes the valid rows to the warehouse along with the model version used.

Common mistake: treating model output as trusted data and loading it directly. Models can return malformed JSON, invented categories, or different answers to the same input across runs. Pipelines must validate every response, retry a bounded number of times on parse failure, and keep the raw input so results can be rerun.

Consequence: a single unvalidated prompt change or model upgrade can silently shift every downstream report. Latency and cost multiply across millions of records, so batching, caching, and cost checks belong in the design from the start.

Use a model where meaning matters and rules fail, and wrap every call in validation, bounded retries, and recorded provenance.

questions.prompt: A bicycle rental company stores 4,000 mechanic repair notes each night. The pipeline is meant to flag notes that mention a brake fault so the bike can be pulled from service. Here is the design. Step 1: the pipeline reads a batch of notes from storage. Step 2: for each note, it builds a prompt that asks for a JSON object with one field, brake_fault, set to true or false. Step 3: it sends the request and parses the JSON response. Step 4: this step is missing from the design and is the one you must identify. Step 5: it writes the valid rows to the reporting table with the model version used. The missing step must make sure that a note whose response fails validation can still be examined and rerun later, so the original note text is kept alongside every result. Which action fills Step 4 in a way that matches the lesson?
choices: Retrain the model on the flagged notes before the next night's run starts.
Send every note to the model twice and keep whichever answer came back first.
Cache each response and skip validation on cached rows to save time and cost.
Keep the raw note text next to each result so the run can be repeated and checked later.
questions.why: Keeping the raw input with each result is what lets a pipeline rerun or audit a record, and the lesson names it as part of the design.

questions.prompt: A freight firm wants to tag shipping complaints such as 'the pallet came in with one corner crushed and the seal was broken'. A colleague proposes a rule that searches for the word 'damaged' only. Which statement best explains why a language model is a better fit for this step?
choices: A model reads the whole sentence and can recognise meaning that a fixed word search misses, such as 'crushed' or 'seal broken' describing damage without the word 'damaged'.
A model is faster than any rule because it skips reading the text and works from the complaint length.
A model always returns the same tag for the same complaint, so the rule is unnecessary.
A model stores every complaint in a lookup table, which is cheaper than searching for words.
questions.why: The lesson explains that models handle meaning that fixed rules cannot, and this complaint describes damage without using the keyword.

questions.prompt: A pipeline sends a warehouse incident note to a language model and asks for a JSON object with a severity field. On three runs of the same note, the model returns a valid severity once, a malformed JSON object once, and a severity value that is not on the allowed list once. What should the pipeline do with these responses?
choices: Retry without any limit until the model returns the same answer three times in a row.
Validate every response, retry only a bounded number of times on parse failure, and mark any note that still fails for review instead of storing a guess.
Take the first response that arrives, since the model is trusted once it has answered.
Average the three severity values and store the result as the final score.
questions.why: The lesson says responses can be malformed or invented, so each one must be validated, retries must be bounded, and unresolved records go to review.

questions.prompt: A retail analytics team upgrades to a newer version of a hosted language model. The new version begins returning the category field with slightly different capitalisation and an extra category name. The pipeline loads every response without checking it against the allowed list. What is the most likely consequence for downstream reports?
choices: Reports can shift silently because the bad values flow into the warehouse with no error raised, and the change is hard to trace without the model version recorded.
The model automatically reverts to the previous version, so the reports stay the same.
Nothing changes, because the warehouse ignores any field whose values it does not recognise.
Reports fail loudly with a clear error message, so the team learns of the problem immediately.
questions.why: The lesson warns that an unvalidated change in the model can silently shift every downstream report, and that the model version must be recorded to trace it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would put a large language model inside a data pipeline instead of a rule-based transform, and name one limit or tradeoff you would design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use an LLM when the input is free text and the task needs meaning that rules cannot capture, such as classifying support emails, pulling fields out of messy notes, or summarizing. A plain rule or SQL expression is still better when the logic is exact, like parsing a fixed-format date or summing a column, because it is faster, cheaper, and gives the same answer every time. The main limit is non-determinism: the same input may produce a different label on another run, and the output can break the expected format. So I would constrain the output to a fixed set of values, parse and validate every response, retry a bounded number of times, route failures to a review queue, and store the model version and raw input so results can be audited and replayed. Per-call cost and latency also scale with volume, so I would batch and cache where possible.
rubricPoints: Names a case where meaning in free text makes an LLM worth using over fixed rules.
Names a case where deterministic rules or SQL are the better choice.
States non-determinism or output format drift as a limit of model output.
Describes validation, bounded retries, or a review path for bad outputs.
Mentions cost or latency scaling with volume and how to contain it.

suggested.rationale: Deciding between a model and a rule for a given pipeline requirement is a judgement best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario.

lessons.plain: Orchestration means deciding the order of work. A data pipeline usually has several steps: pull data from a source, clean or reshape it, and load it somewhere useful. Orchestration is the part that starts each step at the right moment, passes results from one step to the next, waits for slow steps, and decides what happens when a step breaks. Think of a restaurant expediter. They do not cook the food, but they call orders in sequence, check that the oven is ready before the next dish goes in, and send a plate back if something burns. Several AWS services do this coordinating job, each suited to a different shape of work.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your nightly pipeline has three steps: copy files from a server, clean them, then load them into a warehouse. On Tuesday the cleaning step fails halfway through. What should happen to the load step, and what would the system need to remember so that the rerun does not start over from the very beginning?
lessons.teach:
ETL stands for extract, transform, load: pull data out of a source, reshape it, and write it to a destination. Orchestration is the coordination layer that runs those steps as a workflow, meaning a defined set of steps with dependencies, where some steps must wait for others. A state is the recorded fact of which steps have finished, failed, or are waiting. A retry runs a failed step again, usually after a pause. An idempotent step produces the same result whether it runs once or several times.

The services in this objective differ in what they coordinate. AWS Lambda runs short pieces of code when triggered. Amazon EventBridge routes events and fires schedules, so it decides when a workflow starts. AWS Step Functions keeps an explicit state machine, tracking each step's state and handling retries, branches, and waits. AWS Glue workflows chain Glue crawlers and jobs together. Amazon MWAA is managed Apache Airflow, which schedules tasks defined as a directed acyclic graph, a set of steps with one-way dependencies and no loops.

Worked example. Step 1 extracts a file and succeeds, and the orchestrator records that. Step 2 transforms the file and hits a malformed row. The orchestrator marks step 2 failed, retries it twice with a pause, and it still fails. It then halts step 3 so nothing is partially loaded. After the engineer fixes the row, the rerun starts at step 2, reusing step 1's recorded output instead of extracting again.

Common mistake: assuming a rerun is always safe. If the load step appends rows, a rerun after a partial success writes the same rows twice. In a running system, dashboards then double-count revenue until someone finds and removes the duplicates. Steps that write data should be idempotent, for example by overwriting a partition or using a unique key.

An orchestrator does not make a bad step correct. Its value is that it records progress, retries predictably, and stops downstream work when upstream work fails.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs a Step Functions workflow each hour. Step 1 extracts the last hour of sales from an API and succeeds, and the state is recorded. Step 2 transforms the sales records and succeeds. Step 3 loads them into a warehouse table by appending rows. Partway through the load, 4,000 rows are written and the connection drops, so step 3 is marked failed. It is retried once and fails again, and the workflow halts. The engineer needs to rerun the hour, and the load step appends, so a rerun would write those 4,000 rows a second time. The missing step: before rerunning, the engineer changes the load so that it overwrites that hour's partition instead of appending. Which statement correctly explains why this change makes the rerun safe?
choices: Overwriting the hour's partition makes step 3 idempotent, so running it again replaces the hour's rows and the total stays correct.
Overwriting the partition lets the rerun skip step 1, which means the API is called fewer times.
Overwriting the partition makes the connection drop less likely, so step 3 is less likely to fail in the first place.
Overwriting the partition deletes the recorded state, so the orchestrator forgets the earlier failure and retries cleanly.
questions.why: An idempotent step gives the same result whether it runs once or several times, and replacing an hour's partition means a repeat run leaves exactly one copy of each row.

questions.prompt: In orchestration, what is a state?
choices: The recorded fact of which steps have finished, failed, or are waiting in a workflow.
A rule in EventBridge that matches incoming events by pattern.
The schedule that decides how often a directed acyclic graph runs.
The address of the server that runs a Lambda function.
questions.why: A state is the recorded progress of the workflow's steps, which is what lets an orchestrator resume or stop correctly.

questions.prompt: A workflow has step 1 extracting files, step 2 transforming them, and step 3 loading them. Step 2 fails after its retries are used up. What should the orchestrator do with step 3?
choices: Run step 3 anyway, because loading whatever was extracted is faster.
Delete step 1's recorded output so that step 3 starts from a clean state.
Halt step 3 so that nothing is partially loaded from a failed upstream step.
Run step 3 once for each retry of step 2 so that the data is not lost.
questions.why: An orchestrator stops downstream work when upstream work fails, which prevents partial loads from a broken transform.

questions.prompt: A team needs a nightly ETL workflow to start automatically at 02:00 every day without anyone pressing a button. Which service is responsible for firing that scheduled start?
choices: Amazon MWAA worker
AWS Glue crawler
Amazon EventBridge
AWS Lambda
questions.why: EventBridge fires schedules and routes events, so it decides when the workflow starts, while the other services run the steps once started.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we would use a workflow orchestrator instead of one long script that runs every ETL step in order. Explain what the orchestrator adds, and name one limit or tradeoff of adding it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A single script runs top to bottom, and if step three fails, you usually have to start again from step one. An orchestrator records which steps finished, so a rerun can resume at the failed step. It also gives each step its own retry rules, timeouts, and a clear rule that downstream steps wait or stop when an upstream step fails. That reduces partial loads and makes failures visible. The tradeoff is added complexity. There is a separate service to configure, permissions to manage between steps, and a new place where things can break. Also, the orchestrator only resumes safely if the steps are idempotent. If a step appends data, a resumed run can still duplicate rows, so the orchestrator cannot fix that by itself.
rubricPoints: Orchestrator records step state so a rerun can resume at the failed step rather than starting over
Retries, timeouts, and dependency rules are handled consistently per step
Tradeoff: extra complexity, configuration, and permissions to manage
Resumption is only safe if steps are idempotent; the orchestrator does not guarantee that

suggested.rationale: The planned workflow state machine engine would make the learner design step states, retries, and resume-from-failure behaviour, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Building a pipeline that works on a good day is easy. Building one that keeps working is the real job. Performance means it finishes fast enough. Availability means it is up when data arrives. Scalability means it copes when the volume grows. Resiliency and fault tolerance mean that when a step breaks halfway, whether from a crashed machine, a slow database, or a bad record, the system recovers without losing or duplicating data and without someone rebuilding it by hand. Think of a bakery line: more orders should mean more ovens, not a collapsed counter, and a broken oven should not waste the whole batch.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job copies 10 million records from a source into a warehouse. Halfway through, the job crashes. When you rerun it from the start, what could go wrong, and what would you change so a rerun is safe?
lessons.teach:
Four properties carry this objective. Performance is how quickly data moves through the pipeline, measured as throughput (records processed per second) and latency (the time from arrival until the data is usable). Availability is whether the pipeline keeps accepting and processing data when parts of it are unhealthy. Scalability is how well capacity grows when volume rises, usually by adding more workers rather than a bigger single machine, which is called horizontal scaling. Resiliency and fault tolerance are the ability to keep going, or to recover cleanly, when a step fails.

The core mechanism is decoupling: place a durable buffer, such as a managed queue or stream, between producers and consumers. The buffer absorbs spikes, so a slow consumer builds a backlog instead of losing data, and you can add consumers to drain it faster. A consumer should record a checkpoint (a marker of how far it has processed) only after its output is safely written.

Worked example. A consumer reads a batch of 100 order events from a queue. It writes 40 rows to the warehouse, then the machine crashes before it records the checkpoint. On restart, the consumer re-reads from the last checkpoint, so those 40 events are processed again. If each write is an upsert (insert the row, or update it if its unique event ID already exists), the second pass overwrites the same rows and the result is correct. A step with this property is called idempotent: running it twice has the same effect as running it once.

Common mistake: treating retries as free. Plain inserts double-count on retry. Scaling consumers without checking the database's rate limit also fails, because a flood of workers can be throttled and fail in the same way.

In a running system, a pipeline with a durable buffer, idempotent writes, and a dead-letter queue (a holding area for records that keep failing) can be restarted at any point without corrupting the data.

questions.prompt: A parcel-tracking team pushes scan events from its handheld devices into a managed queue, which is a durable buffer that holds messages until a consumer processes them. A sudden spike adds 500,000 scan events, and the backlog is growing. The team's plan has three steps: (1) add more consumer workers so they process the queue in parallel, (2) missing step, and (3) watch the backlog shrink on a dashboard. Which choice correctly fills step 2?
choices: Delete the consumer checkpoints so every worker starts reading the queue from the beginning.
Increase the queue's retention period so that no scan events expire while waiting.
Confirm that the warehouse's write rate limit can absorb the extra consumers' writes before adding more of them.
Replace the consumers with one much larger machine so there is only one writer to coordinate.
questions.why: Adding consumers only helps if the downstream database can accept the extra writes, because a flood of workers can be throttled and fail just like the original bottleneck.

questions.prompt: In a data pipeline, what is the main job of a durable buffer such as a managed queue placed between producers and consumers?
choices: It permanently stores every record so that the warehouse never needs to be updated.
It converts each record into the format the consumer expects before the consumer sees it.
It automatically removes duplicate records so consumers never have to handle them.
It holds incoming records so that a slow consumer builds a backlog instead of losing data, and more consumers can drain it.
questions.why: A durable buffer absorbs spikes and keeps records safe while consumers work through them, which is the decoupling that protects against data loss when one side slows down.

questions.prompt: A consumer reads a batch of 75 meter readings, writes its output to a database, and then records a checkpoint, which marks how far it has processed. Which change makes the pipeline safer if the consumer can crash at any moment?
choices: Skip the checkpoint entirely and rely on the queue to remember what was read.
Keep the current order: write the output first, then record the checkpoint only after the write is safely stored.
Write the batch in parallel threads so the checkpoint is recorded sooner.
Record the checkpoint before the batch is written, so the consumer never reprocesses readings.
questions.why: A checkpoint must follow a safe write; if it is recorded first, a crash leaves the checkpoint ahead of the data and readings are lost.

questions.prompt: A retry job writes sensor reading rows to a ledger table using plain inserts. A network timeout occurs after 30 rows were written, the job retries, and the ledger now shows 30 readings twice. Which design change fixes the root cause?
choices: Stop retrying entirely and accept that some readings will be missing from the ledger.
Make each write an upsert keyed on a unique reading ID, so a repeated write overwrites the same row instead of adding a new one.
Add a longer timeout so the first attempt never appears to fail.
Send all retries to the dead-letter queue so they are never processed again.
questions.why: Plain inserts double-count on retry, and an upsert keyed on a unique ID makes repeated execution have the same effect as a single execution, which is idempotence.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make a pipeline that reads events from a queue and writes them to a database resilient to a consumer crash. Name one limit or tradeoff of your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put a durable queue between the producer and the consumer, so events survive if the consumer dies and a traffic spike becomes a backlog rather than lost data. The consumer processes events in batches and advances its checkpoint only after the database write commits. That means a crash causes reprocessing, not loss, so the write must be idempotent: each row is keyed by a unique event ID and written as an upsert, so a second pass changes nothing new. Records that keep failing after retries with backoff go to a dead-letter queue for inspection instead of blocking everything else. The tradeoff is that delivery is at least once, so duplicates are expected and the consumer must tolerate them, and batching and extra components add latency and operational work. I would also check the database's write limits before adding consumers, because more workers can trigger throttling.
rubricPoints: Uses a durable buffer between producer and consumer so crashes and spikes do not lose data
Advances the checkpoint only after the write succeeds, so a crash causes reprocessing
Makes the write idempotent, for example an upsert keyed by a unique ID, so repeats are harmless
Names a tradeoff such as at-least-once delivery, added latency, or downstream throttling limits

suggested.rationale: That design exercise asks you to plan an ingest path that must handle load and failure, which applies this objective directly.

lessons.plain: A serverless workflow is a recipe for a multi-step job that runs on a cloud platform without you managing servers. Think of a kitchen order ticket passed along a line: one station chops, the next cooks, and a manager tracks which ticket is at which station and reruns a station if something goes wrong. For data work, the steps might be check that a file arrived, transform it, load it into a warehouse, and send an alert if anything fails. Serverless means you pay for steps while they run and the platform handles the machines underneath. The hard part is not any single step but keeping the whole chain correct when a middle step fails, times out, or runs twice.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job has three steps: copy files, transform them, load them. The transform step fails partway through after a timeout. Without any orchestration tool, what would you need to know before you could safely restart the job, and why?
lessons.teach:
A workflow is an ordered set of steps where each step's output feeds the next, along with rules for what happens on success, on failure, and while waiting. A serverless workflow runs those steps on managed compute, so you do not keep a machine running between runs. An orchestrator is the component that holds the workflow definition and tracks each run. AWS Step Functions is the AWS orchestrator. In generic terms it is a state machine: a definition of states and transitions that the platform executes and records. The individual steps are often short functions, for example on AWS Lambda, a managed function service.

Why it works: the orchestrator saves the run's state after each step, so a failure in step two does not lose the result of step one. It can retry a failed step with a growing pause between attempts, wait for a time or an event, branch on a value, or run steps in parallel and join the results. Because you pay for execution rather than idle machines, cost follows the work done.

Worked example: a daily file load. State 1 checks that the source file exists. State 2 transforms it and returns a row count of 10,000. State 3 loads the rows, but the load times out. The orchestrator retries State 3 twice with a pause between tries, and the second retry succeeds. State 4 marks the run complete. Because State 2's output was saved, the transform did not run again.

Common mistake: assuming retries are harmless. If State 3 wrote some rows before timing out, a retry can insert them a second time. Any step that writes must be idempotent, meaning running it twice with the same input leaves the same result, for example by tagging each batch with a unique key that the write checks.

In a running system, a workflow with no retry limit and no failure path can stall silently, and new runs pile up behind it. Every workflow needs an explicit failure path that alerts a person.

questions.prompt: A small online shop builds a refund workflow. Step 1 checks that the order exists and is less than 90 days old. Step 2 calculates the refund amount and returns three line items totaling 84.50. Step 3 posts the refund to the payment provider and is set to retry three times with a growing pause between tries. Step 4 emails the customer a confirmation. The team wants the run to end in a clean, visible state if Step 3 still fails after all three retries. Which addition completes the design?
choices: Set Step 3 retries to unlimited so the step never reaches a failure.
Add a failure path after Step 3 that records the run as failed and alerts a person.
Delete the retry setting on Step 3 so the orchestrator stops saving state during the post.
Move the confirmation email ahead of Step 3 so the customer hears first.
questions.why: A failure path is the explicit route the run takes once retries are used up, so it records the failure and alerts a person instead of stalling silently.

questions.prompt: In generic terms, what is the main job of an orchestrator in a serverless workflow?
choices: It holds the workflow definition, tracks each run, and saves state after each step.
It rewrites each step's code to be idempotent before the step runs.
It runs each step's code on machines the team keeps switched on between runs.
It stores the source data so later steps can query it directly.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the orchestrator as the component that holds the workflow definition and tracks each run, saving state after each step.

questions.prompt: A four-step workflow finishes Steps 1 and 2, then Step 3 fails. Step 2's output was saved. When the run resumes from its saved state, what happens to Step 2?
choices: Step 2 runs again from the start, because its output was not kept.
Step 2 runs again but only its second half, because the first half was saved.
The run must be restarted by hand from Step 1 so that Step 2 can rebuild its output.
Step 2 is not run again; its saved output is used.
questions.why: Because the orchestrator saves each completed step's output, a later failure does not cause earlier successful steps to be rerun.

questions.prompt: A workflow step charges a customer's card and is set to retry. The step is not idempotent, and the first attempt timed out partway through. What is the most likely risk when the retry runs?
choices: The charge is cancelled automatically before the retry starts, so no money moves.
Nothing changes, because retries only ever repeat read-only steps.
The orchestrator blocks the retry to protect the customer's card.
The charge may be applied twice, because the first attempt may have partly taken effect.
questions.why: A retry of a non-idempotent write can repeat an effect that already partly happened, which is why such steps need a unique key or similar guard.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a serverless workflow saves state between steps, and name one limit or tradeoff of retrying failed steps automatically.
lessons.modelAnswer: A serverless workflow keeps a record of each run after every step, so if a later step fails, the run can resume from the last saved result instead of starting over. The platform runs each step on managed compute and charges only while work happens, so we do not keep a server up waiting. The tradeoff is retries. When a step times out, the platform cannot tell whether the work partly happened, so a retry can duplicate writes, such as inserting the same rows twice. So every writing step needs to be idempotent, for example by checking a batch key before inserting. I also cap the number of retry attempts and route final failures to an alert, because an unlimited retry loop hides the problem and lets runs queue up behind it.
rubricPoints: The orchestrator saves state after each step so a run can resume rather than restart.
Managed compute means no idle servers, and cost follows execution time.
Automatic retries can duplicate work when a step partly succeeded before failing.
Writing steps should be idempotent, and retries need caps and a failure path that alerts someone.

suggested.rationale: The planned workflow state machine engine would have the learner design retries, branches and failure paths that match this objective directly.

lessons.plain: When a data pipeline breaks at 3 a.m., someone needs to hear about it, and the pipeline should not stall just because the alert could not be delivered. Two building blocks on AWS handle this. Amazon SNS, the Simple Notification Service, is a broadcast point: the pipeline publishes one message to a topic, and every subscriber, such as an email address or a queue, receives a copy. Amazon SQS, the Simple Queue Service, is a holding line: messages wait in the queue until a worker picks them up and confirms it finished. Used together, the pipeline announces an event once, and each tool gets its own durable copy to work through at its own pace.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your nightly pipeline rejects some records and needs to alert both an on-call team and a dashboard tool. Would you send the alert directly from the pipeline to each recipient, or send it to one place that copies it to them? Why?
lessons.teach:
A topic is a named channel in Amazon SNS. A publisher, here your pipeline, sends one message to the topic, and SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber. A subscriber might be an email address, an HTTP endpoint, or an SQS queue. This pattern is publish and subscribe, often called fan-out: one event, many recipients, and the publisher does not need to know who they are.

A queue is a holding area. Amazon SQS stores messages until a consumer, a worker process that reads them, pulls one off and deletes it after handling it. While a consumer works on a message, the queue hides that message for a set visibility timeout. If the consumer crashes before deleting it, the message reappears for another attempt. A message that keeps failing can be moved to a dead-letter queue, a separate queue kept for a person to inspect.

Why combine them? SNS pushes to a subscriber when it can, so a plain email or endpoint that is down may simply miss the alert. An SQS queue behind the topic gives each consumer a durable buffer that survives its downtime.

Worked example: a load job rejects 37 of 50,000 rows. Step 1: the job publishes one message to a topic called load-alerts. Step 2: SNS copies it to an SQS queue read by an on-call triage tool and to a second queue read by a dashboard. Step 3: the triage tool is offline for an hour, but its queue keeps the message. Step 4: when the tool returns, it reads the message, handles it, and deletes it.

Common mistake: making the pipeline wait on the alert. If the job calls the notification service synchronously and that call fails, the load can fail for a reason unrelated to the data. Publish the alert as a side step and keep the job's own success tied to the data it loaded.

Consequence: standard SQS queues can deliver a message more than once and out of order, so every consumer must tolerate duplicates.

questions.prompt: A team runs a nightly export of 120,000 customer records into a data lake. When the export finishes, its job publishes one message to a topic called export-status. Step 1: the job publishes the message to export-status. Step 2: SNS copies it to an SQS queue read by a finance reconciliation service and to a second queue read by an operations dashboard. Step 3: the reconciliation service pulls the message and begins work, then its process crashes before it deletes the message from its queue. Step 4: what happens to that message next?
choices: The queue deletes the message permanently, and the dashboard queue is told to retry the reconciliation.
Once the visibility timeout expires, the message becomes visible in the queue again and another consumer attempt can pick it up.
The export job notices the missing acknowledgement and publishes the message again under a new topic.
SNS resends the message straight to the reconciliation queue within a second, without waiting.
questions.why: A consumer that crashes before deleting a message leaves it hidden only until the visibility timeout runs out, after which SQS makes it visible again for another attempt.

questions.prompt: In one sentence, why do teams often place an SQS queue behind an SNS topic instead of having SNS push directly to a subscriber that might be offline?
choices: The queue lets SNS skip the subscriber's filter so every message is delivered faster.
The queue stores messages durably so a consumer that is down can still read them when it returns.
The queue converts the message into an email so a person can read it during an outage.
The queue deletes messages after one minute so the subscriber never sees stale alerts.
questions.why: SNS pushes when it can and a plain endpoint that is down may miss the alert, whereas an SQS queue holds each message until the consumer comes back and deletes it.

questions.prompt: A consumer of an alert queue reads a message, starts handling it, and its process is killed before it deletes the message. The consumer's visibility timeout is 60 seconds. What is the most accurate description of the message's state afterwards?
choices: The message is moved to the dead-letter queue immediately on the first failed read.
The message is hidden for 60 seconds, then visible again so another attempt can read it.
The message is permanently removed because it was read once.
The message is sent back to the SNS topic so every subscriber receives a copy again.
questions.why: A message is hidden during the visibility timeout and reappears when that timeout ends if it was never deleted, so the next attempt can process it.

questions.prompt: A pipeline loads 8,400 sales rows into a warehouse. The load job calls an alerting service synchronously after loading. The alerting service is down, the call errors, and the job is marked as failed, even though all 8,400 rows loaded correctly. Which change best fixes the design?
choices: Raise the alerting service's timeout so the synchronous call never fails.
Run the alert call twice so that at least one attempt succeeds.
Skip alerting entirely and check the warehouse table by hand each morning.
Publish the alert as a separate side step and tie the job's success only to the data it loaded.
questions.why: Keeping the alert off the critical path means an unrelated notification failure cannot mark a successful data load as failed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a pipeline that must alert several tools should publish to an SNS topic that feeds SQS queues, rather than calling each tool directly. Name one limit or tradeoff of this design.
lessons.modelAnswer: The pipeline publishes one event to a topic, so it does not need to know how many tools listen or handle their failures. Each tool gets its own SQS queue, which holds the message until that tool is ready, so an outage in one tool does not lose the alert or block the others. The job itself stays focused on loading data, and a failed notification does not make a good load look failed. The tradeoff is that standard queues may deliver duplicates or out-of-order messages, so each consumer has to be idempotent, meaning handling the same alert twice does no harm. There is also one more moving part to monitor, since a queue can quietly grow if its consumer stops, which is why a dead-letter queue and a depth alarm are worth setting up.
rubricPoints: SNS topic publishes once and fans out copies to many subscribers without the publisher knowing them
SQS queue buffers messages so a slow or offline consumer does not lose them
Decoupling keeps the pipeline's success independent of alert delivery
Standard queues can duplicate or reorder messages, so consumers must be idempotent

suggested.rationale: A planned messaging engine would let the learner wire a topic to queues and watch fan-out and buffering behave under a simulated outage.

lessons.plain: Optimizing pipeline code means making a data job finish faster, or use less time and cost, without changing what it produces. Imagine sorting a box of mail: you can check every envelope against a full list of addresses for each one, which gets slower as the pile grows, or you can file them into labeled bins first and only look in one bin at a time. Most slow pipelines are slow for one of a few reasons: repeating an expensive lookup over and over, reading far more data than needed, or handling records one at a time when they could move in groups. Finding the real bottleneck comes before changing anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A transformation job joins 1 million sales rows against a 500,000-row product list by scanning the whole product list for every sales row. Without running anything, what single change would most likely cut the runtime sharply, and why?
lessons.teach:
Runtime is how long a job takes from start to finish. A bottleneck is the step that consumes most of that time, and it is the only place where a change will noticeably help. Much slow pipeline code comes down to three things: repeated lookups done with the wrong data structure, reading more data than the job needs, and processing records one at a time when they could be grouped.

A list is a plain sequence. Finding an item means checking entries one by one, so the work grows with the length of the list. A hash table, which Python calls a dictionary, stores values under keys and jumps close to the right entry directly, so a lookup costs roughly the same however large the table is. Big O notation describes how work grows with input size: O(n) means work grows in step with n, and O(n squared) means it grows with the square of n.

Worked example. Suppose 1,000 sales rows must each find a product name from a list of 1,000 products. Scanning the product list for every sale does up to 1,000 times 1,000, about one million comparisons. Instead, build a dictionary from product id to name once, which costs 1,000 insertions. Then each sale does one lookup, another 1,000 operations. The total is about 2,000 steps, roughly five hundred times less work, and the output is identical.

The common mistake is optimizing before measuring. Profile the job first, find the step that dominates, and change only that. Reading every column of a wide file when the job needs two columns wastes time in the same way.

In a running system, a quadratic step that is harmless on a test file can push a nightly job past its window, so the next run starts while the previous one is still going and the backlog grows each day.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm must match 4,000 parcel scans to a list of 900 depot codes so each scan can show its depot name. Worked plan: (1) Scanning the depot list for every scan costs up to 4,000 times 900, about 3.6 million comparisons. (2) Building a dictionary from depot code to depot name costs 900 insertions, done once. (3) Each scan then does one dictionary lookup, costing 4,000 operations in total. Missing step (4): state the total number of operations for the dictionary approach.
choices: 3.6 million operations
900 operations
4,900 operations
4,000 operations
questions.why: The dictionary approach costs the one-time 900 insertions plus the 4,000 lookups, which adds to 4,900 operations.

questions.prompt: A pipeline must match 2,500 clickstream events to a list of 600 campaign codes to find each campaign name. Which change most reduces the work needed to find each name?
choices: Store the campaign codes in a list and scan it from the end
Load the campaign codes into a dictionary keyed by code, then look up each event
Read the campaign file twice so the list is already loaded in memory
Keep the campaign codes in a list and sort that list once a day
questions.why: A dictionary lookup takes roughly the same time regardless of table size, while a list lookup checks entries one by one and grows with the list length.

questions.prompt: A team's job runs in 12 minutes on a small test file but takes 9 hours on the full production file. An engineer wants to make it faster. What should they do first?
choices: Profile the job on a production-sized run to find the step that consumes most of the time
Remove the logging statements from every function in the job
Add more memory to every machine in the cluster
Rewrite the entire job in a different programming language
questions.why: The teaching text says to measure first, find the dominant bottleneck, and change only that step, rather than optimizing by guesswork.

questions.prompt: A nightly transformation job's runtime roughly quadruples each time its input size doubles. What growth pattern does this suggest, and why does it matter for a running system?
choices: O(n), so the job will keep finishing in the same window as input grows
O(log n), so the job is safe to ignore until the data becomes very large
O(n squared), so each doubling of input can push the run past its window and create a growing backlog
O(1), so runtime will not change as the input size changes
questions.why: Work that grows with the square of input size quadruples when input doubles, and if the run overruns its window the next run starts before the previous one finishes, letting the backlog grow each day.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a nested loop that joins two datasets can become the slowest part of a pipeline as data grows, how a lookup structure fixes it, and what tradeoff that fix brings. Name one limit of the fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: A nested loop compares every row on one side with every row on the other, so the work is roughly the size of one side times the size of the other. Doubling both sides roughly quadruples the time, which is why it looks fine on a sample and then falls over in production. Building a hash table keyed on the join column turns each lookup into a near-constant step, so the total work becomes roughly the sum of the two sizes instead of their product. The tradeoff is memory: the table has to hold the lookup side, and it must be built before probing starts. If the lookup side is too large to fit in memory, the fix stops being simple and the job needs to partition the data or use a distributed join. I would also confirm with a profile that the join is the real bottleneck before changing it.
rubricPoints: Explains that a nested loop costs roughly the product of the two input sizes.
Explains that a hash-based lookup makes each probe near-constant time.
Names the memory cost of holding the lookup side in memory.
Mentions measuring first to confirm the bottleneck before changing code.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner choose between hash tables and lists for lookups, which is the core decision in this objective.

lessons.plain: A Lambda function is a small piece of code that AWS runs for you when something happens, such as a new file landing or a message arriving, so you do not manage a server between those events. Concurrency is how many copies of that code can run at the same moment. Configuring a function for a data pipeline means choosing how many copies may run, how much memory and time each copy gets, and what happens when work arrives faster than the copies can finish it. Set it wrong and the pipeline falls behind, drops work, or overwhelms the systems it writes to. It is like sizing the checkout lanes in a shop: too few and the queue grows, too many and the back room cannot keep up.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function takes 2 seconds to process one batch of records. If 5 copies can run at once, roughly how many batches can it finish per second, and what happens to batches that arrive faster than that?
lessons.teach:
Concurrency is the number of invocations of a function running at the same time. An invocation is one run of the function on one unit of work, such as one batch of records. Reserved concurrency is a cap you set on one function. It limits that function to a maximum number of simultaneous copies and also sets aside capacity for it, so one busy function cannot consume the whole account's pool. Provisioned concurrency keeps a number of copies initialized in advance, which avoids the cold start delay, meaning the pause while AWS prepares a new copy and loads your code. The memory setting also controls the CPU share, so more memory often means a shorter run. The timeout is the longest one invocation may run before it is stopped. Throttling happens when incoming work exceeds the available concurrency; the excess is held back or rejected, depending on how the function is triggered.

Throughput is roughly concurrency divided by the average duration of one invocation. Worked example: a function averages 0.5 seconds per batch and has reserved concurrency of 20. Twenty batches run at once, each finishing in 0.5 seconds, so about 40 batches complete per second. A surge brings 100 batches per second. The backlog grows by 60 per second, so after one minute about 3,600 batches are waiting.

The common mistake is raising concurrency without checking the downstream limit. Raising it to 50 would match the arrival rate, but then 50 copies would open connections to a database that may allow only 30. The function pool is cheap to scale; the database connection limit is what fails. A second mistake is setting the timeout below the real run time, which causes retries and duplicate writes.

In a running system, a pipeline that is throttled without anyone noticing shows growing lag, and if the source keeps data for a limited time, unprocessed records can expire and be lost.

questions.prompt: A team runs an order-events function. Each batch averages 0.8 seconds, and reserved concurrency is set to 25. Throughput is concurrency divided by average duration: 25 divided by 0.8 is 31.25 batches completed per second. A surge then delivers 60 batches per second. The one step not yet done is working out how fast the backlog grows. The backlog grows by the net rate, which is ____ batches per second. Which completion is correct?
choices: 35 per second, the arrival rate plus the completion rate
60 per second, the full arrival rate
31.25 per second, the completion rate
28.75 per second, arrivals minus completions
questions.why: The backlog grows by the amount that arrives each second minus the amount completed each second, so 60 minus 31.25 gives 28.75 per second.

questions.prompt: An account-level function has reserved concurrency set to 10. Which statement describes what this setting does?
choices: It keeps 10 copies of the function initialized in advance so no cold start delay occurs.
It stops any invocation that runs longer than 10 seconds.
It limits the whole account to 10 simultaneous copies across every function.
It caps this function at 10 simultaneous copies and sets aside that capacity so other functions cannot use it.
questions.why: Reserved concurrency is a per-function cap that also sets aside capacity, while the cold start fix is provisioned concurrency and the timeout is a separate setting.

questions.prompt: A function averages 1.2 seconds per batch and has reserved concurrency of 15. Roughly how many batches can it complete per minute if it keeps running at that concurrency with no throttling?
choices: 900 per minute
18 per minute
12.5 per minute
750 per minute
questions.why: Throughput is 15 divided by 1.2, which is 12.5 batches per second, and multiplying by 60 seconds gives 750 per minute.

questions.prompt: A function has its timeout set to 3 seconds, but its batches typically take about 4 seconds to finish. What is the most likely result in production?
choices: Each run is stopped before it finishes and is retried, so some writes may happen twice.
The function finishes faster, because a short timeout forces the platform to allocate more CPU.
The function runs normally, because the timeout only produces a warning in the logs.
Throughput rises, because stopped invocations free their concurrency for new batches sooner.
questions.why: A timeout is a hard stop, so a run cut off at 3 seconds is retried by the trigger, and any writes already made before the stop can be repeated.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose the concurrency setting for a Lambda function that writes records into a database with a fixed connection limit. Name one limit or tradeoff your answer depends on.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from throughput. Concurrency divided by the average run time gives roughly how many batches per second the function can finish, so I compare that with the arrival rate at peak. Then I check the database, because the number of simultaneous copies is effectively the number of connections it must accept. If the database allows 30 connections and I set concurrency to 50, the extra copies fail or wait, and the failures look like random write errors. So I cap concurrency at or below the connection limit, leaving headroom for other clients. The tradeoff is that a lower cap means a longer backlog during a surge, so I accept some lag and make sure the source retains data long enough to cover it. I would also confirm the timeout is longer than the slowest normal batch, so a retry does not write the same records twice.
rubricPoints: Throughput is roughly concurrency divided by average duration, compared against the arrival rate
Concurrency sets how many simultaneous connections or calls the downstream system receives
Raising concurrency can overload a downstream limit, so the cap must respect it
Tradeoff: lower concurrency means backlog and lag during surges, which must fit within source retention

suggested.rationale: That mission has you diagnose a throttling incident under a traffic surge, which exercises how concurrency limits shape a serverless workload.

lessons.plain: Data engineers write small programs that move, clean, and reshape data. The languages they reach for are a short list: Python and SQL are the everyday workhorses, Scala and Java are common where big processing engines run across many machines, R shows up mostly in statistics-heavy work, and Bash and PowerShell are scripting languages for the command line on Linux and Windows. Knowing what each language is typically used for, and why, matters more than memorising syntax, because the choice shapes how a pipeline is built, tested, and run.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job must read a million sales records, total them by region, and write the totals to a file. Before reading on, which would you pick first: Python, SQL, Scala, R, Bash, or PowerShell? Say why in one sentence.
lessons.teach:
A programming language is the notation you write instructions in. A framework is a library of ready-made building blocks, such as a processing engine that splits work across many machines. A data pipeline is a chain of steps that ingest data from a source, transform it, and load it somewhere useful. An ETL job is one such step that extracts, transforms, and loads.

Python is the most common general-purpose language in data work because its libraries handle files, APIs, and cloud calls with little code. SQL (Structured Query Language) is declarative: you describe the result you want, such as totals grouped by a column, and the database engine decides how to compute it. Scala and Java run on the Java Virtual Machine and are the native languages of Apache Spark, a distributed processing framework that runs one job across a cluster. R is strongest for statistics and analysis. Bash and PowerShell are shell languages for scripting the command line: Bash is standard on Linux, and PowerShell is standard on Windows and also runs on Linux.

The underlying idea is to pick the language whose engine does the heavy lifting. Row-by-row work in a loop is slow at scale, while a set-based SQL query or a Spark job pushes the work into an engine built for it.

Worked example: total order amounts by region. Step 1: write the SQL statement SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY region. Step 2: the engine scans the table once and groups the rows by region. Step 3: it adds the amounts within each group and returns one row per region. A Python loop doing the same job would read each row into memory and add it in the interpreter, which is far slower on a billion rows.

Common mistake: writing a Python loop over data that one SQL statement or Spark transformation could handle, or assuming Bash can safely parse structured data such as JSON.

Consequence in a running system: a loop that finishes in seconds on a test file can run for hours on production volume and miss the nightly deadline, so choosing the language is an operational decision as well as a style choice.

questions.prompt: A ride-sharing company stores 2 billion trip records in a data lake, which is a large store of raw files on cloud storage, and needs to flag trips with a negative fare. A junior engineer's draft loops over each record in Python and appends bad ones to a list. The reworked approach has one step missing. Step 1: recognise that the loop pulls every record through a single Python interpreter, which will be slow at this size. Step 2: express the condition as a filter in Spark, a distributed processing framework, so each worker machine in the cluster checks its own share of the records. Step 3: [missing]. Which completion finishes the job correctly?
choices: Keep the Python loop and let it run longer on a bigger machine.
Load the same records into R and run a per-row check there.
Convert the records to a Bash script that greps for negative signs in the raw files.
Write the filtered rows out as the job's output, which is the step that delivers the result from the cluster.
questions.why: The filter only produces a delivered result once the output is written, and Spark runs that filter across the cluster instead of through one interpreter loop.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's nightly job must total invoice amounts per insurer across 80 million rows. Which approach fits this kind of work best?
choices: An R loop that calls sum() on one row at a time.
A Python for loop that reads each of the 80 million rows and adds amounts in a dictionary.
A Bash script that uses awk to sum the third column of each CSV line.
A single SQL statement that groups the rows by insurer and sums the amounts, so the database engine does the work.
questions.why: SQL is declarative and set-based, so the engine computes the grouped totals in one pass rather than through row-by-row work in a loop.

questions.prompt: A Python script finishes in seconds on a 10,000-row test file. Why might the same script miss a nightly deadline on production volume?
choices: Production servers always run PowerShell, which blocks Python from starting.
Python cannot read files larger than the test file's size.
Per-row work in the interpreter grows with the row count, so run time rises far beyond what the test showed.
SQL results are cached in the test file, which makes the script look fast.
questions.why: A loop that is quick at small size can take hours at production volume, which is why language choice is an operational decision.

questions.prompt: A team wants to pull nested JSON events from an API and reshape them reliably. Which choice is the safest?
choices: Use Python or another language with a real JSON parser.
Split the text on commas with a one-line Bash command.
Load the raw text straight into a shell variable and index into it.
Parse them with Bash string tools such as grep and sed.
questions.why: Bash is a shell language that is not built to parse structured data such as JSON, so a language with a proper parser is the safer choice.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to data work why a data engineer might use SQL for an aggregation but Python for calling an external API, and name one limit of relying on SQL alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: SQL is built for asking a set of rows a question, such as totals by group, and the database engine can run that across all the rows efficiently and with its own optimiser. Calling an external API is different: it involves sending HTTP requests, handling authentication, retrying failures, and parsing responses, which Python's libraries do well and SQL does not do natively. A limit of relying on SQL alone is that it has no general way to talk to outside services or handle messy, nested input files, so a pipeline usually needs a general-purpose language like Python alongside it. Another limit is that SQL is harder to unit test in isolation than a Python function, so the logic you put there needs deliberate testing. The practical rule is to put set-based work in the engine and I/O-heavy or branching work in code.
rubricPoints: SQL suits set-based aggregation because the engine processes many rows at once.
Python suits calling APIs, handling retries, and parsing varied inputs.
A stated limit of SQL alone, such as weak support for external calls or harder testing.
Choose the language by where the work runs most efficiently, not by habit.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner read a CSV and produce JSON in Python, which is the closest existing hands-on practice for choosing and using a data language.

lessons.plain: Data pipelines are programs that move and reshape data on a schedule or as it arrives. Engineers who build them borrow habits from software development so that changes can be undone, checked before they run, and understood when something breaks. Version control keeps a dated history of every change to the pipeline's code and settings. Testing runs small automated checks before a change goes live. Logging writes down what each step did, and monitoring watches those records over time so someone is alerted when a run fails or slows down. Together these turn a fragile script into something a team can trust.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job that reshapes sales data broke last Tuesday, and nobody noticed until Friday. Without looking anything up, what two or three practices would have caught the problem sooner, and why would each one help?
lessons.teach:
Version control is a system, such as Git, that records every change to a set of files as a commit, so you can see who changed what and when, and return to an earlier state. A pipeline's transformation code, its schema definitions, and its configuration belong in version control, because a pipeline you cannot reproduce is one you cannot reliably repair. Testing means writing automated checks that run before code is deployed. A unit test feeds a small known input into one transformation and asserts the output. A data test checks properties of real results, such as no null keys or a row count within an expected range. Logging means recording structured events from each step, such as start time, rows read, rows rejected, and errors, in a form you can search later. Monitoring means evaluating those records continuously and raising an alert when a measure crosses a threshold, such as a failed run, a run that takes twice its usual time, or an output with zero rows.

Why it works: each practice shortens the gap between a change and its discovery. A test catches a bad transformation before it touches production data, a log tells you which step failed, and a monitor tells you without someone having to look.

Worked example: a job reads orders, drops rows with a missing customer ID, and writes Parquet files. Step 1, a developer changes how dates are parsed. Step 2, a unit test feeds three sample rows, one with a blank date, and asserts that the blank row is rejected and the others keep their values. The test fails, revealing that the new parser crashes on blanks. Step 3, the fix is committed together with the test, so the history explains why the rule exists. Step 4, each run logs rows read and rows rejected, and a monitor alerts when output row count falls below half of the previous day's.

Common mistake: logging only the final status. A job that writes zero rows and reports success passes every check unless someone measured the row count.

Consequence in a running system: a silent bad load often costs more than a loud crash, because downstream reports keep running on wrong numbers until someone notices.

questions.prompt: A water utility runs a nightly job that reads pressure readings from field sensors, converts them to psi, and writes Parquet files. Step 1: an engineer changes the conversion so it assumes every reading is in kPa. Step 2: a data test on staging checks that every pressure falls between 0 and 150 psi, and it reports 4 of 90,000 rows outside that range. Step 3 is not shown. Step 4: the run logs rows read (90,000) and rows rejected (4), and a monitor alerts whenever any rows are rejected. Which choice best completes Step 3?
choices: Find the cause in the four rows, add a rule covering both unit formats, and add a unit test for both before deploying.
Deploy the change now, since four rows in 90,000 is too small to matter, and let the alert report them when it fires.
Raise the upper limit in the data test to 200 psi so the four rows pass and the run completes without any warning at all.
Delete the data test, because it was written before the new formula and no longer matches how the data arrives at the utility.
questions.why: The data test on real output exposed a genuine mismatch in the input, so the correct move is to find its cause, handle both formats in the transformation, and cover that with a unit test before deploying.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain's nightly inventory job should produce roughly 42,000 rows. Which check is a data test, as opposed to a unit test?
choices: Checking the real nightly output for no null SKU values and a row count between 40,000 and 45,000.
Recording the job's start time and error count in a searchable log after each run.
Confirming that the job's code file is stored in version control with a descriptive commit message.
Feeding three made-up stock records into the unit-price parser and asserting the parsed price for each.
questions.why: A data test checks properties of real results, such as no null keys or a row count within an expected range, while a unit test feeds a small known input into one transformation.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointment-sync job finishes at 3 a.m. with status success but writes zero rows because an upstream API renamed a field. Which practice would most directly have surfaced this without a person looking at the output?
choices: Version control, so the field-name change is recorded as a commit that someone can later review.
A monitor that evaluates the logged output row count and raises an alert when it drops to zero.
Structured logs of each step's start time, with no monitor reading them and no alert configured.
Unit tests on the parser, which would have passed anyway because the sample data used the old field name.
questions.why: Monitoring evaluates recorded measures continuously and alerts when a threshold is crossed, such as an output with zero rows, whereas logs alone need someone to read them.

questions.prompt: A team's job logs only its final status, and a transformation change begins dropping every row whose currency field is empty. Downstream dashboards keep refreshing. What is the most serious consequence of this kind of silent failure?
choices: Nothing is lost, because the job reports success and the source files are retained, so a later rerun repairs every affected report without any further action.
Reports keep running on wrong numbers until someone notices, which can cost more than a loud crash would have.
The job crashes at once, so the failure shows up in the run status the same night and the team reacts quickly.
Version control blocks the deployment automatically because the commit lacks an accompanying test file.
questions.why: A bad load that reports success lets downstream reports keep running on wrong numbers until someone notices, which is often more costly than a loud failure.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to data engineering why a pipeline should have version control, tests, logs and monitoring, and name one limit that testing alone does not cover.
lessons.modelAnswer: Version control gives us a history of every pipeline change, so if a deploy breaks the output we can see exactly what changed and revert it, and the reasons for each rule stay next to the code. Tests run the transformation against small known inputs before it touches real data, which catches logic errors early. Logs record what each run actually did, such as rows read, rows rejected and errors, so we can diagnose failures afterward. Monitoring watches those numbers continuously and alerts us when they go wrong. The limit of testing is that a test only checks the cases someone thought of, and production data often breaks assumptions nobody wrote down, such as a source suddenly sending dates in a new format. Monitoring covers that gap: a sudden drop in row count raises an alert even when every test passed.
rubricPoints: Version control records every change to pipeline code and configuration so changes can be reviewed and reverted.
Tests check transformations against small known inputs before deployment.
Logs record what each run did, such as row counts and errors, in a searchable form.
Monitoring evaluates those records continuously and alerts when a threshold is crossed.
A named limit: tests only cover anticipated cases, so monitoring is needed for unexpected data.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you repair a CI pipeline, which exercises the version control and automated checks this objective covers.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code means describing the cloud resources a system needs, such as storage buckets, message queues, permissions, and pipelines, in a text file instead of clicking them together in a web console. A tool reads that file and builds or updates the resources so they match the description. Because the description is text, it can be stored in version control, reviewed like any other change, and used to rebuild the same setup in a test account or another region. AWS CloudFormation takes a template written in YAML or JSON. The AWS CDK lets you write the same kind of description in a general programming language and then produces the template. Both aim for repeatable deployment: the same input gives the same environment every time.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you deploy the same infrastructure description twice, once to an empty test account and once to an empty production account, what would you expect to be the same between them, and what might still differ?
lessons.teach:
A stack is one deployed set of resources that CloudFormation manages together, such as a bucket, a queue, and the role a job uses to read the bucket. A template is the file that describes a stack. Each resource in it has a logical name, a type, and a set of properties. CloudFormation compares the template with what currently exists and then creates, updates, or deletes resources to match. Because the file is the source of truth, a second copy of the template can build the same environment somewhere else. The AWS CDK, the Cloud Development Kit, lets you write this description in a programming language such as Python or TypeScript, using objects called constructs. Running the CDK's synth step turns that code into a CloudFormation template, which is then deployed the same way.

Worked example: a template declares one S3 bucket with versioning off. You deploy, and the stack creates the bucket. You then change the template so versioning is on and deploy again. CloudFormation first produces a change set that lists the planned update. You review it, and it then modifies the existing bucket rather than creating a new one.

Common mistake: someone turns versioning off in the console. The live bucket now differs from the template, which is called drift. The next deploy may silently revert the console change or fail, depending on the property involved. Consequence: a pipeline that depends on that bucket can break during a routine deploy, long after the manual change was made. Infrastructure as code is only repeatable when every change goes through the template.

questions.prompt: A retail data team writes a CDK app in TypeScript that defines a DynamoDB table for order events and a role that a Glue job uses to read that table. Here is their path. Step 1: they run the synth step, which turns the TypeScript constructs into a CloudFormation template. Step 2: this step is missing from the trace. Step 3: CloudFormation creates the table and the role together as one stack. Which choice correctly fills step 2?
choices: They deploy the generated template through CloudFormation the same way they would deploy any template
They create the table and role in the console first and then let the template adopt them
They deploy the TypeScript file straight to AWS, which skips the template entirely
They hand-edit the generated template file to add the table's capacity settings before anything else runs
questions.why: Synth produces a CloudFormation template, and that template is deployed through CloudFormation like any other template, which is what makes the stack.

questions.prompt: Why can a second copy of a template be used to build the same environment in another place?
choices: Because the template is the source of truth that describes the stack
Because CloudFormation copies live resources from one environment to another
Because the template stores the data inside each bucket and queue for restore
Because the CDK saves a nightly backup of every stack it has ever deployed to a separate account
questions.why: The template file describes the intended stack, so any account that deploys it gets the same set of resources, which is why it is the source of truth.

questions.prompt: A team's template sets a stream's retention to 24 hours. An engineer changes the same setting to 48 hours in the console and does not touch the template. What is the main risk?
choices: The stream is deleted immediately because the live setting no longer matches
The live setting no longer matches the template, so a later deploy may revert it or fail depending on the property
Nothing happens, because the console change is recorded in the template automatically
CloudFormation refuses every future deploy until the stream is recreated under a new name
questions.why: A manual change creates drift, the gap between the live resource and the template, and the next deploy may silently revert it or fail depending on the property involved.

questions.prompt: A developer writes a CDK app in TypeScript that defines a Kinesis stream. What does running the synth step produce?
choices: A compiled binary that CloudFormation executes directly
A Terraform state file that the console reads
A running Kinesis stream already present in the account
A CloudFormation template describing the same resources, which is then deployed
questions.why: Synth turns the CDK code into a CloudFormation template, and that template is then deployed the same way as any other template.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what infrastructure as code gives you over creating resources by hand in the console, and name one limit or tradeoff of working this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Infrastructure as code means the environment is described in a file that lives in version control.
