That gives us repeatability: we can build the same stack in a test account and in production, review changes before they happen through a change set, and see who changed what and when. The description is the source of truth, so we can rebuild a broken environment from it. The tradeoff is that the file only controls what it describes. If someone edits a resource in the console, the live resource drifts from the template, and the next deploy may revert that change or fail. We also have to keep the template and the running system in step, which means discipline about never making manual changes. CloudFormation and the CDK both make this workable, but they do not stop someone from bypassing them.
rubricPoints: Describes infrastructure in a file that can be version controlled and reviewed
Gives repeatable deployment across accounts or regions from the same description
Names drift: manual console changes diverge from the template
Notes that the CDK generates a CloudFormation template rather than replacing it

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly facts about how stacks, templates, change sets, and the CDK relate, which is best learned by reading the official concepts and then checking your understanding against the explanation prompt.

lessons.plain: Serverless means you hand a cloud provider small pieces of code, such as a function that runs whenever a new file lands, and the provider runs and scales them for you. Packaging and deploying means turning your project into a bundle the cloud can run, then creating the cloud resources around it: the function, its permissions, what triggers it, and where its output goes. AWS SAM is a tool and template format that lets you describe all of that in one file and then build, upload and deploy it the same way every time. The goal is that the pipeline can be recreated exactly from the file, instead of being rebuilt by hand in a web console.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you built a small data pipeline that runs a function every time a file arrives in storage, what would you need to write down so a colleague could recreate the exact same setup in a different account next week?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as code means describing cloud resources in a text file instead of clicking them into existence. AWS SAM, the Serverless Application Model, is an extension of AWS CloudFormation, the general service that builds groups of resources from such files. A stack is a set of resources that CloudFormation creates, updates and deletes together. SAM adds short forms for serverless parts: one function declaration can imply its execution role (the identity the function runs as, and the permissions it holds), its event trigger and its log group, which would otherwise take many lines of plain CloudFormation. A transform line near the top of the file tells CloudFormation to expand these short forms first.

The workflow has three steps. Build collects your source code and its dependencies into a deployable form. Package uploads those files, called artifacts, to an object storage bucket and rewrites the template to point at the uploaded copies instead of local folders. Deploy hands the packaged template to CloudFormation, which computes a changeset (a preview of what will be added, changed or removed) and then applies it.

Worked example: a function converts CSV files to Parquet whenever an object lands in a raw bucket. The template declares the function with its memory and timeout, grants it permission to read the raw bucket and write the curated bucket, and attaches an event that fires on object creation. Build installs the Parquet library into the bundle. Package uploads the bundle and rewrites the code location. Deploy creates the function, trigger and permissions in one stack. If any resource fails to create, CloudFormation rolls the stack back to its previous state.

Common mistake: editing the function in the console after deploying. The live stack no longer matches the file, a condition called drift, and the next deploy can silently undo the manual change or fail. Make every change in the template and redeploy.

For a running pipeline, the template is the record of what exists. Keep it in version control so every deployed version can be traced and reproduced.

questions.prompt: A reporting team has a SAM template for a function that compresses daily ledger extracts when they land in an intake bucket. Their pipeline run log shows the steps in this order: build (which installs the compression library into the bundle), then a missing step, then deploy. The template still points at the local folder ./bundle, so the function code in the stack was never the uploaded copy. The missing step is the one that uploads the bundle's files to the artifacts bucket and rewrites the template's code location to point at those uploaded copies. Which step name fills the blank in build, ____, deploy?
choices: Rollback
Drift detection
Package
Changeset review
questions.why: Package is the step that uploads the built artifacts to object storage and rewrites the template to reference the uploaded copies, which is exactly what the log shows was skipped.

questions.prompt: In AWS SAM, what is the job of the transform line near the top of a template?
choices: It tells CloudFormation to expand the short serverless forms into full resource declarations before creating anything
It uploads the function's source code to an object storage bucket
It rolls the stack back to its previous state if a resource fails
It compares the live stack with the template and reports drift
questions.why: The transform line tells CloudFormation to expand SAM's short forms first, so the template's shorthand becomes the full resources that are then built.

questions.prompt: A team changes a function's memory setting directly in the cloud console after a deploy, and does not change the template. What is the main risk for the next deploy?
choices: The changeset will be empty, so the function will run with the new memory forever
The live stack no longer matches the template, so the next deploy may silently undo the manual change or fail
CloudFormation will refuse to deploy any change until the console edit is reverted by a rollback
The function's execution role is deleted automatically to protect the account
questions.why: A manual edit creates drift, meaning the live stack and the template disagree, and the next deploy works from the template and can overwrite or conflict with the console change.

questions.prompt: A new stack deploy creates a function, its event trigger and its permissions, but the log group creation fails halfway. What does CloudFormation do by default?
choices: It deletes the template file from the artifacts bucket and stops
It leaves the stack half-built so the team can finish it by hand
It rolls the stack back to its previous state, which for a first deploy means the stack is removed
It keeps the successfully created resources and retries only the log group indefinitely
questions.why: If any resource fails to create, CloudFormation rolls the stack back to its previous state, and on a first deploy there is no previous state to return to, so the stack's resources are removed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what AWS SAM does for a serverless data pipeline, walking through build, package and deploy, and name one limit or tradeoff of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: SAM lets us describe a serverless pipeline in one template: the functions, their permissions, their triggers and their output locations. Build gathers the code and dependencies into a bundle. Package uploads that bundle to S3 and rewrites the template to point at it. Deploy sends the template to CloudFormation, which previews a changeset and applies it as one stack, rolling back if something fails. The tradeoff is that SAM is tied to the CloudFormation model. Its shorthand hides a lot of generated resources, so when something breaks you still need to read the expanded template, and any change made outside the template creates drift that the next deploy may overwrite. SAM does not make a pipeline fault tolerant by itself; retries, dead-letter handling and idempotent processing still have to be designed into the code.
rubricPoints: Describes SAM as an extension of CloudFormation that expands shorthand into full resources
Explains build, package and deploy as distinct steps with their purpose
Notes that manual console changes cause drift and get overwritten or break the next deploy
Names a real limit, such as hidden generated resources or no automatic fault tolerance

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly about the deployment workflow and template structure, which is best understood by reading the explanation and then explaining it back rather than by an existing or planned hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: A Lambda function is a small piece of code that runs on demand and then stops, so it has no permanent disk of its own. Sometimes a function needs files: a large lookup table, a model file, or a place to leave intermediate results. There are two ways to give it storage. The first is a small scratch area called /tmp that each running copy gets for free, and that can disappear when that copy is recycled. The second is attaching a shared network file system, so the function reads and writes files the way a program on a normal server would, and several functions can see the same files. Choosing between them depends on how much space you need, how long the data must live, and who else needs to see it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A pipeline runs 500 copies of a function in parallel. Each copy writes its output to its own local scratch space, and then a later step reads that output. Will the later step always find every file? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A Lambda function is a unit of code that a cloud service runs when triggered. Each running copy lives inside an execution environment, meaning an isolated sandbox that the service creates, reuses for later requests, and eventually discards. Every execution environment gets a scratch directory at /tmp. Its size is configurable, from 512 MB up to 10,240 MB, and it is cheap and fast because it is local to that sandbox. The catch is that it belongs to one environment only. Two parallel copies have two separate /tmp directories, and when the environment is recycled, its contents are gone.

A shared network file system is the other option. Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) is a managed file system that many machines can mount at once over the network. To use it from Lambda, the function must run inside your virtual network, the file system needs a mount target in a subnet the function can reach, and an access point sets the directory and the user ID the function sees. The function then mounts it at a path that begins with /mnt/. The function's execution role also needs permission to use the file system.

Worked example: a nightly job needs a 2 GB rates file. First, copy the file into an EFS file system. Second, place the function in the right subnets with a security group that allows NFS traffic. Third, create an access point for the /rates directory. Fourth, mount it at /mnt/rates. Fifth, the function opens /mnt/rates/rates.csv like any local file.

Common mistake: writing a result to /tmp and assuming a later step can read it. Different invocations may run in different environments, so the file may be missing. Use /tmp only for temporary working space within one invocation, and use a shared store when another step must see the output.

In a running system, a function attached to a file system in a virtual network adds setup work and depends on network reachability, so a misconfigured subnet or security group makes every invocation time out. Many writers to one shared file also need coordination to avoid corrupting data.

questions.prompt: A clinic's scheduling team runs a Lambda function every five minutes to send appointment reminders. It needs a 300 MB holiday calendar file. The team follows these steps. First, they copy holidays.csv into an Amazon EFS file system, a managed network file system that many machines can mount at once. Second, they attach the function to the private subnets of their virtual network, with a security group that allows NFS traffic. Third, they create an access point that points at the /calendars directory. Fourth, the step that is missing from their notes. Fifth, the function opens /mnt/calendars/holidays.csv like a local file. Which fourth step completes the setup?
choices: Raise the function's /tmp size to 10240 MB so the calendar fits in scratch space.
Create a second Lambda function that copies the file into its own /tmp and invokes the reminder function.
Write the calendar into /tmp at the start of every run so the function has a local copy.
Give the function's execution role permission to use the file system, then mount the access point at a path beginning with /mnt/.
questions.why: The function needs both permission on its execution role to use the file system and a mount at a /mnt/ path, and only option C supplies the missing access and mount step while the others rely on the per-environment /tmp scratch space that the text warns is not shared.

questions.prompt: A payroll team's first Lambda function writes a per-run summary file to /tmp. A second Lambda function, started by a queue message after the first finishes, tries to open that file and fails. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The second function was given too little memory to read the file.
The queue message deleted the file from /tmp once it was delivered.
The file was written in the wrong format for a Lambda function to read.
Each execution environment has its own /tmp, and the second function may run in a different environment where the file does not exist.
questions.why: /tmp belongs to a single execution environment, so a later invocation running in another environment cannot see the file, which is why shared output needs a shared store.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team attached a Lambda function to an EFS file system in their virtual network. The access point and file permissions are correct, but every invocation times out before the function code runs. Which check is most likely to fix this?
choices: Confirm the function's subnets can reach the file system's mount target and that the security group allows NFS traffic.
Lower the function's memory setting so the mount starts faster.
Change the access point's user ID to root so the mount is allowed to start.
Increase the function's /tmp size so the mount has more room.
questions.why: A misconfigured subnet or security group blocks network reachability to the mount target, causing every invocation to time out, and checking that path is the right first step.

questions.prompt: A forecasting team expects to need 4 GB of reference data in a Lambda function's scratch space on each run. Which statement about this plan is true?
choices: The /tmp size can be set to 4096 MB, since the configurable range goes up to 10,240 MB, but the data is lost when the environment is recycled, so it suits only temporary per-environment work.
The function must be attached to a shared file system, since /tmp cannot exceed 512 MB.
The data can be kept permanently in /tmp because the environment never discards it.
The 4 GB file can be shared between parallel copies of the function, because each copy reads the same /tmp directory.
questions.why: The configurable /tmp range runs from 512 MB to 10,240 MB, so 4096 MB is allowed, but each environment has its own copy that disappears when the environment is recycled, which makes it unsuitable for data that must persist or be shared.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when a Lambda function should use its local /tmp space and when it should mount a shared network file system instead. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Local /tmp is the right choice for scratch work that lives only inside one invocation, such as unpacking an archive or converting a file before uploading the result. It is fast and needs no extra setup, but it is private to one execution environment, it can be wiped when that environment is recycled, and its size is capped by the function's configured ephemeral storage. A shared network file system such as EFS suits data that several functions must read or write, or reference data that must survive between runs. The tradeoffs are setup and reliability. The function must run inside a virtual network with a route to the mount target, the access point and permissions must be right, and network latency is higher than local disk. If two functions write the same file at once, we also need a locking or naming scheme. So I default to /tmp for temporary work and use a shared mount only when the data must be shared or kept.
rubricPoints: Local /tmp is private to one execution environment and can be lost when it is recycled.
A shared network file system lets several functions read and write the same files and keeps them between runs.
Mounting a shared file system needs the function in a virtual network, a mount target, and correct permissions.
The shared option adds latency and setup work, and concurrent writes need coordination.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between local scratch space and a shared mount under a stated requirement is an exam-style reasoning task, and no listed mission covers Lambda storage directly.

lessons.plain: Continuous integration and delivery for data pipelines means treating pipeline code like software that gets built, tested, and released automatically every time someone changes it. Instead of an engineer copying a script onto a server by hand, every change follows the same checked route: it is stored in version control, automatically tested, packaged, and deployed to a test environment before production. Continuous integration (CI) is the automatic checking of each change against the rest of the code. Continuous delivery (CD) is the automatic, repeatable release of tested changes. The payoff is that a broken transformation is caught before it touches real data, and getting back to a known good version becomes a routine action rather than a panic.
lessons.guessPrompt: A data engineer fixes a bug in a transformation script by editing the file directly on the production server, and the output looks correct afterward. Why is this still a risky way to ship the change?
lessons.teach:
Continuous integration (CI) means each change to pipeline code is automatically built and tested when it is merged into a shared repository. Continuous delivery (CD) means tested changes are released to environments through a repeatable process, with people choosing when to promote them. Version control records every change to code so any earlier state can be restored. An environment is a separate copy of the pipeline and its infrastructure, such as development, staging, and production. An artifact is the packaged, versioned output of a build. Infrastructure as code describes cloud resources such as storage, job definitions, and permissions in files that a tool creates the same way every time.

It works because the same artifact moves through every environment, so what was tested is what runs in production. Automation removes the manual steps where mistakes creep in.

Example: a developer changes a transform that converts CSV files to Parquet and renames a column. First, the change is committed and CI runs unit tests on a small sample file. One test fails because a downstream column name no longer matches the expected schema. The developer fixes the mapping, the tests pass, and CI builds one versioned artifact. That artifact deploys to staging, where the pipeline runs on sample data and row counts are compared. After approval, the same artifact is promoted to production.

Common mistake: editing the production pipeline by hand. The live code now differs from the repository, so the next deployment silently overwrites the fix or fails, and nobody can reproduce what is running.

In a running system, this drift makes rollback unreliable, because the last known good artifact no longer describes what is live. Repeatable releases are what make data pipelines safe to change.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a job that joins shipment records with depot codes. The team follows these steps: (1) the change is committed to version control; (2) CI runs unit tests on a 50-row sample and they pass; (3) CI builds the versioned artifact depot-join-3.1.0; (4) that artifact is deployed to staging and its row counts are compared with the previous run; (5) ____; (6) the same artifact, depot-join-3.1.0, is deployed to production. Which step belongs in the blank?
choices: The team rebuilds the job from the latest commit directly inside the production environment
A person reviews the staging results and approves promoting artifact depot-join-3.1.0
The developer edits the production job file by hand so it matches the staging copy
The team deletes the staging environment so that only production remains
questions.why: Continuous delivery releases the already tested artifact through a repeatable process, with a person choosing when to promote it, so the blank is the human approval of that same artifact.

questions.prompt: In a pipeline's delivery process, what is an artifact?
choices: The packaged, versioned output of a build that can be deployed as is
An email alert sent to the on-call engineer when a job fails
A temporary folder that holds the logs from the last failed run
A live copy of the production database used for reporting
questions.why: An artifact is the packaged, versioned output of a build, and the same artifact is what moves through each environment.

questions.prompt: A data engineer fixes a broken production job by editing the script directly on the production server. The next scheduled deployment from the repository runs and the fix disappears. What is the root problem?
choices: The repository has no version number, so the deployment cannot tell which code is newer
The staging environment did not have enough sample rows to catch the bug before release
CI ran too many unit tests, which slowed the deployment until the fix was overwritten
The live code no longer matches the repository, so the deployed state cannot be reproduced or reliably rolled back
questions.why: Editing production by hand creates drift between the live code and the repository, which makes the deployed state unreproducible and the fix is overwritten by the next release.

questions.prompt: A team releases a new version of a transform that converts CSV files to Parquet, and the output turns out to be wrong. Which option gives them a reliable way to restore the last known good state?
choices: Use the version control history to recover the earlier code and redeploy its earlier artifact
Edit the transform by hand on the server until the output looks correct to the team
Read the production logs until the cause is found, then patch the live script
Rerun the failed job with more memory so it finishes and overwrites the bad output
questions.why: Version control records every earlier state and the earlier artifact describes exactly what ran before, so redeploying it restores a known good state, whereas hand edits or reruns do not.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only ever deployed pipelines by copying scripts to a server what continuous integration and continuous delivery add, and name one limit or tradeoff of automating releases this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: CI means every change to the pipeline code is pulled into the shared repository and automatically built and tested straight away, so a broken transform is caught before anyone runs it on real data. CD means that once a change passes, the same tested package can be deployed to staging and then production by a repeatable process, instead of someone copying files by hand. The main benefit is that what we tested is what we run, and rolling back means redeploying a previous package. The tradeoff is that automated tests only check what someone thought to write. A pipeline can pass every test and still process bad data if the test data is too small or the data-level checks are missing. The pipeline also needs upkeep: a flaky test or a slow build can push people to bypass the process, which defeats the point. So I would treat the test suite as part of the pipeline design, not an afterthought.
rubricPoints: Defines CI as automatically building and testing each change when it is merged.
Defines CD as promoting the same tested artifact through environments by a repeatable process.
Notes that tests only cover what was written, so data-level checks are still needed.
Names a tradeoff such as flaky tests or slow builds tempting people to bypass the process.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a failing CI pipeline makes the learner practise the build, test, and gate stages this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: Distributed computing means splitting one big data job across several machines that work on different slices of the data at the same time, instead of making a single machine do everything. The data structures and algorithms part is about choosing the right way to store and look up items, and knowing how long each step takes as the data grows. A data pipeline needs both. You split the rows into chunks, send each chunk to a worker, then combine the results. An analogy: a kitchen with several cooks. Splitting the orders among the cooks is distribution. Keeping the spices sorted so nobody searches the whole shelf is the data structure choice. Both decide whether the kitchen keeps up at peak time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A job takes 10 minutes to process 1 million records. If each record must be compared with every other record once, would you guess doubling the input to 2 million takes about 20 minutes, or much longer? Why?
lessons.teach:
Distributed computing means running one job across several machines, each handling a slice of the data at the same time. Each slice is called a partition. A shuffle is the step where records move between machines so that records sharing a key, such as a customer ID, end up on the same machine. Big O notation describes how work grows as the input size n grows. O(n) means work doubles when data doubles. O(n squared) means work quadruples. A hash table finds a value by its key in about one step on average, while a plain list may have to check every item, which costs O(n) per lookup.

Why this works: if each partition can be processed without looking at the others, adding machines divides the time roughly evenly. Hashing the key picks the machine deterministically, so every record for one customer lands in the same place.

Worked example: count orders per customer across 4 workers. Step 1: for each order, compute customer ID modulo 4 to choose a worker. For customer 37, 37 mod 4 is 1, so worker 1 handles it. Step 2: each worker counts its own customers in a hash table. Step 3: no worker needs another worker's data, so the per-worker counts are simply combined at the end.

Common mistake: assuming more machines fix everything. If one customer has most of the orders, all those records go to one worker. This is called data skew, and the job finishes only when that overloaded worker finishes. An O(n squared) step inside each partition also will not become fast just because more machines are added.

In a running system, the slowest partition sets the end-to-end time of the pipeline, so balancing keys and choosing the right lookup structure matter as much as the number of machines.

questions.prompt: A bank counts transfers per account across 6 workers. Step 1: for each transfer, compute account ID modulo 6 to choose a worker. Account 1409 gives 1409 mod 6 = 5, so worker 5 handles every transfer for that account. Step 2: [missing step: what worker 5 does with the records it has received]. Step 3: once all workers finish, their per-account totals are combined into the final report. Which choice correctly fills in step 2?
choices: Worker 5 sends its records to worker 0, which keeps the counts for everyone.
Worker 5 keeps a hash table keyed by account ID, so each update takes about one step on average.
Worker 5 scans a plain list of every account for each transfer, which costs O(n) per lookup.
Worker 5 waits until all six workers have finished before it starts counting anything.
questions.why: Each worker must count only its own accounts in a hash table keyed by account ID, which keeps each lookup at about one step on average, while the other choices break the rule that each partition is processed without needing other workers.

questions.prompt: In this teaching text, what is a partition in distributed computing?
choices: A lookup structure that finds a value by its key in about one step on average.
One slice of the data that a single machine processes at the same time as the other slices.
The step where records are moved between machines so that matching keys meet on one machine.
A measure of how the work grows as the input size n grows.
questions.why: The text defines a partition as each slice of the data handled by one machine in a distributed job, while the other options describe a shuffle, a hash table, and Big O notation.

questions.prompt: A clickstream pipeline splits events across 10 workers by hashing the sensor ID. In one hour, 80 percent of events come from a single sensor, and every one of those events is hashed to the same worker. The team adds 20 more workers and the job still runs as long as before. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: The job is limited by the number of sensors, so only adding sensors would help.
The hash function is broken and must be replaced, because hashing never spreads records evenly.
The shuffle is failing silently, so the extra workers receive no records at all.
Adding workers cannot shorten the job, because the 80 percent overload on one worker makes the job wait for that worker to finish.
questions.why: This is data skew: the overloaded worker sets the end time of the job, so more machines do not help while one partition still holds most of the records.

questions.prompt: A step in a job takes O(n squared) time. The input grows from 500 records to 1000 records, which is double the data. Roughly how much more work does the step now take?
choices: Four times as much work.
The same amount of work, because O(n squared) only depends on the number of machines.
Eight times as much work.
Two times as much work.
questions.why: Under O(n squared), doubling n makes the work grow by a factor of four, which is the rule the text gives for quadratic growth.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why adding more machines to a slow pipeline sometimes does not make it faster, and name one limit or tradeoff of splitting data across machines.
lessons.modelAnswer: Adding machines only helps when the work can be split evenly. If the job has a step that grows quadratically within each partition, each worker still takes too long on its share, and more workers only shrink the share a little. Also, if one key, like a single very active customer, sends most records to one machine, that machine becomes the bottleneck and the rest sit idle. The tradeoff of splitting is the shuffle: moving records between machines to group matching keys costs network time and can fail partway. So before adding capacity, I would check the growth rate of each step and how evenly the keys are spread.
rubricPoints: Explains that the slowest partition or the most loaded machine sets the total time
Names a limit such as data skew, a step whose work grows too fast, or the cost of the shuffle
Connects lookup choice or growth rate (O(n), O(n squared)) to how the job scales
Uses plain language and gives a concrete example

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner compare how work grows with O(1), O(n) and O(n squared), which is the core skill this objective needs for judging whether a pipeline scales.

lessons.plain: Choosing a storage service means picking the place where data will live, based on how the data will be used, how fast answers must come back, how much data there is, and what it costs to keep and read. Think of a warehouse, a filing cabinet, a notepad, and a conveyor belt: each is good for one job and wasteful for others. This objective covers seven AWS services, including a warehouse for large analysis, a database for transactions, a fast lookup table, and two streaming services for live data. The skill is matching the access pattern to the store before looking at price.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop wants to keep every order a customer places, and also wants to run a yearly report that sums sales by region across ten years of orders. Before any teaching, which kind of store would you reach for first for the order-by-order records, and which for the yearly report, and why?
lessons.teach:
Choosing a store means matching the shape of your access to the store's design. Ask four questions: how is data read (by a single key, by a row, or by scanning many rows for totals), how fast must each read return, how much data is there, and does cost follow idle capacity or each request. Cost follows design, so a store that is cheap for one pattern is often expensive for another.

Amazon Redshift is a columnar data warehouse: it stores each column together, so aggregate SQL over huge tables reads only the columns asked for. Amazon EMR runs managed Spark or Hadoop clusters that process files in bulk, and you pay while the cluster runs. Amazon RDS is a managed relational database for row-level transactions with joins. Amazon DynamoDB is a managed key-value store that returns single items by key in milliseconds and bills per request or reserved capacity. AWS Lake Formation is not a store; it is a permissions and catalog layer over data held in object storage. Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon MSK (managed Apache Kafka) are streams that keep ordered records for a retention period so consumers can read them live or replay them.

Worked example: a team stores 8 TB of order history and runs a nightly report summing revenue by region. Step 1: the query reads two columns across all rows, so a columnar warehouse fits, and Redshift reads only those columns. Step 2: the same team also needs one customer's order by order ID in under 10 ms for a checkout page, so a key-value store such as DynamoDB fits that path. Step 3: the two stores coexist, each doing the job it is built for.

Common mistake: putting the nightly report on DynamoDB because it is managed and fast by key. A report needs a full scan, which reads and bills every item, and it is slow compared with a warehouse.

Consequence: a scan of a large DynamoDB table can consume far more read capacity than live traffic needs, throttling the checkout path it was meant to serve. Pick the store for the pattern, then check the cost.

questions.prompt: A logistics company stores 40 TB of parcel scan events. Each week an analyst runs one query that averages transit time per carrier, reading only two columns across all rows. A driver app also needs the current status of one parcel, looked up by its tracking number, in under 10 ms. Step 1: the weekly query reads few columns across many rows, so a columnar warehouse such as Amazon Redshift fits that path. Step 2: the status lookup returns one item by key in milliseconds, so a key-value store such as Amazon DynamoDB fits that path. Step 3 is the one missing step, and it completes the design: which action belongs here?
choices: Use a Kinesis Data Stream as the place that answers the single-parcel status lookup, since streams return records by tracking number.
Put AWS Lake Formation in front of the status table as its store, since it holds the parcel rows and the catalog together.
Keep the weekly report off the key-value table, because a full scan there reads and bills every item and can throttle the lookup path.
Move the status lookups into the warehouse, since the warehouse can answer any question faster than a key-value store.
questions.why: A scan of a key-value table reads and bills every item, which can consume capacity that the single-key lookups need, so the report belongs on the warehouse path.

questions.prompt: A team needs a second consumer to re-read yesterday's ordered click events after the first consumer has already finished with them. Which property of Amazon Kinesis Data Streams or Amazon MSK makes this possible?
choices: Records are stored as rows that can be updated in place with joins to other tables.
The service keeps ordered records for a retention period, so consumers can replay them.
Each record is deleted as soon as one consumer reads it, so the data stays small.
The stream is a cluster you must keep running all day, which keeps old records alive.
questions.why: Streams keep ordered records for a retention period so that consumers can read them live or go back and replay them, which is the property the team needs.

questions.prompt: A startup runs one Spark job on Amazon EMR for four hours each night, then leaves the cluster running for the other twenty hours because restarting it feels risky. What cost problem does this create?
choices: EMR is a permissions layer, so keeping it running adds fees for catalog lookups.
EMR bills per request, so the idle hours cost nothing extra.
EMR charges for the time the cluster runs, so the twenty idle hours are paid for even though no work is done.
EMR stores the data at the highest price tier whenever a cluster exists.
questions.why: EMR bills while the cluster runs, so leaving an idle cluster up means paying for capacity that does no processing.

questions.prompt: A product team stores 50,000 sensor readings per second in Amazon RDS, a managed relational database, even though each reading is written and read by a single device ID and the team never joins readings to other tables. Which statement best describes the mismatch?
choices: RDS is the right store because any relational database is always the cheapest choice at high write rates.
The mismatch is only in cost; RDS and DynamoDB perform identically for single-key access at any volume.
RDS cannot store numbers, so the readings must be converted to a stream before anything can be saved.
RDS is built for row-level transactions with joins, while single-key, high-volume reads and writes match the key-value design of Amazon DynamoDB, which bills per request or reserved capacity.
questions.why: The access pattern is single-key and high volume with no joins, which matches DynamoDB's key-value design better than RDS's transactional, join-capable design.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Redshift, DynamoDB and Kinesis Data Streams for a new system, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the access pattern, not the brand. If the team runs SQL reports that total many rows, I would pick Redshift, because its columnar layout reads only the columns a query needs. If the application fetches single records by a known key with low latency, I would pick DynamoDB, which is built for that and bills per request. If events arrive continuously and several consumers need them in order, I would put Kinesis Data Streams in front, since it keeps records for a retention window so consumers can read or replay them. The tradeoff is that each choice is strong at one pattern and weak at others. DynamoDB makes scans expensive and awkward for ad hoc analytics, Redshift is not built for millisecond key lookups, and Kinesis holds data only for its retention window, so anything older must be saved elsewhere. Cost belongs in the choice too: I would estimate reads, writes and storage for the real pattern before committing.
rubricPoints: Chooses the store by access pattern: scans and aggregates versus single-key lookups versus continuous streams
Names a concrete limit of at least one choice, such as DynamoDB scan cost or Kinesis retention window
Explains that cost follows how the store is read and billed, not only its price list
Notes that a system can use more than one store, each for the job it suits

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers store selection, so a scenario to reason through under exam-style conditions adds the most.

lessons.plain: Storage configuration means setting up where and how your data is kept so that the way people read and write it is fast and affordable. Think of a filing room: if you know you will always look up invoices by month, you file them by month, and you put rarely opened boxes in a cheaper back room. The same data can be arranged very differently depending on whether you need one record quickly, want to scan millions of rows for a report, or need an archive nobody touches. Before picking any setting, you describe the access pattern: how often data is written, how often it is read, how fast answers must come back, and which fields the questions filter on.
lessons.guessPrompt: A monthly report almost always asks for one country on one day, out of five years of stored events. Would you keep all the events in one big file or split them into separate pieces by date and country, and why?
lessons.teach:
An access pattern is a description of how data is actually used: who reads it, how often, how much each read touches, how quickly the answer is needed, and which fields the questions filter on. Configuring a storage service means turning that description into concrete settings, such as how the data is laid out, which file format it uses, how it is partitioned (split into separate slices, usually named by a column value like date), and which storage tier it sits in. A storage tier is a price level: cheaper tiers hold data for less money but charge more or take longer to fetch it.

Why it works: a storage system is fastest on the reads it was arranged for. If a query filters on date and the data is physically separated into one folder per date, the engine can skip every folder that does not match. This skipping is called partition pruning. A columnar format, such as Parquet, stores each field together, so a query needing three columns out of fifty reads only those three.

Worked example: clickstream events are kept as files in object storage, partitioned by year, month, day and region. A report asks for region EU on 14 March. Step one, the query engine reads the partition layout and finds the folder for 2024/03/14/eu. Step two, it ignores every other day and region folder. Step three, inside that folder it reads only the columns the report needs. The scan shrinks from the full history to one day of one region.

Common mistake: partitioning on a field with millions of distinct values, such as user ID. Each partition then holds a few tiny files, and the engine spends more time opening files and listing folders than reading data, so cost and latency both rise.

In a running pipeline a poor layout does not fail loudly. Dashboards just get slower and the bill grows with each new report. Pick the partition key from the most common filter in the access pattern, keep files reasonably large, and move cold data to a cheaper tier.

questions.prompt: A logistics company stores truck telemetry as Parquet files in object storage. The team partitions the data by week_start and warehouse_id, so each partition is a folder such as 2025-06-02/W-17. Analysts nearly always ask for one warehouse in one week. Step one: the query engine reads the partition layout. Step two: a query asks for warehouse W-17 in the week starting 2 June 2025. Step three: [MISSING STEP: what the engine does with the folders that do not match]. Step four: inside the matching folder, the engine reads only the columns the query names. Which completes step three?
choices: The engine copies every partition into memory and then filters the rows by warehouse and week.
The engine rewrites the matching files into one folder per truck so the filter runs faster next time.
The engine reads every file, decompresses it, and filters rows, because partitioning only speeds up writes.
The engine opens only the folder that matches both filter values and skips every other folder, which is partition pruning.
questions.why: Partition pruning means the engine skips folders whose partition values fail the filter, so only the folder for W-17 in that week is opened.

questions.prompt: A table of 40 columns is stored in a columnar format such as Parquet. A query needs only 2 of those columns. What is the main effect on the data read?
choices: The engine reads the 2 columns twice, once for the filter and once for the output, doubling the scan.
The engine reads every row of all 40 columns and discards the unused ones afterward.
The engine reads only the stored data for those 2 columns, so less data is scanned.
The engine must convert the whole table to a row format before it can answer the query.
questions.why: A columnar format stores each field together, so a query naming two columns can read just those two and skip the rest.

questions.prompt: A support-ticket table has about 3 million tickets. Most reports filter on the day each ticket was created. A new engineer proposes partitioning by ticket_id, which is unique per ticket. Why is this a poor choice?
choices: Ticket IDs are stored as text, and text partitions are always ignored by the query engine.
A key with millions of distinct values creates a huge number of tiny partitions, so the engine spends its time opening and listing folders instead of reading data.
Partitioning by ticket_id makes date filters impossible to run at all.
Partitioning by ticket_id forces every report to scan the full table, but only when the table is larger than 1 TB.
questions.why: A partition key with millions of values yields many tiny partitions, which raises overhead and slows queries, while the actual filter field is created date.

questions.prompt: A finance team moves three-year-old invoice files into the lowest-cost storage tier to save money. Each month, an auditor needs a sample of those invoices within a few minutes for a report. What is the most likely problem?
choices: Lower-cost tiers charge more to store data, so the monthly bill will rise.
Moving files between tiers changes their columns, so the auditor's report will fail to parse them.
The cheapest tier is slower to fetch from, so it can miss the few-minutes need of the monthly report, and the team should match the tier to how fast the data is needed.
Lower-cost tiers delete files older than one year, so the invoices will be gone.
questions.why: Cheaper tiers hold data for less money but take longer or cost more to fetch, so the tier must match how quickly the answer is needed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would configure storage for a dataset that is written once a day and mostly queried by customer ID and date range. Name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing down the access pattern: one daily batch write, reads that filter by customer ID and date range, and occasional full-history scans for finance. Customer ID has far too many distinct values to partition by, so I would partition by date, which lets queries skip whole days they do not need. Within each partition I would use a columnar format so reports read only the columns they need, and I would keep files reasonably large instead of creating one file per customer. The tradeoff is that a query filtering only by customer ID still has to scan every date partition, so it stays slow for that pattern. If that lookup is frequent and latency-sensitive, a different store or a separate lookup structure may be the right answer, and I would raise that with the team rather than hide it in the partitioning.
rubricPoints: Starts from the access pattern: write frequency, read filters and latency needs.
Partitions on a low-cardinality filter column such as date rather than a high-cardinality key.
Uses a columnar file format and sensibly sized files so queries read little data.
Names the tradeoff: queries filtering on other fields still scan widely.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a layout for a described access pattern is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario and checking its consequences.

lessons.plain: A data store is the place where a system keeps information so it can be read and changed later. Choosing one means asking how the data will be asked for: by a known key, by searching many fields, or by large summary reports. Some stores keep their working data in fast memory, which makes reading a value almost instant. A key/value store works like a very large labelled filing cabinet: you give a label and get back the thing filed under it. The skill is matching the shape of the questions to the store that answers them quickly and safely.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your mobile app needs a user's current session data returned in under a millisecond, and losing that data on a server restart would log users out. Would you choose a store that keeps everything only in memory, a store that keeps everything only on disk, or a store that is built for big summary questions? Why?
lessons.teach:
A key/value store holds items, each identified by a unique key, and returns the value stored under that key. Amazon MemoryDB is AWS's managed, Redis-compatible database. It keeps its working data in memory, so reads and writes typically finish in well under a millisecond. Every change is also written to a durable transaction log, which is copied across several availability zones (separate data centres within one region) before the write is confirmed. Because of that log, MemoryDB can serve as a primary database, not only as a disposable copy.

Why it works: memory is far faster than disk, so a lookup skips the slow disk read. Durability comes from confirming a write only after the log is replicated, so a failed machine can be replaced without losing acknowledged writes. A cache is different: it is allowed to forget data, because the true copy lives somewhere else.

Worked example. A ride app stores each driver's live status under the key driver:4471. Step 1: the dispatcher writes the status 'available' under that key; the write goes to memory and is replicated to the log. Step 2: another service reads driver:4471 and gets 'available' back in about a millisecond. Step 3: the primary node fails, a replica takes over using the logged data, and the status is still there. The use case matches: a fast lookup by a known key, where losing the value would matter.

Common mistake: choosing MemoryDB for questions that search by any field, such as 'all drivers within 2 km', or for large reports. A key/value store answers by key. Scanning many items by a different attribute is slow or unsupported, so that workload belongs in a store built for queries or analytics.

Consequence: if you put data you cannot afford to lose into a plain cache, a restart can wipe it and users see missing or stale state. If you put sub-millisecond session reads on a disk-based store, latency targets slip under load. Match the store to the access pattern first, then to the durability you need.

questions.prompt: A language-learning app stores each learner's current lesson position under a key such as learner:88213, so the app can resume the lesson instantly. The team has two needs. First, when a learner opens the app, it must fetch that position in well under a millisecond, and the position must survive a server failure. Second, each month the team wants a report counting learners by country and by lessons completed. Step 1: split the requirements into two access patterns, a lookup by a known key and a scan across many items by other attributes. Step 2: the lookup by learner key matches MemoryDB, because a fast read by key is its strength and the logged writes survive failover. Step 3: [missing step] The monthly report needs to scan and group by country and lesson count, which is not a key lookup, so the report belongs in
choices: a plain cache, since the report data can always be rebuilt from memory
MemoryDB with a longer read timeout set on the report job
MemoryDB as well, since it is fast enough to scan every item in a month
a store built for queries or analytics, kept separate from the key lookup
questions.why: A key/value store answers by key, and scanning by other attributes such as country belongs in a store designed for queries or analytics, so the correct choice is that separate store.

questions.prompt: What property lets Amazon MemoryDB serve as a primary database rather than only a disposable copy?
choices: It keeps all data on local disk so memory loss never matters
It discards old keys automatically so the working set stays small
It answers queries by any field, so no separate store is needed
Every change is written to a durable transaction log replicated across availability zones before the write is confirmed
questions.why: The durable log, replicated across several availability zones before confirmation, is what allows acknowledged writes to survive a failed machine.

questions.prompt: Which access pattern is the poorest match for a key/value store such as MemoryDB?
choices: Storing a session token and reading it back by session ID in under a millisecond
Looking up the current inventory count for a product by its SKU
Finding every film released in 1998 that features a named actor, searched across the whole catalogue
Fetching a user's saved preferences by their user ID
questions.why: That question searches by attributes that are not the key, which a key/value store answers slowly or not at all, so it belongs in a store built for queries.

questions.prompt: A team uses a plain in-memory cache to hold shopping cart contents, and after a cache restart customers see empty carts. What is the root problem?
choices: The cache was too small, so it evicted carts too early
The cart data was stored only in a store that is allowed to forget data, and no durable copy existed elsewhere
Cart reads should have used a disk-based analytics store instead
The team should have used a longer key name for each cart
questions.why: A cache is allowed to forget data because the true copy lives elsewhere; when the cart had no durable copy, a restart erased it, so the store was chosen for data it could not safely hold.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between MemoryDB and a relational database for a new service that stores customers' shopping carts. Name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the access pattern. A cart is read and written by customer ID, which is a key lookup, and it is needed on every page view, so an in-memory key/value store fits. MemoryDB keeps the data durable through its replicated transaction log, so a node failure should not empty every cart. That is why I would pick it over a plain cache, which is allowed to forget data. The tradeoff is that it answers by key. If the business later wants reports such as carts abandoned by region last week, or joins with order history, those queries will be slow or awkward there. I would export the data to an analytics store for that rather than bend the cart store to do it. Memory also costs more per gigabyte than disk, so I would keep only the fields that live carts need.
rubricPoints: Starts from the access pattern: lookups by a known key, and how often they happen
Explains that MemoryDB is in-memory with a durable replicated log, so it is more than a cache
Names a real limit: it answers by key and is weak for ad hoc queries or reports
Mentions cost or scope: memory is pricier, so store only what is needed, and export for analytics

suggested.rationale: Choosing a store from a scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, and no listed mission covers store selection.

lessons.plain: When you search a huge pile of data by meaning rather than exact words, you first turn each item into a list of numbers that captures what it is about, then look for the items whose numbers sit closest to your query's numbers. Checking every item is slow once the pile is large, so a vector index is a shortcut structure that finds close matches quickly. It trades a small chance of missing the very best match for a large gain in speed. Two common shortcut designs are HNSW and IVF, and they make different tradeoffs.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you have ten million product descriptions turned into number lists, and you want the ten closest to a new query, would you rather compare the query against every list one by one, or first sort the lists into neighbourhoods and only look in the nearby ones? What do you give up with the second choice?
lessons.teach:
A vector is a list of numbers, often hundreds or thousands long, that an embedding model produces so that items with similar meaning get similar lists. A nearest-neighbour search finds the stored vectors closest to a query vector under a distance measure such as cosine distance. An exact search compares against every row, which is accurate but slow at scale. An approximate nearest-neighbour index trades a little accuracy for speed. Recall is the share of the true nearest items that the index actually returns.

HNSW, Hierarchical Navigable Small World, builds a multi-layer graph. Each vector links to a few neighbours. Upper layers hold few vectors with long links, so a search can make big jumps. The bottom layer holds every vector with short links. A query starts at the top, hops greedily toward the target, drops a layer, and repeats. Two settings matter: m, the number of links per vector, which affects memory and recall, and ef_search, how many candidates are kept during a query, which trades speed for recall. HNSW accepts new rows without a full rebuild, but it uses more memory.

IVF, inverted file, first clusters all vectors around a set of centroids, which are cluster centres found by k-means. Each vector is filed under its nearest centroid. A query finds the closest few centroids, controlled by probes, and searches only those lists. IVF uses less memory and builds faster, but its recall depends heavily on probes, and clusters built from too little data are poor.

Worked example, in Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension: a table holds 1,000,000 document embeddings. You create an HNSW index with m set to 16 and ef_construction set to 64. A query asks for the 10 nearest. The search enters the top layer, moves to the closest node, descends, and at the bottom keeps about ef_search candidates, then returns the best ten.

Common mistake: building an IVF index on an empty or tiny table and then loading the data. The centroids then describe nothing useful, and results quietly degrade. Consequence: a retrieval-augmented app answers from the wrong documents with no error raised, so you must measure recall against an exact search before trusting either index.

questions.prompt: A travel company's support team stores 300,000 ticket-text embeddings in Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension. Their steps are: (1) create an HNSW index on the embedding column with m set to 24 and ef_construction set to 100; (2) choose 200 sample queries and run an exact nearest-neighbour search for each, saving the true top 10 results; (3) MISSING STEP; (4) if average recall is 0.84, raise ef_search and repeat the missing step until recall is acceptable. What belongs in the missing step?
choices: Reload all 300,000 rows so the HNSW graph is rebuilt with new centroids.
Set probes equal to the number of centroids so that every list is searched.
Run the same 200 queries through the HNSW index and compare its results with the saved exact results to measure recall.
Drop the HNSW index and switch to IVF, because HNSW uses more memory.
questions.why: Recall is the share of true nearest items the index actually returns, so it can only be measured by comparing approximate results against the exact results saved in step 2.

questions.prompt: A media company adds about 50,000 new image embeddings every hour and cannot afford a full index rebuild during the day. Which index type fits this need best, and why?
choices: A flat exact search with no index, because new rows never affect exact search.
IVF with probes set to zero, because an empty probe list skips the rebuild step.
HNSW, because it accepts new rows without a full rebuild, at the cost of more memory.
IVF, because its centroids are updated instantly for every new row and it uses less memory.
questions.why: HNSW accepts new rows without a full rebuild but uses more memory, which matches the stated constraint; the other choices misstate how IVF or exact search behave.

questions.prompt: A logistics team builds an IVF index with 500 centroids on Aurora PostgreSQL and sets probes to 1 to make queries faster. What is the most likely result?
choices: The index is corrupted and must be dropped, because probes can only be set to a value equal to the number of centroids.
Results stay identical because probes only changes the order of the returned rows, not which rows are searched.
Recall rises because fewer rows are compared, so the closest matches are found sooner.
Recall falls because true neighbours in unsearched clusters are never examined; raising probes trades speed back for recall.
questions.why: Probes controls how many centroid lists a query searches, so setting it to 1 can miss true neighbours that sit in other clusters, lowering recall.

questions.prompt: An HNSW index has already been built with m set to 16 on a product-catalogue table, and the team finds recall too low for their queries. They want a change that takes effect without rebuilding the index. Which setting should they adjust, and why?
choices: Raise ef_search at query time, because it sets how many candidates are kept during a search and trades speed for recall.
Lower m to 4, because fewer links per vector always increases recall.
Switch the distance measure to exact search for every query, because exact search is the only way to raise recall.
Change ef_construction on the existing index, because it is applied at every query.
questions.why: ef_search is a query-time setting that controls how many candidates are kept during a search, so raising it can improve recall without a rebuild, while m is fixed when the graph is built.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how HNSW and IVF differ in the way they find nearest vectors, and name one limit or tradeoff of the index you would pick for a workload with frequent inserts.
lessons.modelAnswer: HNSW builds a layered graph in which each vector links to nearby vectors. A search descends from sparse top layers to a dense bottom layer, hopping toward the query at each step. IVF instead splits the vectors into clusters around centroids and, at query time, scans only the few clusters closest to the query. The tradeoff with HNSW is memory: the links take space and building is slower, but it handles inserts well and gives strong recall that you can tune with ef_search. IVF is smaller and quicker to build, but its recall depends on how many clusters it probes, and it needs representative data at build time, so frequent inserts can make its clusters stale. For a workload with frequent inserts, I would pick HNSW in Aurora PostgreSQL, watch its memory use, and measure its recall against an exact search, because both index types are approximate.
rubricPoints: HNSW uses a layered graph that a search descends through from sparse to dense layers.
IVF groups vectors into clusters around centroids and searches only the nearest clusters.
HNSW handles inserts well but uses more memory; IVF is smaller but depends on probes and representative build data.
Both are approximate, so recall should be measured against an exact search.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between HNSW and IVF for a described workload is an exam-style reasoning task that benefits more from a scenario than from reading alone.

lessons.plain: Many businesses still exchange data as files: a partner drops a daily CSV, or a vendor sends an export. Integrating a transfer or migration tool means connecting the step that receives those files to the rest of your processing system, so the files arrive safely in storage, get noticed, and feed the next steps. Think of a warehouse loading dock. The delivery truck unloads at a managed door, the goods are placed on a shelf in a known spot, and a worker is told something new has arrived. The real job is making that hand-off reliable, not just getting the door to open.
lessons.guessPrompt: A partner uploads a 2 GB file to your server every night, and your nightly job starts at 02:00 by looking for new files. What could go wrong if the upload is still running at 02:00, and how would you prevent it?
lessons.teach:
A managed file-transfer service is a hosted server that speaks standard file protocols, such as SFTP (file transfer over SSH) and FTPS (FTP over TLS), so existing partner tools keep working while the provider runs the machines. AWS Transfer Family is the AWS example: it receives uploads and writes them into object storage (Amazon S3) or a network file system. A processing system is whatever reads that data next, such as a scheduled job, an event-driven function, or a pipeline step. Integrating the two means agreeing on where files land, how the system learns a file is complete, and what happens to duplicates.

Why it works: storage decouples the sender from the processor. The transfer service only has to receive bytes reliably into a known location, and the processor only has to react to finished objects. A completion signal, such as a marker file or a storage event, tells the processor when it is safe to read.

Worked example. Step 1: the partner uploads orders_2024-05-01.csv to the inbound folder, which maps to the S3 prefix inbound/orders/. Step 2: the upload finishes and the object is complete in the bucket. Step 3: the partner uploads an empty orders_2024-05-01.done marker last. Step 4: the processor triggers only on the marker, reads the matching CSV, loads it, then moves the file to processed/ and records its name so a rerun does not load it again.

Common mistake: triggering on the data file the moment it appears. A large upload can be visible while still incomplete, so the processor loads a truncated file.

Consequence: downstream reports look plausible but undercount, and nothing fails loudly. Marker files, checksums, and a processed-files record make the hand-off safe.

questions.prompt: A clinic network's lab vendor sends daily results to a managed file-transfer endpoint, which writes into the S3 prefix labs/inbound/. A nightly processor loads them into a reporting table. Here is the flow. Step 1: the vendor uploads results_0612.json to labs/inbound/. Step 2: the upload finishes and the object is complete in the bucket. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the processor triggers on the signal, reads results_0612.json, loads it into the reporting table, then moves the file to labs/archived/ and records its name so a rerun skips it. What belongs in the missing Step 3?
choices: The vendor uploads an empty results_0612.ready marker file after the data file, which tells the processor the data is safe to read.
The vendor renames results_0612.json to include the current time, so the processor can sort files by upload order.
The processor deletes results_0612.json from labs/inbound/ before loading it, so the vendor cannot resend it.
The processor begins reading results_0612.json while the vendor's upload is still in progress, to save time.
questions.why: A completion marker uploaded after the data file is the signal the processor waits for, so it never reads a partly uploaded object.

questions.prompt: In this teaching text, what is the main job of a completion signal such as a marker file or a storage event?
choices: It compresses the data file so it transfers faster over SFTP.
It encrypts the file so only the processor can open it.
It tells the processor when a file is finished and safe to read.
It sets the retention period that decides when the file is deleted.
questions.why: The text says a completion signal tells the processor when it is safe to read, which is what the marker does here.

questions.prompt: A supplier uploads a 6 GB order file through a managed file-transfer endpoint that writes into an S3 prefix. A scheduled processor starts at 02:00. The upload began at 01:45 and typically finishes at 02:30. Which hand-off design is safe?
choices: Have the processor trigger on the order file's arrival, then wait a fixed 10 minutes before reading.
Have the processor start at 02:00 and read whatever is in the prefix, since the file is already there.
Have the supplier upload an empty marker file after the order file finishes, and have the processor trigger only on that marker.
Have the processor delete the partial file at 02:00 and wait for the supplier to resend it.
questions.why: Triggering on the marker after the data file completes avoids reading a truncated object, while the other options either read early or rely on guesswork.

questions.prompt: A processing job crashed halfway through loading a batch of files from an inbound prefix, then was rerun from the start. The reporting table now shows duplicate rows. Which missing element would have prevented this?
choices: A longer schedule gap between runs, so the rerun never overlaps the first one.
Turning off the completion marker, so the job reads every file as soon as it lands.
A larger processing instance, so the first run would have finished before the crash.
A processed-files record that stores each file's name and is checked before loading.
questions.why: Recording which files were already loaded and checking that record before loading lets a rerun skip them, which is the duplicate protection the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would connect a managed file-transfer service to a nightly processing job so that partial or repeated files do not corrupt the data. Name one limit or tradeoff of your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would have the transfer service write into a dedicated inbound prefix in object storage, so the sender never touches the processing area. Processing should not start on the data file as it appears, because an upload can be partial. I would require a completion marker written after the data file, and the job triggers only on that marker. After loading, the job moves the file to a processed prefix and records its name, so a rerun or a duplicate upload does not load the same rows twice. The tradeoff is that the partner must follow the marker convention. If a marker is missed, the load is delayed, so we need an alert on files that sit unmarked past a deadline.
rubricPoints: Separates the landing area from the processing area.
Waits for a completion signal rather than the first sign of a file.
Makes reruns and duplicate uploads safe, for example by moving or recording processed files.
Names a tradeoff, such as depending on the sender to follow a convention or delayed loads when signals are missed.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises managed file transfer into a processing pipeline, so reading the concepts and the hand-off pattern is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Sometimes the data you need lives in more than one place: a live operational database, a pile of files in cheap storage, and a summary you check often. This objective covers three ways a data warehouse can reach those places. One reads the live database directly when you ask a question, so you see fresh rows without copying them. Another reads files sitting in object storage as though they were tables. The third saves the result of a slow question so the next person gets it instantly. Each trades freshness, speed, and cost differently, and choosing among them is the skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a daily report needs yesterday's orders from a live database and last year's clickstream files stored in cheap object storage. Would you copy both into the warehouse every night, or leave them where they are and query them in place? What would you give up with each choice?
lessons.teach:
A data warehouse is a database built for large analytical questions. Amazon Redshift is the AWS warehouse this objective names. Three features let it answer questions about data it does not store itself.

Federated query lets Redshift run a query against a live operational database, such as an Aurora or RDS database. You create an external schema, which is a named link inside the warehouse that points at the source database. The link uses credentials kept in a secrets store rather than typed into SQL. Rows are read at query time, so results are current, but every query adds load to the source system.

Redshift Spectrum lets Redshift read files in object storage, such as Amazon S3, as if they were tables. You define an external schema that points at a catalog, such as the AWS Glue Data Catalog, which records each table's columns and where its files live. Nothing is loaded. Spectrum scans the files when you query, and columnar formats and partition filters reduce how much it reads.

A materialized view is a saved query result stored as a real table in the warehouse. It is precomputed, so reads are fast, and it is refreshed on demand or on a schedule. It can sit on top of federated or Spectrum sources, giving fast answers to expensive questions, but its data is only as current as its last refresh.

Worked example: a dashboard counts daily orders. Step one: a federated external schema exposes the live orders table in RDS. Step two: a Spectrum external schema exposes the S3 archive of older orders. Step three: a materialized view unions the two and aggregates by day. Step four: a refresh job runs every hour, and the dashboard reads the view. The dashboard is fast but can show data up to an hour old.

Common mistake: assuming federated queries are free to run often. Each one hits the production database, so a dashboard refreshing every minute can slow live transactions.

Consequence: a materialized view that looks correct can stay stale for hours after its source changes, so the refresh schedule is part of the design. Choose the access path by deciding how fresh the answer must be, how much load the source can bear, and how often the same question is asked.

questions.prompt: A hotel group wants a dashboard of nightly occupancy per property. Step one: a federated external schema exposes the live bookings table in an RDS database, with its credentials held in a secrets store. Step two: a Spectrum external schema exposes three years of past bookings stored as files in S3, described by the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Step three: a materialized view unions the two sources and counts occupied rooms per property per night. Step four is missing. Step five: the dashboard reads the view. The managers accept figures up to 15 minutes behind, and the RDS database can take only light load. Which step four completes the design?
choices: Query the live RDS bookings table directly from the dashboard on every page load, so the figures are always exact.
Skip any refresh, because a materialized view picks up source changes automatically as they happen.
Replace the materialized view with a plain view, so no refresh is needed and the Spectrum files are read only once.
Set a refresh of the materialized view every 15 minutes, matching the staleness the managers accept and keeping load on RDS low.
questions.why: A refresh schedule sets how stale the stored view can be and how often the live source is hit, so a 15-minute schedule matches the tolerance the managers gave while limiting load on RDS.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a federated query in Amazon Redshift?
choices: It reads rows from a live operational database at query time, so answers are current but the source takes extra load.
It saves a query result as a table that stays fixed until someone drops it.
It copies the operational database into the warehouse overnight, so later queries never touch the source system and the copy stays fixed for every reader.
It scans files in S3 as if they were tables, without any link to a live database.
questions.why: A federated query reads rows from a live source at query time through an external schema, which keeps answers current but adds load to that source system.

questions.prompt: A team has eight years of sensor files in S3 and wants to ask occasional questions of them in Redshift without loading the files into warehouse tables. Which feature fits?
choices: Redshift Spectrum, which reads the files in place through an external schema over a catalog.
A materialized view, which stores a full copy of the files as warehouse tables.
A federated query against the S3 bucket, which reads rows through a secrets store.
A plain view, which is fast because it caches the contents of the files.
questions.why: Spectrum reads files where they sit in object storage through an external schema that points at a catalog, so nothing is loaded and the files are scanned at query time.

questions.prompt: A materialized view built on a federated source shows yesterday's totals even though the operational table changed this morning. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The view stores a saved result that is current only as of its last refresh, so this morning's change has not reached it yet.
Federated queries are not allowed to read rows that changed on the same day.
Redshift Spectrum has locked the S3 files, so the view cannot read the new rows.
The view is corrupt and must be dropped and rebuilt from the Spectrum files.
questions.why: A materialized view is a precomputed, stored result whose freshness depends on its last refresh, so a source change stays invisible until the next refresh runs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use a federated query, a Spectrum external schema, or a materialized view instead of copying the data into the warehouse. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would leave data where it lives when copying it would add cost or delay and the question only needs it occasionally. A federated query fits a small, fresh lookup against an operational database, since it reads current rows at query time. A Spectrum external schema fits large history stored as files in S3, since the warehouse scans the files without loading them. A materialized view fits a question asked constantly over either source, since it stores the precomputed answer. The tradeoff with federated queries is load: every run hits the live source, so heavy use can slow production. The tradeoff with materialized views is freshness: results are only as current as the last refresh, so the refresh schedule must match what the business accepts.
rubricPoints: Federated query reads live operational data at query time, with fresh results but load on the source.
Spectrum reads files in object storage through a catalog without loading them into the warehouse.
A materialized view stores a precomputed result that is fast to read but only as fresh as its last refresh.
A good answer names a concrete limit, such as source load or staleness, and ties the choice to freshness and cost needs.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between live, file-based, and precomputed reads is best practised by writing and comparing SQL queries, which the planned SQL lab would provide.

lessons.plain: When two people try to change the same thing at once, the database has to decide who goes first. A lock is the database's way of saying 'I am using this right now, wait your turn.'
