Worked through: Step one, open the DAG processing log group and find a parse error reporting that the module 'pricefeed' cannot be imported. Step two, confirm 'pricefeed' is not listed in the environment's requirements file. Step three is missing. Step four, after the update, wait for the next parse cycle and confirm the DAG reappears in the interface. What should step three be?
choices: Give the execution role write permission on the inventory bucket
Increase the worker count so the DAG can parse faster
Open the task instance log for the last successful run
Add the missing package to the requirements file and update the environment so it installs
questions.why: The parse error names a missing package, so the fix is to supply that package through the requirements file and let the environment install it before the DAG can be read again.

questions.prompt: A data team's Airflow setup has tasks where task C must wait until tasks A and B finish, and no chain of arrows ever leads back to its starting task. What is this structure called?
choices: A scheduler that decides which runs are due and hands them out
A requirements file that lists extra Python packages
A task instance with its own queued or success state
A DAG
questions.why: A DAG, a directed acyclic graph, is the set of tasks and ordering arrows with no loops that Airflow uses to define a pipeline.

questions.prompt: A reporting task has sat in the queued state for forty minutes, and its code has not changed. Which explanation does the teaching text point to first?
choices: The execution role lacks permission to read the source bucket
A parse error in the DAG file, which hides it from the interface
Too little worker capacity or a missing dependency
The task's SQL has a syntax error that the scheduler has not yet found
questions.why: The teaching text says a task stuck in queued usually points to too little worker capacity or a missing dependency, not to the task's code or permissions.

questions.prompt: A task fails with an access denied error when it tries to write files to a storage bucket. Where should troubleshooting start?
choices: The execution role's AWS permissions
The package versions in the requirements file
The number of rows the query returned
The DAG processing logs looking for a parse error
questions.why: Access denied errors point to the execution role, which is the set of AWS permissions the workers use to read and write data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would troubleshoot a managed Airflow workflow whose last run finished green but produced wrong numbers. Name which logs you check first, one limit of relying on task status alone, and where the check belongs in the pipeline.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by confirming which run and which task instance produced the bad figures, then open that task's log in CloudWatch rather than trusting the green status. Green only means the code exited cleanly, so the log is where I look for row counts, the date parameter used, and the paths read. If a DAG is missing from the interface entirely, I would check the DAG processing log first, because a parse error means the file never ran. The limit of task status is that Airflow cannot judge whether the data is right. The fix belongs in the pipeline itself: a data quality task after the load that fails on zero rows or on a sudden drop against the last run, placed before any downstream refresh. That way the bad run stops before anyone sees the dashboard, and the team gets an alert from the failed check.
rubricPoints: Green task status only shows the code exited without error, not that the data is correct.
Check the log group matching the failing layer: DAG processing logs for missing DAGs, task logs for bad values.
Identify the specific run and its parameters, such as the run date, that produced the bad output.
Place a data quality check, such as a row-count or threshold test, that fails the run before downstream refresh.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario where a pipeline ran but produced wrong numbers requires reasoning across logs, data, and checks, which adds more than reading facts alone.

lessons.plain: An SDK (software development kit) is a ready-made library that lets a program talk to a cloud service without you building each web request by hand. Instead of writing the low-level message yourself, you call a function such as 'start this job' or 'list these files', and the library sends it, handles the login details, and returns the answer. Calling AWS SDKs from code means your own scripts can start, check, and stop data services like storage buckets, transformation jobs, and query engines, so the work runs the same way every time. The catch is that a remote call can fail, time out, or return only part of the answer, so good code checks each result.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your script starts a data transformation job through a cloud SDK and the call returns successfully within a second. Can you say the job has finished and its output is correct, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
An AWS SDK is a language library, such as boto3 for Python, that wraps AWS service APIs (the published set of requests each service accepts) in ordinary functions. A client is the handle your code creates for one service, such as object storage or a data catalog. Credentials are the identity the calls run under. In production they should come from an attached role, which provides temporary permissions, rather than long-lived keys pasted into code.

Why it works: each function call becomes a signed HTTPS request, the service does the work, and the response comes back as a structured object your code can read. Long jobs are usually asynchronous. Starting a job returns an identifier right away, the job keeps running on the service side, and you check its state later.

Worked example: a script needs to run a transformation job. Step 1, it calls the start function and receives a run ID. Step 2, it asks for that run's status. Step 3, the status says RUNNING, so it waits and asks again. Step 4, the status says SUCCEEDED, and only then does the script move on. If the status says FAILED, the script reads the error message and stops the pipeline instead of continuing.

Two more rules matter. Throttling (the service refusing calls because you send too many) and transient network errors should be retried with increasing waits, not in a tight loop. List calls are paginated: one response may hold only part of the results plus a continuation token, so the script must keep asking until no token is returned.

Common mistake: treating the start call as proof of success. A successful start only means the request was accepted. Another mistake is ignoring pagination, which quietly processes the first page of files and drops the rest.

Consequence: a script that drops a page of files still exits cleanly, so downstream tables load with fewer rows and nothing raises an error. That is exactly the kind of wrong number a data quality check should catch before a dashboard does.

questions.prompt: A small script in a data team's repository lists the files that a parts retailer, Northgate Parts, uploads each night to an object storage bucket. A continuation token is a marker the service returns when a list response holds only part of the results and more remain. Step 1: the script creates a client for the storage service, using the team's attached role rather than stored keys. Step 2: it calls the list function for the prefix nightly/ and reads the file names from the response. Step 3: it counts the names and writes that count to a log. Some nights the load is about 40 percent short, yet the log shows a successful run. A step is missing between Step 2 and Step 3. Which completion fills that gap?
choices: Sort the file names alphabetically before counting them
Call the start function for the nightly load again to confirm the count
Retry the list call with longer waits, but only when it returns an error
Pass the continuation token from the response into the next list call and repeat until the service returns no token
questions.why: Because the list response is paginated, the script must keep requesting the next page with the continuation token until none is returned, otherwise it counts only the first page.

questions.prompt: In an AWS SDK, which description best fits a client?
choices: A signed HTTPS request sent for each function call
The published set of requests a service accepts
The identity your calls run under, such as a role
A handle your code creates for one service
questions.why: A client is the handle the code creates for one service, such as object storage or a data catalog, and the other options describe the API, credentials, or the request itself.

questions.prompt: A script starts a data export on a warehouse service and gets an identifier back with no error. It then immediately reads the export's output folder and finds it empty. Which explanation is most likely?
choices: The output folder must be created by hand before any export starts
The credentials were rejected silently
The SDK does not return identifiers for exports
The start call only confirmed the request was accepted, and the export had not finished writing output yet
questions.why: A successful start call means only that the request was accepted, so the script must check the job's state until it completes before reading results.

questions.prompt: A script reads records from a streaming service. When it sends requests too fast, the service refuses some with a throttling response, and the script retries in a tight loop with no wait, so it keeps getting refused. Which change follows the guidance for throttling?
choices: Retry immediately in a tight loop with a higher attempt count
Switch to long-lived keys so the service stops throttling
Retry with increasing waits between attempts
Remove the retry and log each refusal as a success
questions.why: Throttling should be retried with increasing waits rather than in a tight loop, because repeated fast retries add to the load that caused the refusal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a script that calls an AWS SDK to start a data job should not treat the start call as the end of the job. Name one limit or tradeoff of checking job status by polling.
lessons.modelAnswer: The start call only confirms the service accepted the request. The job runs asynchronously, so it can still be running, fail later, or finish with bad output. The script has to read the run's status, wait while it is RUNNING, and act only on SUCCEEDED, stopping on FAILED. The tradeoff is that polling adds calls and waiting time. Too frequent polling can get throttled, and too infrequent polling delays the pipeline. Good code uses increasing waits between checks, sets a maximum wait, and still verifies the output with a row count or quality rule, because a job marked successful can still produce incomplete data if the script also skipped paginated input.
rubricPoints: The start call only means the request was accepted, not that the job succeeded.
The script must poll the job status and act on SUCCEEDED or FAILED.
Polling has a cost: throttling risk, extra calls, or delayed completion.
Output should still be verified, since a successful job can produce incomplete data.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario about async job status, retries, and pagination adds more than a read because the SDK behaviour is easy to misjudge in context.

lessons.plain: Processing data means taking raw records, such as sales events or sensor readings, and transforming them into something useful, like daily totals or cleaned tables. On AWS, three services do this work in different ways. Glue runs transformation jobs without you managing servers. EMR gives you a managed group of machines running big data engines, so you can tune them yourself. Redshift is a data warehouse: you load data into it and transform it with SQL. Choosing well means knowing what each one is good at and what it asks you to look after. This lesson gives you the vocabulary to tell them apart and to spot which feature protects a pipeline from producing wrong numbers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job must join two large files and total sales per store. You could run it on a fleet of servers you configure yourself, on a managed job service that starts and stops compute for you, or with SQL inside a warehouse where the data already lives. If the data is already in a warehouse table and the work is a join and a sum, which would you try first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A transformation job reads data, changes it, and writes results somewhere else. This is often called ETL, meaning extract, transform, load. Three AWS services commonly run these jobs, and each reflects a different level of control.

AWS Glue is a serverless service: you submit a job, often a Spark script, and Glue provisions and releases the compute. Spark is an open-source engine that splits work across many machines. A crawler scans stored data and records its shape in the Data Catalog, a shared index of tables and columns. Job bookmarks remember what was already processed, so a rerun does not count the same rows twice.

Amazon EMR is a managed cluster of big data engines such as Spark and Hadoop. You choose instance types, scaling, and configuration. That gives control and tuning power, but you also operate more.

Amazon Redshift is a columnar data warehouse, meaning it stores each column together so queries that read a few columns across many rows are fast. Distribution keys decide which node holds which rows, and sort keys decide the order rows are stored in, which lets queries skip data outside a date range. Materialized views store precomputed results.

Worked example: a table holds one million sales rows. A query groups by store_id and sums amount. The warehouse reads only those two columns, uses the sort key on date to skip irrelevant blocks, and returns one total per store.

Common mistake: assuming a clean run means correct numbers. A rerun that loads the same file twice, or a join that multiplies rows, finishes without errors and produces inflated totals.

In a running system, that silent doubling flows straight into a dashboard until someone notices. Row counts and reconciliation checks catch it earlier than any error log does.

questions.prompt: A hotel group, Northwind Stays, runs a nightly Redshift job that joins booking records to a room rate table, then sums revenue per hotel. Here is the trace. Step 1: the booking table holds 4,000 rows, one per booking. Step 2: the rate table has three rows for each room type, one row per season, and the join matches each booking on room type only. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the reported revenue is three times the true revenue for the night, and the job finished without any errors. Which statement correctly fills in step 3?
choices: The sort key on the booking table forces the join to read each booking only once, leaving 4,000 rows.
The hotel name is used as the join key, so each hotel's bookings are summed once before the join runs.
The join output has 12,000 rows, because each booking now matches all three seasonal rate rows.
The job drops bookings that have no matching rate, so the join output is smaller than 4,000 rows.
questions.why: Because the join matches each booking to every seasonal rate row for its room type, the row count grows from 4,000 to 12,000, which multiplies the revenue total and is the silent inflation the trace describes.

questions.prompt: A small analytics team needs a managed big data cluster where they choose the instance types and tune the Spark settings themselves, accepting that they must also operate the cluster more. Which AWS service fits this need?
choices: AWS Glue, because it is serverless and the team never chooses instance types
Amazon EMR, because it is a managed cluster where the team controls configuration and scaling
Amazon Redshift, because it is a columnar warehouse that tunes its own nodes
The Glue Data Catalog, because it stores the table definitions the cluster needs
questions.why: Amazon EMR is the managed cluster option where you pick instance types, scaling, and configuration, which gives control but adds operating work, while Glue is serverless and hides that choice.

questions.prompt: A nightly Glue job failed halfway through and was restarted. The team wants the rerun to skip rows already processed in the earlier attempt so no row is counted twice. Which Glue feature provides this?
choices: A crawler, which scans stored data and records its shape in the Data Catalog
A distribution key, which decides which node holds which rows
Job bookmarks, which remember what was already processed so a rerun does not count the same rows twice
A materialized view, which stores precomputed results for faster reads
questions.why: Job bookmarks record what a job has already processed, so a rerun skips those rows; a crawler only records table shape, and the other two options are Redshift features unrelated to rerun tracking.

questions.prompt: A reporting team's Redshift queries filter a very large table to one month of dates and read only three columns, yet the queries still scan most of the table. The table's sort key is set to customer_id, not to the date column. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Redshift cannot read a table that has more than three columns in a query
The sort key is not date, so the rows for that month are spread through storage and cannot be skipped
Materialized views were not created, so the query must always read every row in the table
The distribution key was set to the date column, so each node scans the whole table
questions.why: Sort keys set the order rows are stored in, so only a sort key on date lets queries skip blocks outside the date range; a sort key on another column leaves the matching rows scattered and forces a wider scan.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Glue, EMR, and Redshift for a transformation step. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from where the data lives and how much I want to operate myself. If the data is already in Redshift tables and the transform is SQL, I would keep it there, using a view or materialized view, because there is nothing new to run and the warehouse handles joins and aggregation. If the data sits in files in S3 and the work is Spark-style, Glue is my default, since it is serverless and its bookmarks track what was already processed. I would pick EMR when I need a specific engine version, custom cluster tuning, or long heavy workloads where I want control over instance types, and I accept that I patch, scale, and watch the cluster myself. The tradeoff I would name for Glue is that startup time and cost are less predictable for tiny jobs. For Redshift, if I skip loading and sort-key design, the cost shows up later as slow queries on a growing table.
rubricPoints: Matches the service to where the data lives and the work style, such as SQL in a warehouse or Spark over files.
Explains Glue as serverless with less operating effort, and EMR as managed but configured by the user.
Names a real tradeoff, such as control versus operating burden, or cost and startup behavior.
Notes that a clean run does not prove correct numbers, so checks are still needed.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among these processing features depends on product facts and console-level behavior that are best learned from reading, and no current mission or planned engine covers them directly.

lessons.plain: A data API is a doorway a program uses to ask another system for data, usually over the internet, by sending a request and getting a structured reply back. Consuming one means your pipeline is a customer of that doorway: it has to ask in the right format, stay within the limits the owner sets, and handle replies it does not expect. Maintaining one means the work does not stop after the first successful call. The owner changes fields, retires versions, rotates keys and slows down under load, so your code has to notice when answers change shape or stop arriving. Think of a shop that orders from a supplier through a catalogue window: you need the right form, a limit on how often you knock, and a plan for the day the catalogue changes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job calls a vendor's data endpoint and gets back only the first 100 records out of 25,000, with no error. What do you suspect first, and what single check would prove it?
lessons.teach:
A data API (application programming interface) is a published set of addresses and rules that lets one program request data from another. Most pipelines consume them over HTTP: your code sends a request to an endpoint, which is a specific address for one kind of data, includes credentials, and receives a response, usually JSON text holding records. Three things decide whether this works in production.

First, pagination. Few APIs return a large dataset in one reply. They return a page plus a marker, often called a next-page token, that says where the following page starts. A job that reads only the first page does not fail loudly; it quietly under-counts.

Second, rate limits. The owner caps how many requests you may make in a time window. Going over produces a refusal, commonly a status meaning too many requests. The correct response is to wait and retry with growing gaps between attempts, called exponential backoff, not to push harder.

Third, versioning and schema drift. The owner may add fields, rename one, or change a type. Your parser should verify the fields it depends on rather than assume yesterday's shape still holds.

Worked example: the job needs 25,000 vehicle records, and the API returns 100 per page. Step 1: request page one. Step 2: read the next-page token. Step 3: request that page. Step 4: repeat until the token is empty. Step 5: compare the collected row count with the total the API reports, and fail the run if they differ.

Common mistake: treating a successful HTTP status as proof the data is complete and correct. The consequence is that a dashboard shows a dip that looks like real demand, and nobody finds the cause until a reconciliation weeks later. A row-count check and a schema check on each run catch this before anyone reads the table.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company publishes a data API. Its endpoint, the web address for attendance records, returns 40 records per reply, and each reply ends with a cursor, a string that marks where the next reply begins. The reply also reports a total of 1,860 records. A job follows the cursor across 47 replies and collects 1,860 rows. Its steps are: follow each cursor until it comes back empty; write the rows to the table. Yesterday the table had the right row count, but total ticket revenue came in about 30% low. The cause was that from reply 19 onward, the vendor replaced the integer field price_cents (a price in whole cents) with price, a decimal text value such as "24.50". The job does not check field names or types before writing. Which step was missing, and what would it have caught before the table was written?
choices: A check that total revenue matches last month's figure, which would show the drop only after the table is already built
A schema check that confirms each record has the expected fields with the expected types, and fails the run before writing if they do not
A retry of every reply that returned a success status, to be sure no page was served from a cache
Raising the page size from 40 to 100 so that fewer replies are needed to collect the records
questions.why: The row count was correct, so only a check on field names and types, run before the write, would have caught the change from integer cents to decimal text.

questions.prompt: In data API work, what is a next-page token?
choices: A marker in a response that says where the following page starts
A status code that tells the job it has sent too many requests
A secret credential that proves the job is allowed to read the data
A count of how many records the API holds in total
questions.why: A next-page token is the marker a paged reply includes so the job can request the page that follows; the other options describe totals, credentials, and rate-limit responses.

questions.prompt: A reporting API caps each client at 300 requests per minute. A job begins receiving refusals with a too-many-requests status once it passes that cap. Which response is correct?
choices: Treat each refusal as an empty page and move on to the next token
Run the same job on several machines so each gets its own separate allowance
Wait, then retry the refused request with longer gaps between each attempt
Retry the refused request immediately in a tight loop until one of them succeeds
questions.why: The correct response to a rate limit is to wait and retry with growing gaps (exponential backoff), not to push harder or try to evade the cap.

questions.prompt: A job reads a vehicle-data API. The vendor renamed the field vehicle_speed to speed_kmh in a recent version. Every request returns a success status, the row count matches the reported total, and the job writes the table with no errors logged. Which check should have caught the problem before the table was written?
choices: Retrying the job with exponential backoff, because the requests were refused
A row-count check, because the number of rows would have been wrong
A schema check that confirms the fields the parser depends on still exist with the expected names before writing
Adding more pages to the reading loop, because the job stopped too early
questions.why: The row count was correct and the status was successful, so only a schema check on the field names the parser depends on would have flagged the rename.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would consume a paginated, rate-limited data API in a nightly pipeline, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would call the endpoint page by page, following the next-page token until it is empty, and keep every record in a staging area rather than writing to the final table as I go. If the API answers with a too-many-requests refusal, I wait with growing gaps between retries and cap the total number of attempts, so the job does not hang all night. Before publishing, I compare the collected row count with the total the API reports and check that the fields I depend on are present and typed as expected. The tradeoff is time: waiting for rate limits makes a large pull slower, so the schedule needs slack. A second limit is that a row-count check only proves completeness, not correctness, so I still run value-level quality rules on the loaded data.
rubricPoints: Explains pagination and following the next-page marker until it ends
Describes retrying rate-limit refusals with backoff and a retry cap
Names a completeness check such as comparing row counts against the reported total
States a tradeoff such as slower runs or the gap between completeness and correctness

suggested.rationale: That mission builds the log-reading habit for finding out why an API is failing, which is the troubleshooting half of maintaining one.

lessons.plain: Before anyone can calculate anything, raw data usually needs tidying: dates written three different ways, blank cells, numbers stored as text, duplicate rows. Data preparation is that tidying step, done before the data is transformed into something useful. AWS offers two places to do it visually. One is a tool called DataBrew, where you point at a file, look at a summary of what is wrong with it, and build a list of cleaning steps you can rerun. The other is SageMaker Unified Studio, a shared workspace where a team finds data, works on it inside projects, and opens the right tools without juggling separate setups. The skill is knowing what each one is for and how to check that the cleaning actually worked.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dataset has 10,000 rows and you preview your cleaning steps on the first 200. The preview looks perfect. What could still be wrong with the full run, and how would you find out?
lessons.teach:
Data preparation means making raw records consistent and trustworthy before transformation: standardising formats, handling missing values, and removing duplicates. A profile is a summary a tool computes over a dataset, such as how many cells are empty, how many distinct values a column holds, and what range the numbers fall in. A recipe is an ordered list of cleaning steps, such as trimming spaces, converting text to a date, or removing rows that fail a condition. A sample is a subset of rows used for quick interactive previews. A data quality rule is a condition a column must meet, such as no blank values or amounts above zero.

AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual tool built around these ideas. You connect a dataset, run a profile job to see its problems, and build a recipe whose steps you preview on a sample and then apply to the full data in a job. Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is a shared workspace for data and analytics teams. It organises work into projects and gives access to data and to tools such as notebooks, so preparation can sit inside the team's wider workflow.

Worked example: a trip file has an amount column where most values are numbers, some are blank, and two rows say N/A. Step one, the profile shows that about 3 percent of amounts are not numeric. Step two, the recipe converts the text to numbers, so N/A becomes a missing value instead of breaking the load. Step three, the recipe fills or flags missing amounts according to the team's rule. Step four, you preview on a sample, run the job on all rows, and profile the output again.

A common mistake is trusting the preview. A sample of a few hundred rows may contain none of the rare bad values, so the recipe looks correct and then fails on the full run or, worse, passes silently. The consequence in a running system is that unnoticed bad amounts flow into the warehouse and shift every average on the dashboard, and nobody sees it until someone questions the numbers. Profiling the full output and applying explicit quality rules is what catches this before anyone looks at a dashboard.

questions.prompt: A bookstore exports an orders file with 60,000 rows and an order_date column. A profile job shows that about 5 percent of dates are written in a second format, such as 03/14/2024 next to 2024-03-14. Step one is done: the profile found the mixed formats. Step two is done: the recipe converts every date to one standard format. You preview the recipe on a sample of 400 rows, the preview looks clean, and you run the job on all rows. The missing step is the one that checks whether the converted output is trustworthy before anyone uses it. Which step fills that gap?
choices: Profile the full converted output and add a data quality rule that order_date is never blank and never later than today.
Increase the sample to 10 rows so the preview is more likely to show a rare bad value.
Trust the clean sample preview and publish the output to the sales dashboard.
Delete every row whose original date was in the second format so the column is uniform.
questions.why: Profiling the full output and applying an explicit rule checks all rows, not just the small sample, so rare bad dates are caught before the dashboard uses them.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a data quality rule in data preparation?
choices: A tool setting that decides how many rows a sample should contain.
A summary of how many cells are empty and how many distinct values a column holds.
A condition a column must meet, such as no blank values or amounts above zero.
A saved list of cleaning steps that run in a fixed order.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a data quality rule as a condition a column must meet, so the correct choice names a condition; the others describe a sample, a recipe, and a profile.

questions.prompt: A warehouse receipts file has 90,000 rows. A preview of 500 random rows shows no negative quantity values, and the recipe looks correct. What is the most reliable next step before trusting the output?
choices: Remove the quantity column so negative values cannot reach the warehouse.
Profile the full output and check quantity against an explicit rule such as quantity is zero or greater.
Rerun the preview with the same 500 rows to confirm the result is stable.
Assume the file is clean because the preview showed no negative values.
questions.why: A small sample can miss rare bad values, so profiling the full output and testing an explicit rule is what catches them.

questions.prompt: A recipe converts a weight column from text to numbers. Some rows contain the text unknown, and after conversion those rows become missing values rather than breaking the load. Later, a dashboard average of weight shifts noticeably because the missing rows were treated as zero by a downstream step. What is the best explanation?
choices: The recipe converted the text correctly, but the downstream step treated missing values as zero, and no rule checked for that.
The sample preview should have been larger, because the conversion itself always produces zeros.
DataBrew cannot handle text values, so the whole column should have been dropped.
The profile job ran too early, so the weight column was still in text form on the dashboard.
questions.why: Converting unknown to a missing value is the intended behaviour, and the shift comes from how a later step handled those missing values, which a quality rule or profile of the output could have flagged.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks when you would pick DataBrew over the wider SageMaker Unified Studio workspace for cleaning a new dataset. Explain the choice in your own words, and name one limit of checking your cleaning steps on a sample.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with DataBrew when the main job is profiling a dataset and building a repeatable set of cleaning steps for it, because the profile shows problems at a glance and the recipe is a reusable ordered list of steps. I would use the Unified Studio workspace when the cleaned data needs to be shared with others in the project, when it feeds notebooks or other analytics tools, or when access should follow the team's project structure. The limit is the sample. Interactive preview runs on a subset of rows, so a rare bad value can look fine in the preview and only appear on the full run. So after the full job I would profile the complete output and check it against explicit quality rules, rather than trusting the preview. Either tool can produce a wrong cleaning if nobody checks the complete result.
rubricPoints: Profiling reveals the problems before any cleaning decisions are made.
A recipe is a reusable, ordered list of cleaning steps.
Unified Studio is a shared workspace for projects, data access and tools, not only a cleaning tool.
A sampled preview can miss rare bad values, so the full output must be checked.
Explicit quality rules, checked after the full run, are what catch wrong numbers before a dashboard does.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between two preparation tools in a realistic situation is best practised by reasoning through a scenario, which goes beyond any single listed mission.

lessons.plain: Amazon Athena lets you ask questions of data in plain SQL without loading that data into a database first. The data sits in files in cloud storage, and Athena reads those files when you run a query. You pay for the amount of data each query reads, and there are no servers to set up. Think of it like searching a filing cabinet by describing what you want rather than walking through every drawer yourself. The real skill is not only writing the question, but making sure it reads only the drawers that matter and that the answer is correct.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company stores a year of website click logs as one folder of files per day in cloud storage. An analyst wants yesterday's click count. Before any teaching: would you expect the query to read all 365 days of files, or only yesterday's? Why?
lessons.teach:
Amazon Athena is a serverless query service: you submit standard SQL, it runs the query on data that stays in Amazon S3 (object storage, where files are kept in named containers called buckets), and you pay for the bytes scanned. Serverless means you do not manage machines; the service allocates the compute for each query.

Three terms matter. A table in Athena is not stored data. It is a definition in the AWS Glue Data Catalog (a shared metadata store) that says which storage location to read, what the columns are, and what format the files use. A partition is a grouping of files by a key, usually stored as sub-folders such as day=2024-05-14, that lets a query skip whole folders. A columnar format such as Parquet stores each column's values together, so a query naming three of forty columns reads only those three.

Why it works: Athena reads only what the query needs. If your WHERE clause filters on the partition column, Athena prunes the other folders and never opens them.

Worked example: the click logs are partitioned by day. The query counts rows where day equals 2024-05-14. Step 1: Athena looks up the table definition in the catalog. Step 2: it sees that day is a partition key and that the filter matches one folder. Step 3: it reads that one folder, about 1 GB, instead of all 365 GB. Step 4: you are billed for roughly 1 GB scanned.

Common mistake: writing the filter so Athena cannot prune, such as wrapping the partition column in a function or filtering on a plain column that merely looks like a date. Then every folder is scanned. A second mistake is assuming new folders are visible. If a partition was never registered in the catalog, the query silently returns fewer rows, which looks exactly like a real drop in traffic.

Consequence: a dashboard that runs an unfiltered scan every few minutes can cost far more than expected and slow other work, while a missing partition produces wrong numbers that no error reports. A query's row count should be reconciled against the source system before anyone trusts it.

questions.prompt: A clinic keeps appointment logs in S3, with one folder per day named appt_date=YYYY-MM-DD, and the table is partitioned on appt_date. On July 1 a new folder was uploaded to S3, but nobody registered that partition in the Glue Data Catalog. An analyst runs a count of appointments for appt_date = '2024-07-01' and gets 0. Here is the trace. Step 1: Athena looks up the table definition in the catalog. Step 2: Athena checks which partitions the catalog lists, and it sees that appt_date is a partition key. Step 3: the 2024-07-01 folder is not in the list of registered partitions, so Athena does not know it exists. Step 4: what does Athena do with that folder?
choices: It reads the folder straight from S3 anyway and counts the rows it finds there.
It silently leaves that folder out of the scan, so the count comes back lower than the real number with no warning.
It reads the folder but counts every row in it as zero.
It stops the query and returns an error saying the partition is missing from the catalog.
questions.why: Athena only reads partitions the catalog registers, and an unregistered folder is skipped without any error, which is why the count is too low and looks like a real drop.

questions.prompt: In Athena, what is a table?
choices: A definition in the Glue Data Catalog that names the storage location, the columns, and the file format.
A sub-folder such as day=2024-05-14 that groups files by a key.
A copy of the data stored inside Athena so queries run faster.
The S3 bucket that holds the files for one dataset.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an Athena table as metadata in the Glue Data Catalog that points to data in S3, not as stored data itself.

questions.prompt: A table is partitioned by event_date. An engineer filters with WHERE MONTH(event_date) = 6 and notices the query scans the whole dataset. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Athena does not support partitions on date columns.
The S3 bucket is in the wrong region.
The filter wraps the partition column in a function, so Athena cannot match whole folders to prune.
The data is stored in Parquet, which always forces a full scan.
questions.why: Wrapping the partition column in a function prevents Athena from pruning folders, so every folder gets scanned, as the teaching text warns.

questions.prompt: A 40-column dataset is stored in Parquet format and a query selects only three of those columns. Why is it cheaper than reading a row-based CSV file?
choices: Parquet keeps each column's values together, so Athena reads only the three columns the query names.
The Glue Data Catalog caches the three columns in memory.
Parquet files are always stored in the same folder as the catalog.
Parquet compresses the whole file into a single block that is read at once.
questions.why: A columnar format stores each column together, so a query naming a few columns reads only those, which lowers the bytes scanned and the cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used a relational database why an Athena query over a year of partitioned logs can be cheap or expensive, and name one limit of Athena's approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Athena runs SQL directly on files in S3, and you pay for the data each query scans, so the cost depends on how much the query has to read. If the logs are partitioned by day and the WHERE clause filters on the day column, Athena skips every other folder and reads only one day's worth. If the filter is missing, or wraps the partition column in an expression that stops pruning, it reads the whole year and the bill grows with it. The limit to name is that Athena has no indexes and no storage of its own: the catalog only knows the partitions someone registered. A new day that was never added is simply invisible, so the query returns a smaller, wrong count without any error. That is why a row count check against the source should run before a dashboard trusts the number.
rubricPoints: Athena runs standard SQL on files in object storage and bills by the amount of data scanned.
A filter on the partition column lets Athena skip folders, which lowers both cost and run time.
Missing filters or unregistered partitions can silently produce expensive or wrong results.
A reconciliation check against the source row count catches missing data before dashboards use it.

suggested.rationale: The planned SQL lab would let the learner write and check partition-filtered Athena-style queries against sample data, which is the hands-on core of this objective.

lessons.plain: AWS Lambda lets you run a small piece of code without keeping a server switched on to run it. You write a function, tell the cloud what should wake it up, such as a new file landing in storage or a message arriving in a queue, and the platform starts a copy of it for each event and stops it afterward. You pay only for the time it runs. For data work this suits small, frequent jobs, like cleaning one file as it arrives. Each run is short-lived and keeps no memory of earlier runs, so the code has to be written with that in mind.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new file lands in a storage bucket, and a function is set to run once for each new file. Suppose the platform sometimes delivers the same notification twice. What could go wrong in the output data, and what would you change in the function to prevent it?
lessons.teach:
Serverless means you do not manage the machines that run your code. AWS Lambda runs a function in response to an event. An event is a signal, such as a new object written to an S3 bucket (Amazon's object storage), a message placed on a queue, or a record arriving in a stream. The function you write is called the handler, and it receives the event as its input. Lambda starts an execution environment when needed and can run many copies at once when events pile up. The number of simultaneous copies is called concurrency.

Why it suits data work: each event is small and independent, so the platform scales out without capacity planning. Each invocation has limits you must design around. A maximum run time (15 minutes), a memory setting that also determines the CPU share, and a cap on the size of the event itself. Lambda keeps no state between runs, so anything needed later must live in storage such as a table or an object store.

Worked example: a file orders-2024-06-01.csv lands in the bucket raw-orders. Step 1: S3 sends an event containing the bucket name and object key. Step 2: Lambda starts the handler with that event. Step 3: the handler reads the file, drops rows with an empty order_id, and writes the cleaned copy to a curated bucket under a key derived from the input file name. Step 4: it logs how many rows were kept and dropped.

Common mistake: assuming each event runs exactly once. Asynchronous invocations can be delivered at least once, so a retry may run the handler again for the same file. If the handler appends rows, the second run doubles them and nothing reports an error. The fix is to make the handler idempotent, meaning running it twice on the same input leaves the same result. Overwriting the output under a stable key achieves this.

In a running system, a silent duplicate is worse than a visible failure, because the dashboard still looks plausible while the totals are inflated. Lambda suits short, event-driven transforms; work that needs more than fifteen minutes belongs on a different service.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs a Lambda handler on files named appointments-2024-07-15.csv that land in the bucket intake-clinic. Trace one run. Step 1: S3 sends an event containing the bucket name and object key. Step 2: Lambda starts the handler with that event. Step 3: the handler reads the file and drops every row with a blank patient_id. Step 4 is missing: the handler writes the cleaned rows to the curated bucket. Which completion of step 4 means a retry of the same file leaves the same result?
choices: Write the cleaned rows under a key that includes the current time, so that every run keeps its own separate copy
Write the cleaned rows to the curated bucket, then delete the raw file once the write has succeeded
Write the cleaned rows under a key derived from the input file name, overwriting any earlier output for that same file
Append the cleaned rows to the end of the existing curated file so that earlier rows are kept alongside the new ones
questions.why: Overwriting under a stable key derived from the input name means a repeat run replaces the earlier output instead of adding to it, so the result is the same either way.

questions.prompt: A Lambda handler is meant to keep a running count of rows processed across all files it has ever seen. A developer stores the count in a variable at the top of the handler file. Why will this approach fail?
choices: Variables are limited to 15 minutes, so the count resets when the handler finishes its first file
The event size cap stops the handler from carrying any number forward between invocations
Lambda keeps no state between runs, so the count must be saved in a table or object store
Concurrency copies share one variable, so the count always reflects whichever copy ran last
questions.why: Lambda keeps no state between runs, so anything needed later, such as a running count, has to be written to durable storage like a table or an object store.

questions.prompt: A team wants a Lambda function to transcode a 40-minute video stored in a bucket. Which option best fits the run-time limit described for Lambda?
choices: Raise the memory setting, which extends the maximum run time in proportion to the extra CPU it gives
Shrink the event payload so the handler starts faster and finishes inside the 15-minute limit
Move the transcode to a service built for longer jobs, since one invocation cannot exceed 15 minutes
Raise the concurrency setting so several copies each handle a different part of the same video file
questions.why: The maximum run time of one Lambda invocation is 15 minutes, and memory changes CPU share, not that limit, so work longer than that belongs on a different service.

questions.prompt: A shop's returns-processing Lambda appends each day's returned items to one shared curated file. A retry causes the same daily file to be processed a second time. What is the likely effect, and which design prevents it?
choices: The totals are correct because Lambda runs each event exactly once, and the retry only adds extra log lines
Totals are inflated with no error reported, so write the output under a stable key so a rerun overwrites it
An error is written to the logs straight away, so the duplicate is caught and the run is marked as failed
The second run is blocked by Lambda because the output file already exists, so the totals stay unchanged
questions.why: Appending on a retry silently doubles the rows, and making the handler idempotent by overwriting under a stable key keeps repeated runs from changing the result.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a Lambda function that processes incoming files must be safe to run twice on the same file, and name one limit of Lambda that you have to design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: In the normal case Lambda runs the handler once per event, but the platform can retry after an error or timeout, and asynchronous delivery is at least once, so the same file notification can reach the function twice. If the function appends rows, the second run doubles the counts and nobody gets an error. So I write it to be idempotent: the output key comes from the input file name, so a rerun overwrites the same output instead of adding to it, and the result is identical either way. The limit I design around is run time, since a handler has a fifteen minute ceiling. A file too large to finish in that window needs splitting into smaller pieces or a different service. Memory matters too, because it sets the CPU available. Lambda pipelines are cheap and simple only when each run is short, repeatable, and leaves a clear record of what it did.
rubricPoints: Lambda runs the handler per event, and events can be delivered or retried more than once.
The handler must be idempotent so a repeated run does not duplicate or inflate output.
The run time limit of 15 minutes and the memory setting constrain what fits in one invocation.
Lambda keeps no state between runs, so anything needed later must live in storage.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner write an event handler that stays correct when the same event arrives twice, which is the core safety skill in this lesson.

lessons.plain: Amazon EventBridge is a managed service that works like a switchboard for events. An event is a small message saying something happened, such as a file landing in storage or a job finishing. EventBridge receives events, checks them against rules you write, and passes matching events to the right targets, such as a function or a workflow. It can also start jobs on a timetable, so you can say 'run this every day at 6 a.m.' without keeping a server running just to wait. For a data engineer, it decides when pipelines start and what reacts when they finish.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job must run at 2 a.m., and it should also start automatically whenever a new file is dropped into a storage bucket. Without knowing any particular service, what two kinds of trigger would you need, and what could go wrong if the job ran twice for the same file?
lessons.teach:
An event is a small record saying something happened, usually with a source, a type, a timestamp, and a payload of details. An event bus is the channel events travel on. A rule is a filter on a bus: it holds an event pattern, which describes the events it wants, and one or more targets, the things to invoke when a match arrives. A schedule is a rule that fires on time instead of on an incoming event. It uses either a rate expression, such as every six hours, or a cron expression, a compact calendar notation such as 2 a.m. on weekdays.

Why it works: the router decouples the producer from the consumer. Storage does not need to know which pipeline cares about new files; it only publishes the fact. Delivery is generally at least once, so the same event can reach a target more than once, and a failed invocation is retried for a limited time. Events that still fail can be sent to a dead-letter queue, a holding area for later inspection.

Worked example: a supplier uploads sales.csv under the incoming/ prefix. Step one, the storage service publishes an event with source 'storage', type 'object created', and the file key in the payload. Step two, the bus compares the event with each rule. Step three, a rule whose pattern matches that source, that type, and a key ending in .csv under incoming/ is selected. Step four, its target starts the ingest workflow and passes the file key along. If the workflow errors, retries happen; if they all fail, the event goes to the dead-letter queue.

Common mistake: writing a pattern so broad that it also fires on temporary or partial files, or assuming at-least-once delivery means exactly-once. In a running system, a duplicate delivery starts a second load of the same file, and unless the load is idempotent, the table ends up with doubled counts.

EventBridge routes and triggers work; it does not check whether the data inside the file is correct.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Energy runs a nightly job that compacts turbine readings. Its schedule is the cron expression 30 3 * * *, meaning 03:30 UTC every day. Step one: at 03:30 UTC the scheduler produces a timed trigger, with no incoming data event behind it. Step two: [missing]. Step three: the rule's target, the compaction job, starts and receives the input configured on the schedule. Which sentence correctly fills in the missing step two?
choices: The rule is skipped, because timed triggers call the target directly and never pass through the bus or any rule.
The bus matches the trigger against the schedule rule and selects it, so the rule's target is invoked.
The bus opens every turbine reading file in the bucket to decide whether there is enough data to run the job.
The cron expression is converted into a rate expression of every 24 hours before the rule is checked.
questions.why: A schedule is a rule that fires on time, so the bus matches the timed trigger against that rule and selects it, which then invokes the target.

questions.prompt: A new analyst says an event is a database table that stores the full contents of each file a pipeline loads. Which description of an event is accurate?
choices: A small record saying something happened, with a source, a type, a timestamp and a payload
A timed trigger that fires at a set calendar time
The channel events travel on, through which rules are also attached to filter them and send matches onward
A table row holding every field of a loaded file
questions.why: An event is a small record describing that something happened, not a store of file contents, and the bus is the channel rather than the event itself.

questions.prompt: A team needs its load to start at 6:15 a.m. on Mondays only. Which kind of schedule expression fits, and why?
choices: A rate expression set to every 7 days, since a week is a regular interval
A dead-letter queue, since it holds failed timed runs for later inspection
A cron expression, since it can name a time of day and a weekday
An event pattern on the bus, since patterns decide when rules fire
questions.why: A rate expression only gives regular intervals and cannot pick a specific time on a specific weekday, whereas a cron expression is a calendar notation that can.

questions.prompt: A lab-results loader receives the same event about labs_0412.csv twice, because delivery is generally at least once. The second load would double the row counts. Which change prevents this problem?
choices: Assume delivery is exactly-once, so a second invocation can never happen
Delete the dead-letter queue so that failed invocations are retried indefinitely
Make the load idempotent so that processing the same file a second time leaves the row counts unchanged
Widen the rule pattern so that any file arriving under the lab/ prefix is loaded
questions.why: Because a duplicate delivery can happen, the load itself must be safe to repeat, which is what idempotent means; the other choices either assume a guarantee that does not exist or make the problem worse.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an event rule decides which pipeline to start when a file arrives, and name one limit or tradeoff of triggering a pipeline from events instead of a fixed schedule.
lessons.modelAnswer: When a file arrives, the storage service publishes an event describing it. The event bus compares that event against each rule's pattern, which checks fields like the source, the event type, and the file path. Any rule that matches invokes its target, so the right ingest workflow starts with the file key. The main limit is delivery: events are delivered at least once, so the same file can trigger the workflow twice, and the pipeline has to be idempotent, meaning a second run produces the same result instead of duplicating rows. The tradeoff against a fixed schedule is that event-driven runs start as soon as data arrives, but they can run at unpredictable times and in bursts, so you need to think about concurrency limits and about what happens when several files land at once. A schedule is simpler to reason about but may run when there is nothing new, or late.
rubricPoints: Describes matching an event against rule patterns on fields such as source, type, or path
Notes that delivery is at least once, so duplicates can occur
Explains that the target must be idempotent to tolerate repeats
States a tradeoff between event-driven timing and fixed schedules

suggested.rationale: A planned messaging engine would let the learner build event rules, retries, and dead-letter handling, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Visualizing data means turning rows of numbers into pictures people can read at a glance: a bar chart, a trend line, a table that refreshes. On AWS, two services cover different parts of this job. One is a visual data preparation tool, where you look at a dataset, see its shape and gaps in summary pictures, and clean it before anyone builds on it. The other is a business intelligence dashboard service, which connects to prepared data so people can build charts and share them as dashboards. Think of the first as the workbench where you inspect raw material and the second as the display wall that shows the finished result.
lessons.guessPrompt: A pipeline loads sales records into a warehouse every hour, and a manager builds a dashboard on top of that table. Before any teaching, what would you check first to be confident the chart shows real sales and not a copying or blank-value error? Name one thing you would look at and why it matters.
lessons.teach:
A dataset is a named collection of rows and columns that a tool can read. AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool. You open a dataset in a project, run a profile job that computes statistics for every column (how many values are missing, how many distinct values appear, what the range and spread look like), and then build a recipe, which is an ordered list of cleaning steps such as filling blanks, renaming columns, or removing duplicates. The profile is the picture you check before anyone adds up the data. Amazon QuickSight is a business intelligence service. You connect it to a dataset, build visuals such as bar charts, line charts and tables in an analysis, and publish those visuals as a read-only dashboard. A dashboard shows whatever its dataset contains. QuickSight can load a copy into SPICE, its in-memory engine, which is fast but only as fresh as its last scheduled refresh, or it can query the source directly.

Why it works: a chart is a summary, and a summary can look tidy while being built on wrong rows. Profiling first shows the shape of the data, and every dashboard inherits whatever quality its dataset has.

Worked example: an orders dataset has 10,000 rows. The DataBrew profile shows customer_id blank in 1,200 rows, which is 12 percent. Step 1: add a recipe step that replaces blank customer_id values with the text Unknown. Step 2: run the recipe and write the cleaned output. Step 3: point QuickSight at that output and refresh SPICE. Step 4: the orders-by-region bar chart now shows an Unknown bar of about 1,200 orders instead of silently dropping them from the total.

Common mistake: building a dashboard straight from raw files and trusting the totals because the chart looks finished. Consequence: if a SPICE refresh fails, the dashboard keeps showing the last good copy, and managers read yesterday's numbers as today's unless someone checks the last-refresh time. A dashboard is only as trustworthy as the dataset behind it, so the check belongs before the chart.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company loads a trips dataset of 8,000 rows into DataBrew and runs a profile job. The profile shows trip_id appearing twice or more in 240 rows (3 percent), which means the same trip was logged twice. Step 1: the team notes the duplicate rate from the profile before any totals are built. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the team runs the recipe and writes the cleaned output. Step 4: QuickSight points at that output, SPICE is refreshed, and the trips-per-city bar chart no longer overcounts. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Add a recipe step that removes duplicate rows, matching on trip_id
Switch QuickSight to query the source directly so the duplicates are skipped at read time
Rename trip_id to trip_key in the recipe so the duplicates are hidden from the profile
Run a second profile job on the cleaned output before the first profile is saved
questions.why: The duplicates must be removed inside the recipe, keyed on the column that identifies one trip, so the cleaned output the dashboard reads is correct.

questions.prompt: In AWS Glue DataBrew, what does a profile job produce for each column of a dataset?
choices: Statistics such as the count of missing values, the number of distinct values, and the range and spread
A copy of the dataset loaded into an in-memory engine for fast queries
A read-only dashboard that can be shared with managers
A set of cleaning steps that are applied automatically to the column
questions.why: A profile job computes statistics per column, such as missing counts, distinct counts, and range, which are the picture checked before the data is totalled.

questions.prompt: A manager opens a QuickSight dashboard built on SPICE and sees last week's sales. The most recent scheduled refresh failed. What is the most likely explanation, and what should the team check?
choices: QuickSight deleted the newer rows, so the team should rebuild the analysis from raw files
The dashboard is showing the last good copy in SPICE, so the team should check the last-refresh time before trusting the numbers
The visuals were published as editable dashboards, so the team should lock them to read-only
SPICE is querying the source directly, so the team should restart the source database
questions.why: SPICE keeps its last successful copy when a refresh fails, so the dashboard looks normal while being out of date, and the last-refresh time reveals it.

questions.prompt: A team wants a region chart to show the blank region values as their own visible group instead of silently dropping those rows from the total. Which change achieves this, and where should it be made?
choices: Set the QuickSight chart to hide any category that has a blank label
Increase the SPICE refresh frequency so blank rows are filled in automatically
Delete the rows with blank region values in the source database before profiling
Add a recipe step in DataBrew that replaces blank region values with a labelled text value, then write the output the dashboard reads
questions.why: A DataBrew recipe step replacing blanks with a named value makes those rows appear as their own category in the cleaned output that QuickSight reads.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can point QuickSight straight at the raw landing files and skip DataBrew, since the dashboard is the part people actually see. Explain to them what each tool is for, and name one limit or tradeoff of building the dashboard directly on whatever data is there.
lessons.modelAnswer: DataBrew is where we inspect and clean the data: its profile shows missing values, distinct counts and distributions, and its recipe steps fix those problems in a repeatable way. QuickSight is where we visualize: it builds charts and dashboards from a dataset, but it does not judge whether the rows are right. If we skip DataBrew, the dashboard will faithfully show raw problems such as blank keys, duplicate orders or a half-written file, and the totals will look confident. The tradeoff is freshness. A SPICE copy only updates on its refresh schedule, so if a refresh fails the dashboard keeps showing old numbers. So I would keep the profile and the cleaning step in front of the dashboard, and check the last-refresh time as part of reading it.
rubricPoints: DataBrew prepares and profiles data; QuickSight builds visuals and dashboards
A dashboard reflects whatever data its dataset contains, including errors
Profiling and cleaning should happen before the chart is trusted
A tradeoff such as stale SPICE data after a failed refresh is named

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product facts and console concepts (which tool does what, how refresh and datasets work), so reading the teaching text is the most efficient route, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Verifying data means checking, before anyone trusts it, that the numbers are complete, correctly shaped, and plausible. Cleaning means fixing or removing bad records in a repeatable way. A pipeline can run without errors and still produce wrong totals, because a job that finishes only proves it reached the end, not that its output is right. AWS offers several tools for this work: small functions that run automatically when data arrives, SQL queries over stored files, dashboards for spotting oddities, notebooks for exploring data, and visual preparation tools. The core skill is placing checks where bad data gets caught before a dashboard shows it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job copies one million sales rows and finishes with no errors, but the dashboard total is 40 percent lower than yesterday. Name two checks you would want to run on the output before the dashboard refreshed, and say what each would have caught.
lessons.teach:
A data quality check is a rule that a dataset must pass before anyone relies on it. Common rules are: the row count falls within an expected range, a required field is never empty (a null value), a key such as an order ID is unique, and values fall inside a sensible range. Cleaning means applying fixes, such as trimming text or converting types, in a repeatable way, and setting aside rows you cannot fix rather than deleting them quietly.

Why it works: a job that exits successfully only proves the code ran to the end. It says nothing about whether the output matches what should be there. A check compares the output against an expectation you wrote down in advance, so it can fail loudly.

The tools fit at different points. A Lambda function is a small piece of code that runs automatically when an event happens, such as a new file arriving, so it can run checks as soon as data lands. Athena is a query service that runs SQL over files kept in storage, so it can count nulls or duplicates. QuickSight is a dashboard service; it helps reveal a sudden drop, but it should not be the first place a problem is found. Jupyter notebooks are interactive documents where you explore data with code. SageMaker Data Wrangler is a visual tool for profiling and transforming data before it is used.

Worked example: a nightly file should contain about 9,500 orders. Step 1: count the rows, getting 7,200. Step 2: compare with the expected minimum of 9,000. Step 3: 7,200 is below the minimum, so the check fails. The pipeline holds the file and alerts the team, and the dashboard never refreshes with the short total.

Common mistake: treating a clean exit as proof of correct data, or deleting bad rows silently so the totals look plausible. Silent drops hide the loss from everyone downstream.

In a running system, a check placed right after ingestion stops bad numbers before they reach reports. A check placed only at the dashboard is too late, because someone has already seen the wrong figure.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company exports its weekly trip records to storage. The team expects about 3,000 trips a week, so their rule is that the row count must be at least 2,700. Step 1: a Lambda function counts the rows in this week's file and gets 2,140. Step 2: the expected minimum is 2,700. Step 3: ______. Which step completes the check?
choices: Delete the 560 rows that appear to be missing from the report so the totals look normal.
Wait for the QuickSight dashboard to show the total, then decide whether the drop is real.
Compare the two numbers: 2,140 is below 2,700, so the check fails. Hold the file and alert the team before the dashboard refreshes.
Rename the file and load it anyway, since a weekly count is only a rough estimate.
questions.why: The check compares the measured count against the minimum written down in advance, and a failing comparison should stop the file from being used and raise an alert, as the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a data quality check?
choices: A test that confirms the pipeline's code ran without errors from start to finish.
A visual chart in a dashboard that highlights unusual spikes in the data.
A rule a dataset must pass before anyone relies on it, such as a row count range or a uniqueness rule on a key.
A tool that automatically fixes every bad value so that no row is ever set aside.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a data quality check as a rule that a dataset must pass before use, with examples such as row count ranges, non-empty fields, unique keys, and value ranges.

questions.prompt: A loyalty-points job finishes with a success status every night. One morning an analyst finds that some customer IDs appear twice in the output table, which inflates point totals. Which statement best explains what went wrong?
choices: The success status only shows the code ran to the end; a uniqueness check on the customer ID should have failed before the totals were used.
The success status proves the output is correct, so the duplicates must come from the analyst's query.
The duplicates mean the dashboard refresh was too slow, so the fix is a faster chart tool.
The job should have deleted the duplicate rows quietly so the totals would look plausible.
questions.why: A clean exit says nothing about whether the output is correct, and a uniqueness rule on the key is the check that would have caught repeated IDs before anyone relied on the data.

questions.prompt: A team wants to catch empty values in a required field of a newly landed file of hospital appointment records. Which placement is best?
choices: Right after ingestion: a Lambda function runs when the file lands and uses an Athena query to count empty values, failing the load if any are found.
In a manual review by a staff member after the nightly report has already been published.
Only in the QuickSight dashboard, where a missing-value chart will reveal the gap to managers.
In a Jupyter notebook that someone opens once a month when they have time to explore.
questions.why: The teaching text says a check placed right after ingestion stops bad numbers before they reach reports, while a check placed only at the dashboard is too late.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a pipeline that finished without errors can still need a data quality check, and name one limit of the check you would add.
lessons.modelAnswer: A pipeline that finishes without errors has only shown that its code ran to the end. It has not shown that the output is right. A job can read a truncated file, drop rows during a join, or double-count duplicates, and still exit successfully. So we add checks that compare the output with expectations we wrote down: a row count range, no empty required keys, unique order IDs, and totals within a plausible band. These checks belong right after the data lands, so a failure stops the pipeline and alerts the team before a dashboard refreshes. One limit: a check only catches what it was written to test. If the expected range is set too wide, a 20 percent shortfall passes quietly, and if it is set from an unusual week, it can wrongly block good loads. So thresholds need periodic review, and failing rows should be quarantined for investigation rather than discarded.
rubricPoints: A clean job exit only shows the code ran, not that the output is correct.
A data quality check compares output against a stated expectation, such as row count, nulls, duplicates, or value ranges.
Checks belong early, right after ingestion, so bad data is caught before dashboards show it.
A check only catches what it tests, so thresholds must be sensible, and failing rows should be quarantined rather than silently deleted.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario where a pipeline ran but produced wrong numbers, reasoned through with checks, adds the most here; the fleet report mission is only a loose practice on messy CSV data and does not teach AWS checks.

lessons.plain: Writing SQL means asking a database a question in a structured language: which rows to read, how to filter them, and how to add them up. Amazon Redshift and Amazon Athena both let you do this on large sets of data. A view is a saved question with a name, so you and your colleagues can ask it again without rewriting the logic. The skill here is writing those questions correctly and saving them as views that others can trust. If a filter is wrong, the answer still looks confident and is still wrong, so checking the query is part of the job.
lessons.guessPrompt: A table has 10 trips: 7 have status COMPLETED, 2 have status CANCELLED, and 1 has no status at all (the value is missing). How many rows does the condition WHERE status <> 'COMPLETED' return, and why might that surprise you?
lessons.teach:
A SQL query is a written request that asks a database to read rows from one or more tables and return a result. SELECT names the columns you want, FROM names the table, and WHERE keeps only the rows that pass a test. GROUP BY collects rows that share a value so you can aggregate them, and an aggregate function such as COUNT or SUM turns each group into one number. A view is a named saved query: once it exists, anyone can read from the name as if it were a table. A NULL is SQL's way of marking a missing value, not zero and not an empty string. Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse, a database built for large analytical scans over its own stored tables. Amazon Athena runs SQL directly over files kept in object storage, using table definitions in a catalog that record where the files are and what columns they have. The SQL logic is similar in both, but the storage and cost model differ.

Why it works: the engine reads only what the query asks for, and a view lets you write a business rule once, such as what counts as a completed trip, instead of repeating it in every report. A standard view stores no data; each read reruns the underlying query against current data. A materialized view in Redshift stores a precomputed result that is refreshed on a schedule or on demand, so it can be stale until the next refresh.

Worked example: a view named completed_trips selects trip_id, vehicle_id and trip_date from trips where status equals 'COMPLETED'. Step 1: the engine reads the trips table. Step 2: it keeps only rows where status is exactly 'COMPLETED'. Step 3: it returns the three columns. A report then runs SELECT vehicle_id, COUNT(*) FROM completed_trips GROUP BY vehicle_id, which counts within that filtered set.

Common mistake: writing WHERE status <> 'COMPLETED' expecting it to catch every non-completed trip. Rows where status is NULL are silently dropped, because a comparison with NULL is neither true nor false. Test for missing values explicitly with IS NULL.

Consequence: when a view is the single source for a dashboard, a wrong filter produces a plausible but incorrect number with no error message, so a row-count or null-count check should run before anyone trusts the view.

questions.prompt: A team at a cold-storage logistics company defines a view named open_claims over an Athena table called insurance_claims. The definition is: SELECT claim_id, region FROM insurance_claims WHERE settled_date IS NULL. The engine works through it in three steps. Step 1: Athena reads the claim files, using the column list recorded in the catalog. Step 2: [MISSING STEP]. Step 3: it returns claim_id and region for the rows that remain. Which statement correctly completes Step 2?
choices: It keeps only rows where settled_date is an empty string, because missing dates are stored as blanks in the files.
It keeps rows where settled_date is zero, because SQL treats a missing date as the number zero.
It writes the filtered result to disk so that later reads of open_claims skip the filter entirely.
It keeps only rows where settled_date is exactly NULL, meaning the date is missing, and drops every row that has a real date.
questions.why: IS NULL tests for a missing value, so Step 2 keeps only rows whose settled_date is missing and removes rows with a real date, while a standard view stores no data and reruns this filter on each read.

questions.prompt: A Redshift materialized view named daily_fleet_mileage was refreshed at 06:00. At 10:00 a batch load adds new trip rows to the underlying table, and at 10:30 a dashboard reads daily_fleet_mileage without anyone triggering a refresh. What does the dashboard most likely show?
choices: The totals as of 06:00, because the view holds a precomputed result that changes only at refresh.
The totals as of 10:30, because Redshift refreshes every materialized view automatically on each read.
The totals as of 10:00, because the view reruns its query against current rows at each read.
An error, because a materialized view cannot be read while new rows are loading into its source table.
questions.why: A materialized view stores a precomputed result that is updated only when it is refreshed, so until the next refresh it can show a stale total that predates the new rows.

questions.prompt: An analyst runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM support_tickets WHERE priority = 'HIGH' OR priority <> 'HIGH' and gets fewer rows than the table's total row count. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The COUNT function skips duplicate rows, so repeated ticket IDs are being removed from the total.
The priority column has a data type that the WHERE clause cannot compare, so the engine drops the whole table.
Rows where priority is NULL make both comparisons neither true nor false, so those rows are excluded from the result.
The OR operator only returns the first matching condition, so it stops after reading the HIGH rows.
questions.why: A comparison involving NULL evaluates to neither true nor false, so rows with a missing priority fail both branches of the OR and are silently left out of the count.
