questions.prompt: A data team has a folder of daily CSV files in object storage that they want to query with SQL once, ad hoc, without loading them into a warehouse first. Which service fits, and why?
choices: Amazon Redshift, because it stores files in its own cluster and therefore keeps them queryable without any loading step.
Amazon Athena, because it copies the files into a managed database on first query so that later queries run faster.
Amazon Athena, because it runs SQL directly over files in object storage using table definitions recorded in a catalog.
Amazon Redshift, because it is the only option that can read CSV files directly from object storage without any table definition.
questions.why: Athena runs SQL directly over files kept in object storage, using catalog definitions that record file locations and columns, so no separate loading step is needed for ad hoc queries.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a standard view and a materialized view, and name one limit or tradeoff of building a dashboard directly on a view.
lessons.modelAnswer: A standard view is just a saved query. Nothing is stored, so every time someone reads it, the underlying query runs again against the current table data. That means it is always fresh, but it can be slow on large data because the work repeats on every read. A materialized view, which Redshift supports, stores the computed result. Reads are fast because they hit the stored result, but the result only reflects the data as of the last refresh, so it can be stale until it is refreshed. For a dashboard built on a view, the main tradeoff is that the view's filters and joins become the business rule behind every number, so a wrong filter gives confident but incorrect figures. That is why I would add a row-count and null-count check on the source before the dashboard trusts the view.
rubricPoints: A standard view stores no data and reruns its query on each read
A materialized view stores a precomputed result that can be stale until refreshed
A view's filter logic becomes the rule behind every dashboard number
A wrong filter, such as one that drops NULLs, produces wrong numbers without an error
A data check such as a row or null count should run before the view is trusted

suggested.rationale: Writing queries against sample tables and checking which rows a filter keeps or drops is the core skill, and the planned SQL lab would drive that practice directly.

lessons.plain: A notebook is a shared page where you write small pieces of code, run each piece on its own, and see the result right under it. Athena notebooks let you run that kind of page on Apache Spark, an engine built to process large amounts of data by splitting the work across many machines. You can load a table of files stored in cloud storage, look at a sample, run a calculation, and check whether the numbers make sense before you build anything on top of them. The point is exploration: finding out what the data really looks like, including odd values and missing rows, before anyone trusts it. A notebook is where you learn what to check, not a finished pipeline.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you have a table of one million order rows and want the number of orders per day, would you rather load every row into one laptop's memory and count, or spread the counting across several machines at once? Why?
lessons.teach: Definitions first. Apache Spark is an open-source engine that splits a large data job into pieces and runs those pieces in parallel across a cluster of machines. A Spark session is a running instance of that engine that keeps state, such as the tables you have loaded and the variables you have set, between steps. A notebook is a page of cells; each cell is one block of code you run separately, and its output appears beneath it. An Athena notebook runs its cells in a managed Spark session that Athena provisions for you. It reads table definitions from the AWS Glue Data Catalog, a shared registry that records where a table's files sit in Amazon S3 object storage and what columns they contain. Why it works: the session keeps data loaded between cells, so you load once and ask many questions cheaply, while Spark does the heavy counting in parallel. Worked example: cell one loads the orders table from the catalog. Cell two counts rows grouped by order date. The output shows 30 dates, but one date has zero rows. Cell three lists the raw S3 folder for that date and finds files there, so the rows were lost in a transformation step, not at the source. Common mistake: treating a notebook result as proof. Exploration showed you a number once; it did not create a rule that will catch the same problem tomorrow. Sessions also cost money while they run, billed by the capacity they hold, so an idle session left open keeps charging until it stops. Consequence: if a join in a notebook quietly duplicates customers, any dashboard built on the same logic reports inflated revenue, and nobody notices until the month closes. The notebook finds the problem; a data quality check in the pipeline stops it from coming back.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's analyst loads the events table and the venues table from the AWS Glue Data Catalog into an Athena notebook session. Cell two joins events to venues on venue_id and counts events per city. The output totals 9,800 events, but the events table holds 7,200 rows. Step one, loading both tables, and step two, running the join and count, were done. The analyst never checked whether venues has exactly one row per venue_id before joining. What missing step would have caught the inflated count before the report went out?
choices: Export the grouped result to a spreadsheet and add up the city totals by hand.
Give the Spark session more capacity so the join finishes faster.
Remove the venues table from the session and count events from the raw file alone.
Before joining, confirm venues has exactly one row per venue_id, and compare the joined row count with the events row count.
questions.why: If venues has a repeated venue_id, each matching event is paired with it more than once, so the join multiplies rows, and comparing row counts before and after the join exposes that.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does the AWS Glue Data Catalog hold for a table?
choices: A full copy of every row, so notebooks can read without touching Amazon S3.
The running Spark session that keeps loaded data between cells.
The saved results of past queries, so dashboards can reuse them.
A record of where the table's files sit in S3 and which columns they contain, not the rows themselves.
questions.why: The catalog is a registry of table locations and column definitions; the row data stays in the files in S3.

questions.prompt: An analyst finishes exploring in an Athena notebook, closes the browser tab, and leaves the session running overnight. What is the consequence?
choices: The session is deleted and loaded data is lost, but no charge applies.
The session keeps holding its capacity and keeps billing until it is stopped.
Other users cannot read the catalog until the session expires.
Nothing; the session pauses on its own and costs nothing while idle.
questions.why: Sessions are billed by the capacity they hold while running, so an idle session left open keeps charging until someone stops it.

questions.prompt: In an Athena notebook, a join shows the same customer_id appearing twice in the output. The team wants a pipeline check that stops a run before any dashboard is built from it. Which check fits best?
choices: Restart the Spark session before each run so the duplicates clear.
Add a comment in the notebook explaining that the join repeats customers.
Assert that customer_id is unique in the joined output and fail the run if it is not.
Count the dashboard's rows once a month after the books close.
questions.why: A uniqueness check inside the pipeline turns the notebook finding into a rule that blocks bad data from reaching reports, which exploration alone does not do.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can skip writing a data quality check because we explored the data in an Athena notebook and the numbers looked right. Explain to them what a notebook session is good for, what it cannot guarantee, and one cost or limit you would warn them about.
lessons.modelAnswer: A notebook session is good for finding out what the data really looks like. We load a table, run counts and sample rows, and spot things like a missing date or a suspicious duplicate. It is fast because Spark splits the work across machines and the session keeps the table loaded between cells. But it only shows what we looked at, once, on the day we looked. It does not stop the same problem recurring in tomorrow's load, so the check has to live in the pipeline. The limit I would warn about is cost: a session is billed while it holds capacity, so an idle one left open keeps charging. We should explore, then turn what we learned into a rule that runs every time.
rubricPoints: Describes the notebook as an exploration tool where cells run against a Spark session that keeps state between steps.
Explains that a one-off notebook result does not prevent the same error in future runs.
Names a concrete limit or cost, such as billing while a session is idle.
Connects the finding to a data quality check that runs inside the pipeline.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers Spark notebooks directly, and reasoning through an exam-style case about where a notebook result is trustworthy adds the most.

lessons.plain: Some data services make you rent a fixed amount of computer capacity and keep it running, like booking a whole bus for the day whether it fills or not. Others charge only for the work they actually do and grow or shrink on their own, like a taxi ride. Choosing between these two styles is a trade-off. Fixed capacity gives predictable cost and control, while pay-per-use means less to manage and a cost that follows demand, but it comes with its own limits and surprises. Here you learn to weigh the two options for a given job.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job does its work in one hour and sits idle for the other 23 hours. Would you rather pay for a server that runs all day, or pay only for the hour it works? Why?
lessons.teach:
Provisioned means you decide in advance how much capacity a service has, such as a fixed number of nodes or servers, and you pay for that capacity for as long as it exists, whether it is busy or idle. You also own the sizing and the scaling rules. Serverless means the provider runs the capacity for you, scales it up and down with demand, and bills for what you use, such as compute time, requests or the amount of data scanned. The service still runs on real servers; the difference is that you do not hold them.

Why the trade-off exists: fixed capacity has predictable cost and performance, and it is usually cheaper when the load is steady and high enough to keep the machines busy. Pay-per-use is cheaper when load is spiky or sparse, and it removes the work of sizing, but it has quotas, such as limits on concurrent executions, and its cost follows how much work your queries or jobs do.

Worked example. A nightly job needs 10 node-hours of compute. Option A: a provisioned cluster of 10 nodes at 1 credit per node-hour runs 24 hours, so 10 times 24 equals 240 credits per day. Option B: a serverless service that bills 2 credits per node-hour of work, so 10 times 2 equals 20 credits, and nothing is billed when the job is not running. Option B is far cheaper here.

Common mistake: assuming serverless is always cheaper. If the same job ran continuously at full load, the higher per-unit price of serverless could exceed the fixed cluster cost.

Consequence: a serverless workload that hits its concurrency quota gets throttled during a surge, and an unfiltered query that scans a whole table can produce a large bill overnight. The cheaper option is the one that matches your load shape, and you should check the quota and the cost driver before choosing it.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics firm runs its reporting warehouse on a provisioned cluster of 4 nodes billed at 3 credits per node-hour, switched on around the clock. A serverless alternative bills 5 credits per node-hour of actual work. The reporting job needs 12 node-hours of work per day. Step 1: the provisioned cluster costs 4 times 24 times 3, which is 288 credits per day. Step 2: the serverless job costs 12 times 5, which is 60 credits per day. Step 3 is missing: state which option is cheaper for this load and give the reason from the billing model.
choices: Provisioned: its rate per node-hour is lower.
Serverless: it has no quotas to check.
Serverless: 60 is less than 288, and it bills only the 12 hours used.
Provisioned: serverless costs more at any load.
questions.why: Serverless wins here because its daily total of 60 is far below the fixed 288, and it charges only for the work actually done, not for idle time.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a serverless service?
choices: The service runs without any servers existing anywhere, so it has no hardware costs.
You set the scaling rules yourself but the provider handles the machines.
The provider runs and scales the capacity for you and bills for the work you use.
You pick a fixed number of machines and pay for them whether or not they are busy.
questions.why: Serverless means the provider manages and scales the capacity and charges for usage, while the underlying service still runs on real servers.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's nightly ingestion needs 9 node-hours of work per day. Option one is a provisioned cluster of 6 nodes at 1.5 credits per node-hour, running all 24 hours. Option two is a serverless service billed at 4 credits per node-hour of work done. Which option costs less per day and why?
choices: Serverless, because it costs 36 credits against 216 for the cluster.
Serverless, because the cluster has no quota and so it is cheaper to run.
Provisioned, because 6 nodes at 1.5 credits gives 9 credits a day.
Provisioned, because a fixed cluster always beats pay-per-use on cost.
questions.why: The cluster costs 6 times 24 times 1.5, which is 216 credits, while serverless costs 9 times 4, which is 36 credits, so serverless is cheaper for this sparse load.

questions.prompt: A retail firm's serverless processing service has a concurrency quota of 20, meaning at most 20 jobs can run at the same time. A flash sale triggers 50 jobs at once. What is the most likely result, and what should the team check before choosing this service?
choices: All 50 jobs run, and the bill simply rises with the extra work done.
The service automatically raises its quota, so no jobs are affected, and no check is needed.
The extra 30 jobs are run on a hidden provisioned pool at no added cost.
The extra jobs are throttled, so they are slowed or refused, and the team should check the quota against its peak load.
questions.why: A serverless service that hits its concurrency quota throttles the excess work, so the team must compare the quota with expected surge load before relying on it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a provisioned data service and a serverless one for a new pipeline, and name one limit or tradeoff you would still have to watch after choosing the serverless option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the shape of the load. If the work is steady and busy most hours, a provisioned service is usually predictable and can cost less, because we pay for capacity we keep full. If the work is bursty or runs only a few hours a day, a serverless service fits better, because we pay only for the work done and the provider handles scaling and patching. Then I would check the cost driver and the limits before committing. For the serverless option, the trade-off I would watch is quotas: if a traffic spike exceeds concurrency limits, work gets throttled, so I would add retries and alarms on throttling. I would also watch cost per query or per run, since a query that scans far more data than needed can be expensive, so I would confirm partitioning and filters are in place.
rubricPoints: Provisioned means fixed capacity you pay for whether it is used or not; serverless means pay per use with automatic scaling.
Choose by load shape: steady high load tends to favor provisioned, while spiky or sparse load tends to favor serverless.
Serverless has limits such as concurrency quotas that can throttle work during surges.
Serverless cost follows usage drivers such as data scanned, so unbounded queries can surprise the bill.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between the two styles is a judgment across load shape, cost and limits, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario adds the most.

lessons.plain: Aggregation means boiling a long list of records down to a few useful numbers, like a total, a count, or an average. Think of a teacher who has a sheet with every quiz score from every student and wants the average per class, not per student. Grouping sorts the records into buckets first, so each bucket gets its own summary. A rolling average is a running summary that moves along a sequence, like a car's average speed over the last five minutes, updated as new readings arrive. Pivoting rearranges a long list so that one category becomes separate columns, like turning a tall list of sales into a grid with one column per region.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop writes one row for every sale, with a town name and an amount. Without reading each row yourself, how would you find the total sales for each town, and what would you call that step?
lessons.teach:
Aggregation collapses many rows into a summary value: a count, a sum, or an average. Grouping, written GROUP BY in SQL, splits rows into buckets by one or more columns, and the aggregate function runs once per bucket. A rolling average (also called a moving average) keeps every row but, for each row, averages it together with a fixed number of rows before it, such as the last three. This is a window function: it looks at neighbouring rows without collapsing them. Pivoting turns the values of one column into separate columns, usually with conditional aggregation: for each wanted category you sum a value only when the category matches, so one row per date can show one column per region.

Why it works: the database arranges the rows into sets, then applies the same function to each set. Worked example: five daily readings for truck 7 are 10, 12, 14, 20, 22. A three-day rolling average at day 3 is (10+12+14)/3 = 12. At day 4 it is (12+14+20)/3 = 15.33. At day 5 it is (14+20+22)/3 = 18.67.

Common mistake: averaging per-group averages. If one group has 2 rows and another has 200, the average of the two averages gives the small group equal weight. Recompute from the underlying sums and counts instead.

Consequence in a running system: if a join before the aggregation duplicates rows, SUM quietly double counts and a dashboard shows inflated totals with no error. A data quality rule that compares row counts before and after the join would catch it.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company logs daily rentals at one station: day 1 is 4, day 2 is 8, day 3 is 6, day 4 is 10, day 5 is 12. It wants a three-day rolling average, where each row averages itself with the two rows before it. Day 3 is (4+8+6)/3 = 6.00 and day 4 is (8+6+10)/3 = 8.00. Step to complete: the window for day 5 is ____, so its rolling average is ____.
choices: (6+10+12)/3 = 9.33, the current row plus the two rows before it
(10+12)/2 = 11.00, only the two most recent rows divided by two
(4+8+6+10+12)/5 = 8.00, an average over all five days
(8+6+10)/3 = 8.00, the same window as day 4 repeated
questions.why: A three-day rolling average at each row uses that row and the two before it, so day 5 uses days 3, 4 and 5, giving 28/3 = 9.33.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm stores one row per parcel scan, with a depot column. An analyst runs SELECT depot, COUNT(*) FROM scans GROUP BY depot. What does the GROUP BY clause do in that query?
choices: It splits the rows into one bucket per depot and counts each bucket
It deletes any scan whose depot value is empty before counting
It keeps every scan row and adds a running count beside each one
It joins the scans table to a depots table so the counts can be labelled
questions.why: GROUP BY places rows into buckets by the listed column and the aggregate function runs once per bucket, so COUNT returns one row per depot.

questions.prompt: Depot A has 3 parcels with an average handling time of 10 minutes. Depot B has 300 parcels with an average handling time of 40 minutes. Someone wants the overall average handling time across all 303 parcels and computes the mean of the two depot averages. Which statement is correct?
choices: The overall figure should be the larger depot average, 40 minutes, because it covers most of the parcels
The mean of the two averages, 25 minutes, is correct because each depot counts equally
The mean of the two averages is wrong; the correct overall figure comes from total minutes divided by total parcels, about 39.7 minutes
The mean of the two averages is right only if both depots have the same number of parcels, which they do here
questions.why: Averaging per-group averages gives a small group the same weight as a large one, so the overall average must be recomputed from the underlying sums and counts, which gives about 39.7 minutes here.

questions.prompt: A coffee chain has a table with one row per order, containing an order_date column, a drink column with values such as latte or tea, and a quantity column. The team wants one row per date with one column per drink showing total quantity sold. Which approach produces that layout?
choices: A window function with a rolling three-row frame over the quantity column
For each drink, sum the quantity only when the drink matches, grouped by order_date
Joining the orders table to itself on drink so each drink gets its own copy of the rows
GROUP BY drink alone, which returns one row per drink with no date information
questions.why: Pivoting with conditional aggregation sums a value only where the category matches, and grouping by date gives one row per date with one column per drink.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between grouping and a rolling average, and name one limit or tradeoff of each when you use them on a live pipeline.
lessons.modelAnswer: Grouping collapses rows: every row in a bucket, such as one town or one day, becomes a single summary row, so the output is shorter than the input. A rolling average keeps every row and attaches to each one the average of it and the few rows before it, so the output is the same length but smoother. The limit of grouping is that detail is gone once you aggregate, so you cannot later see which individual record caused a strange total. The limit of a rolling average is the start of the series: the first rows have fewer neighbours, so their averages cover a smaller window and can look misleading unless you handle them on purpose. Both also depend on the order and completeness of the input. A late or missing row changes the result silently.
rubricPoints: Grouping reduces many rows to one summary row per bucket
A rolling average keeps every row and uses a fixed window of neighbours
Grouping loses row-level detail once aggregated
Rolling averages are unreliable at the start of the series or with missing or late rows

suggested.rationale: Writing grouped, rolling, and pivoted queries against sample data is a hands-on SQL skill that the planned SQL lab would exercise directly.

lessons.plain: An audit is a review where someone checks what happened in a system and who did it. Audit logs are the written records a system keeps of actions, such as who changed a setting or read a file, and when. Extracting logs for an audit means pulling a specific slice of those records out of where they are stored, for a defined time range and set of actions, in a form that can be checked later. The goal is to produce evidence that is complete, accurate and unchanged. A sloppy extraction can lose records or make them look different from the originals, and then the audit proves nothing.
lessons.guessPrompt: An auditor asks: Who changed the access settings on the trips table between 14:00 and 16:00 UTC on 11 March 2025? Before reading anything else, what three things would you need to pin down so the answer is trustworthy?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. An audit log is a record, kept automatically by a service, of an action taken in a system: who (the identity, such as a user or a service role), what (the action and the resource it touched), when (a timestamp), and from where. An extraction is a filtered copy of a slice of those records, taken for a stated purpose. A retention period is how long the provider keeps the records before they expire, so an extraction must happen before records age out.

Why it works: a defensible extraction has three parts. First, a fixed scope: a time range written in UTC, the accounts or systems included, and the event types wanted. Second, a faithful copy: the records are read from the original store and never edited, and you record a checksum, which is a fingerprint computed from the file's contents, so any later change shows up as a mismatch. Third, a record of the extraction itself: who ran it, when, with what filter, and how many records came back.

Worked example. The auditor asks about changes to access settings on the trips table from 14:00 to 16:00 UTC on 11 March 2025. Step 1: set the window as 2025-03-11T14:00Z to 16:00Z, and do not use local time. Step 2: choose the source, the account's API activity log (on AWS this is CloudTrail). Step 3: filter by event name for permission-changing actions and by the trips table resource. Step 4: export the matching records to a write-once storage location and compute a checksum. Step 5: count the records and note the count in the extraction log, so a reviewer can rerun it and get the same number.

Common mistake: using the local time zone of the person running the query, so the window quietly shifts by hours and the one relevant change falls outside it. Another is filtering on a field that is empty for some event types, which drops records without any error.

Consequence: a silent gap in the extraction means the audit can report that no changes were found when changes did happen. The failure looks like success, which is why the record count and the checksum matter.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm, Brightwater Freight, wants to know who restored archived invoices from its invoice-archive-eu storage bucket between 22:00 and 01:00 UTC on 4 to 5 June 2025. The analyst set the window as 2025-06-04T22:00Z to 2025-06-05T01:00Z, chose the account's API activity log as the source, and filtered on the restore event name and that bucket. The matching records were exported to a write-once location. The analyst then wrote the record count into the extraction log, but skipped one step between the export and that log entry. Which step belongs there?
choices: Compute a checksum of the exported file so that any later change shows up as a mismatch
Widen the window to a full 24 hours so that late restore events are included
Delete the original records from the activity log once they have been exported
Re-run the filter in the analyst's local time zone to confirm the window is right
questions.why: A checksum is a fingerprint computed from the file's contents, so recording it right after export lets anyone detect a later edit, which is the missing step.

questions.prompt: In an audit extraction, what does the retention period describe?
choices: The time window written in UTC that the auditor requested
How long the extraction job is allowed to run before it times out
The number of records a single export file can hold
How long the provider keeps the records before they expire, so the extraction must run before then
questions.why: A retention period is how long the provider keeps audit records before they age out, which is why an extraction has to happen before that point.

questions.prompt: A team extracts records of storage bucket policy changes by keeping only records where the field requestParameters.bucketName has a value. Their extraction reports zero policy changes for the month, but a manager saw a policy change in the console that same month. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The checksum on the exported file did not match, so the file was rejected without a message
Some relevant events leave that field empty, so the filter silently dropped them
The export tool applied a default size limit that quietly cut the output short before the file was written
Bucket policy changes are never written to the audit log, so no extraction can find them
questions.why: Filtering on a field that is empty for some event types drops those records without any error, so the extraction looks complete while missing real changes.

questions.prompt: A team in Sydney, which is UTC+10 in July with no daylight saving change, wants an audit window covering 09:00 to 11:00 on 14 July 2025 local time. Which UTC window should they write in the extraction scope?
questions.why: Sydney at UTC+10 is ten hours ahead of UTC, so 09:00 local on 14 July is 23:00 UTC on 13 July, and the window ends at 01:00Z on 14 July.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says: We already keep CloudTrail, so audit extraction is just downloading the logs. Explain to them what an audit extraction should include beyond downloading, and name one limit that extraction cannot solve.
lessons.modelAnswer: Keeping the logs is only half the job. An audit extraction needs a fixed scope: an exact time window in UTC, the accounts and resources in question, and the event types that matter. It also needs a faithful copy. Export from the original store, do not edit the file, and record a checksum so anyone can later prove the file is unchanged. Finally, log the extraction itself: who ran it, when, which filter was used, and how many records came back, so a reviewer can rerun it and get the same count. One limit: these records only exist if they were retained and logged. If retention expired before the audit request, or logging was never turned on for that region or service, no extraction can recover the missing events. The honest answer in that case is that the gap is itself part of the finding.
rubricPoints: Defines an audit log and an extraction, and fixes the scope with an exact time window in UTC.
Explains that the extracted records must be an unedited copy, verified with a checksum.
Says the extraction itself is recorded (who, when, filter, record count) so it can be rerun and checked.
Names a limit: records that expired or were never logged cannot be recovered by extraction.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission covers audit extraction directly, so reasoning through an auditor's request about scope, time window and gaps adds the most.

lessons.plain: Auditable and traceable means you can later answer two questions about a data pipeline: what happened, and why did this number come out this way? Logging is the written record a pipeline produces as it runs, much like a shift log kept in a control room. Monitoring watches measurements over time, such as how many rows arrived, and raises a warning when they drift from normal. Deploying this well means building these records and watches into the pipeline from the start, not adding them after something has already gone wrong. When it is done properly, one bad figure on a dashboard can be traced back to the exact run, input and step that produced it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job loads sales totals, and the morning dashboard shows revenue at half of what finance expects. The job reported success. What is the first piece of information you would want written down during each run so you could find out which run produced the wrong number and why?
lessons.teach:
A log is a timestamped line of text that a program writes as it does its work. A structured log writes the same information as named fields, such as run_id, step, row_count and status, so a tool can search and count it instead of a person reading free text. A run ID is a unique label given to one execution of a pipeline, and every log line from that execution carries it. A metric is a number recorded over time, such as rows loaded per run. An alarm is a rule that watches a metric and sends a notification when it crosses a threshold. An audit trail is a record of who or what changed something and when. On AWS this usually means application logs sent to a log service such as CloudWatch Logs, records of API calls kept by CloudTrail, and metric alarms in CloudWatch.

Why it works: a bad number is almost always the end of a chain of steps. If each step records its inputs and outputs under one run ID, you can walk the chain backward. Worked example: run 2024-06-03-a reads 120,000 order rows from a source file and logs row_count=120000. The filter step drops test orders and logs rows_out=118000. The load step writes to the table and logs rows_loaded=118000. A metric records rows_loaded per run, and an alarm fires if that value drops below 90 percent of the seven-day median. A common mistake is logging only 'job finished' or 'success', which tells you nothing about counts. Another is keeping logs for only a day or two, so the evidence is gone before anyone asks. In a running system, a silent partial load can repeat every night for weeks; the counts and the alarm are what expose it on the first night.

questions.prompt: A clinic-booking pipeline runs under run ID clinic-0917-b. The extract step reads 6,000 appointment rows and logs rows_read=6000. The deduplication step removes 600 rows that are duplicate bookings and writes its output, but its log line is left blank in this example as rows_out=____. The load step then logs rows_loaded=5400. Using the run ID to walk the chain, what value belongs in the blank?
questions.why: Deduplication keeps every row except the 600 duplicates, so 6,000 minus 600 gives 5,400, which matches what the load step recorded.

questions.prompt: A nightly billing export job needs its logs to be searchable by a tool that counts rows per run. Which log line best meets that need?
choices: Job bill-88 completed successfully
export step done at 02:14
export finished, 3200 rows, all ok
{"run_id":"bill-88","step":"export","row_count":3200,"status":"ok"}
questions.why: A structured log stores named fields such as run_id, step, row_count and status, so a tool can filter and count them, while free text needs a person to read it.

questions.prompt: A warehouse load's alarm fires when rows_loaded drops below 90 percent of the seven-day median. The seven-day median for a job is 5,000 rows. Last night the job loaded 4,600 rows. What happens?
choices: The alarm fires at 4,500 rows, so 4,600 is still too low
The alarm does not fire, because 4,600 is 92 percent of 5,000, above the 90 percent threshold
The alarm fires only if the load also logs an error status
The alarm fires, because any drop from the median triggers it
questions.why: Ninety percent of 5,000 is 4,500, and 4,600 is above that line, so the threshold rule is not crossed and no notification is sent.

questions.prompt: On a Tuesday, a column was removed from a warehouse table and the pipeline's application logs show only that its scheduled runs succeeded. Which record is most likely to show who made the removal and when?
choices: The pipeline's application log for the Tuesday run
An audit trail of API calls, such as CloudTrail, which records who issued a change and when
A metric recording rows loaded per run
The alarm history for rows_loaded
questions.why: An audit trail records who or what made a change and when, whereas application logs and metrics describe the pipeline's work rather than the identity of whoever altered the table.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make a nightly data pipeline traceable enough that someone could find the exact run behind a wrong dashboard number. Name one limit or tradeoff of the logging and monitoring you would add.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would give every run a unique run ID and write every log line with that ID, along with the step name, input source, row counts before and after each transform, and a final status. I would also publish rows loaded per run as a metric and set an alarm that fires when it falls well below the recent normal, so the problem is caught before the dashboard is read. If someone questions a number, we search logs by the run ID for the date in question, check the counts at each step, and see where they diverge. The main tradeoff is cost and noise: detailed logs and many alarms cost money to store and can cause alert fatigue, so I would log counts and key decisions rather than every row, and tune thresholds against a few weeks of history before trusting them.
rubricPoints: Each run gets a unique ID that is attached to every log line.
Structured logs record inputs, outputs and row counts at each step, not just success or failure.
A metric tracks a key quantity over time, and an alarm fires when it drifts from normal.
Logs are retained long enough to audit past runs, and the tradeoff of cost or alert noise is acknowledged.

suggested.rationale: Building metric alarms with thresholds and notifications directly exercises the monitoring half of this objective, which no listed mission covers.

lessons.plain: A monitoring alert is a message that reaches a person or another system when something measurable goes wrong, such as a job failing or a number falling outside its normal range. Monitoring watches the numbers, and notifications carry the news. The useful pattern is a rule that says when a measurement crosses a line, plus a delivery path that sends the message to the right people or tools. An alert that nobody receives, or that fires every few minutes, is worse than none, because it trains people to ignore the channel. This lesson covers how that chain is built and what makes it dependable.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly pipeline's output row count drops from about 2 million to 40 thousand, but the job reports success. Who should hear about this, and how would they find out before someone opens a dashboard?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a number recorded over time, such as rows written per run or minutes since the last successful load. An alarm is a rule that checks a metric against a threshold, which is a line such as fewer than one million rows. The alarm looks at the metric over a set number of evaluation periods and changes state between OK, ALARM, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA. A notification topic is a publish-subscribe channel: one publisher sends a message to the topic, and every subscriber attached to it receives a copy. Subscribers can be an email address, a phone number, a function, a queue, or a chat webhook. In AWS these are CloudWatch alarms and Amazon SNS topics, but the pattern is generic.

It works because the evaluation and the delivery are separate steps. The alarm runs on its own schedule, and only a state change is published, so one breach produces one message rather than a flood. Fan-out lets the same event reach an on-call inbox and a team channel without the pipeline knowing who they are.

Worked example: the job publishes a RowCount metric after each run. The alarm is set to ALARM when RowCount is below 1,000,000 for one period. At 02:00 the run publishes 40,000. At the next evaluation the alarm sees the breach, moves from OK to ALARM, and publishes once to the pipeline-alerts topic. The topic delivers to the on-call email and the team chat. The next night's run publishes 2,050,000, the alarm returns to OK, and a recovery message is sent.

Common mistake: alerting only on job status. A job can succeed and still write wrong numbers, so the alarm needs a data measurement. A second mistake is treating missing data as healthy. If the job stops publishing, the alarm should move to INSUFFICIENT_DATA and notify, not stay quiet.

In a running system, a threshold that is too tight fires on normal variation and gets muted, while one that is too loose lets a bad load reach a dashboard. Alerting is only useful when the metric, the threshold, and the delivery path are all tested together.

questions.prompt: A dental practice runs a nightly job that loads appointment records into a reporting store and publishes a metric called MinutesSinceLoad after each attempt. An alarm watches that metric. Its rule is ALARM when MinutesSinceLoad is above 90 for one evaluation period, and its notifications go to a topic named practice-ops. Last Tuesday the load finished at 03:00 and published 12, so the alarm stayed OK. On Wednesday the job crashed at 03:00 and published nothing at all. Step 1: at the 05:00 evaluation the alarm finds no data, so it moves from OK to INSUFFICIENT_DATA. Step 2 is missing. Step 3: on Thursday the job reruns, publishes 15, and the alarm returns to OK and sends a recovery message. Which completes step 2?
choices: The alarm stays OK because no value above 90 was ever recorded.
The alarm publishes a new message at every evaluation until a value finally arrives.
The alarm publishes one message to practice-ops for the change to INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
The alarm removes the practice-ops subscribers so that nobody is bothered by a silent job.
questions.why: A state change is published once, and moving to INSUFFICIENT_DATA is a state change that should notify, so the alarm sends one message to the topic rather than staying quiet or flooding the inbox.

questions.prompt: A team's nightly export publishes a metric called FailedRecords after each run. Which part of the system decides whether a notification should be sent?
choices: The alarm, which checks FailedRecords against its threshold over its evaluation periods.
The export job itself, which emails the team directly whenever FailedRecords is nonzero.
The topic, which compares the metric to a threshold before delivering anything.
The email client of the on-call engineer, which filters messages by subject.
questions.why: The alarm is the rule that compares a metric to a threshold across evaluation periods and changes state; the topic only delivers, and the job is not meant to send alerts itself.

questions.prompt: A warehouse load job always finishes with a success status, but last week it wrote a sales total that was 30 percent low because a source table was partly empty. The team's only alarm watches job status. What change would have caught this before a dashboard showed the wrong total?
choices: Changing the job to exit with an error code whenever it runs longer than usual.
Adding an alarm on a data measurement such as the loaded row count or sales total, compared to a threshold.
Lengthening the evaluation period so that the status alarm reacts more slowly.
Adding a subscriber to the alarm topic so that more people see the status message.
questions.why: A job can succeed while writing wrong numbers, so the alarm needs a metric that measures the data itself, which is the mistake the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A topic named finance-alerts has three subscribers: an on-call email address, a queue read by an automated retry function, and a chat webhook. A metric breach occurs once. How many messages does the alarm publish, and who receives them?
choices: One message is published to the topic, and all three subscribers receive a copy.
Three messages are published, one for each subscriber, and each subscriber gets only its own copy.
One message is published, and only the queue receives it because the retry function handles all alerts.
One message is published, but only the email address receives it because it is the first subscriber.
questions.why: A publish-subscribe topic takes one publish and delivers a copy to every attached subscriber, which is the fan-out behaviour the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a monitoring alert travels from a measured number to someone's inbox, and name one limit or tradeoff in choosing its threshold.
lessons.modelAnswer:
The pipeline publishes a metric, such as rows written per run, after each load. An alarm evaluates that metric on a schedule against a threshold. When the value crosses the line for the required number of periods, the alarm changes state and publishes one message to a notification topic. The topic fans that message out to subscribers like an email list, a chat channel, or a function that opens a ticket. The same path also needs a rule for missing data, because a stopped job is a failure too.

The main tradeoff is in the threshold. A tight line catches small problems early but fires on normal day-to-day variation, so people start ignoring it. A loose line stays quiet but lets a wrong load reach a dashboard. A good threshold is based on the historical range of the metric, and it should be reviewed when the data volume changes.
rubricPoints: Describes the chain: metric, then alarm rule against a threshold, then a notification topic, then subscribers
Explains that alarm state changes, not every evaluation, produce the message
Names a threshold tradeoff: too tight causes noise and muting, too loose misses bad data
Notes that missing data or a stopped job needs its own alert behavior

suggested.rationale: The alarm-builder engine would let the learner set a metric threshold and watch the alarm state change, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Troubleshooting pipeline performance means finding out why a data pipeline is slower, more expensive, or more fragile than it should be, and fixing the cause rather than the symptom. A pipeline is a chain of steps that moves and reshapes data, like a kitchen line where each station passes plates to the next. When the whole line slows down, the question is which station is holding things up. You look at timing records, resource use, and how the work is split across workers, then test one change at a time. The core habit is to measure first and guess second.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job that used to finish in 40 minutes now takes 3 hours, and the only known change is that the input data grew by 20 percent. Before reading anything else, what would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Performance troubleshooting starts by finding the bottleneck, meaning the one step whose slowness sets the speed of the whole run. A pipeline is a series of stages, each reading data, transforming it, and writing it out. Total run time is roughly the duration of the slowest stage plus any waiting between stages, so speeding up a stage that is already fast changes almost nothing. Three signals usually locate the problem: per-stage duration in the run logs, resource metrics such as CPU, memory and input and output throughput, and the number of records or bytes each stage handles. Data skew means the work is unevenly split. A partition, which is a slice of the data assigned to one worker and often grouped by a key such as a customer ID, holds far more rows than the others. Most workers finish quickly and then sit idle while one worker grinds on.

Worked example. A nightly job groups 100 million trip events by city. Stage timing shows 95 of 100 tasks finish in about 2 minutes, but one task runs for 90 minutes. Step 1: the task log shows its input is 80 million rows, all carrying one city value. Step 2: the other tasks each handle roughly 100,000 rows. Step 3: the cause is a hot key, a single value that dominates the data. Step 4: the fix is to split that hot key, for example by adding a random suffix so its rows spread across several workers, then combine the partial results in a small second step.

Common mistake: adding more workers or a bigger machine. Extra capacity does not help one oversized partition, so cost rises while runtime barely moves. Measure first, change one thing, and measure again.

A single hot partition can hold a whole run past its deadline, which delays every dashboard that depends on the output.

Pipeline performance is a measurement problem before it is a tuning problem: find the slow stage, then find out why it is slow.

questions.prompt: A parcel company runs a nightly job that counts package scans per depot. The job has 40 tasks, one per slice of data, and each slice is grouped by depot ID. Step 1: the run log shows 39 tasks finished in about 3 minutes, but one task ran for 55 minutes. Step 2: that slow task's input held 6 million scan rows, and nearly all of them carried the depot ID HUB-7; the other tasks each handled roughly 150,000 rows. Step 3: [missing step; the learner must supply the diagnosis]. Step 4: the team decides to split the HUB-7 rows across several workers, then combine the partial counts in a small second step, and then re-run the job to confirm that the slowest task now finishes close to the others.
choices: The output write to the reporting database is slow, so the task spends most of its time waiting to write.
A hot key: one value dominates the data, so one partition holds far more rows than the rest and that worker becomes the bottleneck.
The network between the stages is congested, so every task is slowed down equally by waiting for data.
The depot ID column is too wide, so the workers are running out of memory and swapping to disk.
questions.why: Steps 1 and 2 show one partition with far more rows than the others, all sharing one value, which is the definition of a hot key causing data skew.

questions.prompt: A data pipeline has four stages. Their durations are 4 minutes, 6 minutes, 25 minutes and 3 minutes, with about 2 minutes of waiting between stages. Which change is most likely to shorten the total run time?
choices: Halve the duration of the 3-minute final stage by giving it a larger machine
Speed up the 25-minute stage, because total run time is roughly the slowest stage plus waiting
Remove the 2 minutes of waiting by rewriting the scheduler configuration
Add a fifth stage that runs in parallel with the 4-minute stage
questions.why: Total run time is roughly the slowest stage plus waiting, so the 25-minute stage is the bottleneck and speeding it up is what changes the total.

questions.prompt: A team has a batch job where one partition holds about 70 percent of all rows, and the other workers finish quickly and sit idle. The team responds by doubling the number of workers. What is the most likely result?
choices: Run time stays nearly the same and cost rises, because the one oversized partition still limits the run
Run time drops by about half because the work is now split across twice as many workers
The job fails with a quota error because the data is now too spread out
Run time rises because the extra workers compete for the same input
questions.why: Extra workers cannot split a single oversized partition, so the bottleneck stays and the added capacity mostly adds cost.

questions.prompt: A team wants to find out whether a slow pipeline is caused by uneven data splitting. Which pair of measurements would most directly reveal a partition holding far more rows than its peers?
choices: The total size of the output bucket and the number of days since the job was written
The job's total cost for the month and the count of stages in the pipeline
The average CPU of the whole cluster over a week and the name of the scheduler
The number of rows handled by each task within the same stage, compared with per-task duration
questions.why: Comparing per-task row counts within one stage, alongside how long each task took, shows directly whether the work is unevenly split.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find out why a pipeline run that used to take 40 minutes now takes three hours. Name one limit of your method and one tradeoff in the fix you would choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the per-stage timings from the run logs and the resource metrics, not with the code. Total run time is driven by the slowest stage plus waiting, so the goal is to find the one stage that grew. Once I have that stage, I look at how its work is split. If one partition or key holds most of the records while the rest finish quickly, the cause is skew, and adding workers will not help much. If the work is evenly split but the stage reads far more data than before, I check for a missing filter or partition pruning that stopped working. The limit of this approach is that logs only show what was instrumented, so a stage with no timing can hide the cause. For the fix, salting a hot key adds a second combining step and some complexity, but it attacks the cause instead of paying for more capacity.
rubricPoints: Locate the slowest stage using per-stage timings and resource metrics before changing anything
Distinguish skew (uneven partitions) from simply too much data being read
Explain that adding capacity does not fix a single oversized partition
Name a limit of the method, such as missing instrumentation, or a tradeoff of the chosen fix

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a slow-run situation with logs and a skewed partition adds the most beyond reading the definitions.

lessons.plain: Every time someone or some program asks a cloud account to do something, such as create a table, change a permission, or delete a file, the account can keep a written record of that request. Think of it as a security camera log for the account's control panel. It notes who asked, when, from where, what they asked for, and whether it worked. When a pipeline breaks or a setting changes without anyone admitting it, this record is how you find out what happened and who or what caused it.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a column in your reporting table suddenly changed its data type overnight and nobody remembers touching it, what single kind of record would you want to check first, and what would you hope it tells you?
lessons.teach: AWS CloudTrail is the AWS service that records API calls. An API call is a request sent to an AWS service, whether it comes from the web console, the command line, a software development kit (SDK, a library that lets code call AWS), or another AWS service acting on a role's behalf. Each recorded item is an event. An event holds the identity that made the request (a user or a role), the time, the source address, the event name such as UpdateTable, the parameters, and an error code if the call failed. Events come in two broad kinds. Management events are control actions, like creating a job or changing a permission. Data events are high-volume actions on the data itself, such as reading or writing individual objects in Amazon S3; these are off by default and cost extra. Event history shows recent management events for the last 90 days with no setup. A trail is a configuration that keeps delivering events to an S3 bucket for long-term storage and can also send them to CloudWatch Logs for searching and alerts. Worked example: a transformation job's output starts dropping a column at 02:14. Step 1: search event history for update events on that job over the previous day. Step 2: find an event at 02:09 made by a deployment role, from a build runner's address, whose parameters point to a new script version. Step 3: confirm there is no error code, so the change succeeded. Step 4: review that script version first. A common mistake is assuming the record covers everything forever. Event history is a short window, and data events are not recorded unless a trail turns them on, so last month's object reads may simply not exist. In a running system, the lack of a trail means you can see that something changed but not how far back the change went.

questions.prompt: At Northwind Freight, a currency conversion table started giving totals about 3 percent too low at 16:40. An engineer uses CloudTrail to investigate. Step 1: search event history for update events on the currency table over the previous 12 hours. Step 2: find a 16:31 event made by the role 'fx-sync-role', from a build server address, whose parameters point to a new feed source 'vendor_feed_v2'. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: ask the feed owner to review the new source before anything else. What belongs in step 3?
choices: Query S3 data events for every row read from the table since 16:31, because the update event alone cannot show the change succeeded.
Delete the trail so no further changes are recorded while the investigation runs.
Check that the 16:31 event has no error code, which confirms the update succeeded.
Assume the event history covers the last 90 days, so pull the table's older versions from there.
questions.why: An event with no error code shows the call succeeded, which is the confirmation the investigation needs before reviewing the new source.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm wants to know which of its S3 bucket reads were made by a reporting tool last week. Which kind of CloudTrail event would hold that information, and is it recorded by default?
choices: A management event stored in CloudWatch Logs, recorded automatically once an alarm exists.
A management event, which is recorded by default in event history for 90 days.
A data event, which is off by default and must be turned on through a trail.
A data event, which is always recorded by default and needs no setup.
questions.why: Reads of individual S3 objects are data events, which CloudTrail does not record unless a trail is configured to capture them.

questions.prompt: A payments company's auditor asks for the record of an object read in a bucket that happened three weeks ago. The company has no trail configured. What is the most accurate answer?
choices: The read can be recovered from the CloudWatch alarm history that was enabled last month.
The read cannot be recovered, because object reads are data events and no trail was keeping them.
The read is in event history, since event history keeps everything for 90 days.
The read can be found by searching event history, but only if the object was modified during that time.
questions.why: Data events are not kept unless a trail records them, so with no trail the three-week-old object read does not exist to be found.

questions.prompt: A retail company has a trail that delivers events to an S3 bucket and also sends them to CloudWatch Logs. What does the CloudWatch Logs delivery add that event history alone does not provide?
choices: It stores events permanently in the bucket and blocks any change to the job's parameters.
It turns on data events for every object in the account automatically.
It lets the team edit old events so the record matches the corrected numbers.
It makes events searchable and lets the team set alerts on them, while the S3 delivery is the long-term store.
questions.why: CloudWatch Logs supports searching and alerting on events, whereas long-term storage is the S3 delivery and event history is only a short window.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what AWS CloudTrail records, how that differs from the default event history, and one limit they should know about before relying on it for an audit.
lessons.modelAnswer: CloudTrail records API calls made to an AWS account, so each entry shows who or what made the request, when, from where, what action was requested, and whether it succeeded. The default event history only keeps management events for about 90 days and needs no setup. For anything longer, or for an audit, you need a trail, which continuously delivers those records to an S3 bucket. The limit to warn about is coverage: data events, such as reads and writes on individual S3 objects, are off by default and must be enabled explicitly, and they are billed separately. So if a teammate asks who read a file last month, the answer depends on whether a trail with data events existed then. Without it, the record simply is not there.
rubricPoints: CloudTrail records API calls with the caller, time, source, action, and result.
Default event history covers only recent management events, about 90 days.
A trail delivers events to S3 for long-term retention.
Data events such as S3 object reads are off by default and need explicit enabling.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly service facts and console settings, which a reading lesson covers better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: A data pipeline is a chain of automatic steps that moves data from where it starts to where people use it, such as copying raw records, cleaning them, and summarizing them into a table. AWS Glue and Amazon EMR are two managed services that run the heavy processing step, usually with Apache Spark, an engine that splits work across many machines. Troubleshooting means finding out why one of those jobs failed, ran slowly, or quietly produced bad output, and maintaining the job so problems show up early. This lesson covers how to read the evidence a job leaves behind and how to keep it healthy over time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job that cleans sales records finished with a green status, but yesterday's totals are about half of what they should be. Before reading anything else, what would you check first, and why might a green status not settle the question?
lessons.teach: Definitions first. A Glue job is a managed run of a script, usually Apache Spark, that AWS starts, runs and records for you. Amazon EMR is a managed group of virtual machines, called a cluster, that runs Spark and similar engines, and a step is one unit of work submitted to that cluster. Spark splits data into partitions and spreads them across workers. The Glue Data Catalog is a shared index of tables and their columns, and a crawler is a process that scans storage and updates that index.  Why it works: a job status only says the program exited without an error. It does not say the numbers are right. So you verify with evidence the job leaves behind: the run status, the driver log in CloudWatch Logs, row counts at each stage, and the schema the catalog holds.  Worked example. A Glue job reads 1,000,000 raw order rows, drops rows with an empty customer_id, and writes curated rows. Step 1: the run reports SUCCEEDED. Step 2: the log shows 1,000,000 rows read. Step 3: the log shows 0 rows after the filter, with no warning. Step 4: the source export renamed the column to customerId last Monday, so every customer_id reads as empty and the filter drops all rows. Step 5: the catalog still lists the old column name, which confirms the mismatch. The job did exactly what it was told.  Common mistake: restarting the job as the first fix. If the job wrote partial output before failing, a rerun can duplicate rows unless the write is idempotent, meaning running it twice gives the same result as running it once.  Consequence: a dashboard summing curated orders shows a revenue drop of nearly 100 percent, and someone may act on it. A row-count check that compares output to input and fails the run when output falls below an agreed share would have stopped the load before anyone looked. Pipelines need this routine maintenance: review row counts over time, alert on failed or unusually slow runs, and watch for schema changes at the source.

questions.prompt: An Amazon EMR step (one unit of work submitted to an EMR cluster, which is a managed group of virtual machines) reads 300,000 loyalty-point events and writes one points total per member. Step 1: the step state is COMPLETED. Step 2: the driver log shows 300,000 events read. Step 3: the log shows 300,000 rows after parsing the event_time column, with no warning. Step 4: the output holds 41,000 distinct member_id values, while the prior month's run held 58,000. Step 5 is missing and must be inferred: the source team changed member IDs to carry an 'M-' prefix, and the catalog schema still shows the old format. Which finding best explains the 17,000 missing members?
choices: The prefixed IDs fail to match the member table on the old format, so the join silently drops the rest with no warning.
The step state is COMPLETED, which means every member was written, so the gap must be in the dashboard query.
Spark split the input into partitions and skipped one, so rerunning the step will recover the missing members.
The Data Catalog crawler added 17,000 members to the table, so the output file is smaller than the correct total.
questions.why: The 300,000 rows were read and parsed, so the loss happened in a later stage where the changed ID format stopped matching, and the schema mismatch shows why.

questions.prompt: In this course's terms, what is a step on an Amazon EMR cluster?
choices: One unit of work submitted to the cluster, such as a Spark program run.
The catalog index that lists tables and columns for the cluster.
A scheduled scan of storage that updates table definitions.
A virtual machine in the cluster that holds one partition of data.
questions.why: A step is defined as one unit of work submitted to an EMR cluster, distinct from the machines, the catalog, and the crawler.

questions.prompt: A Glue job run shows the status SUCCEEDED. What does that status tell you?
choices: The output row counts match the source row counts.
The script exited without an error, but it says nothing about whether the numbers are right.
It is safe to rerun the job without duplicating output.
The Data Catalog schema matches what the script wrote.
questions.why: The status only reports that the program exited without an error, so separate evidence such as row counts and schema is needed to judge the data.

questions.prompt: A pipeline reads 88,000 telemetry rows and writes 61,000. The team's rule is that output must be at least 90 percent of input or the run fails. What should happen?
choices: The run is retried before any rule applies.
The run fails, since 61,000 is about 69 percent of 88,000, under the 90 percent floor.
The run passes, because the job reported success.
The run passes, since more than half the rows were kept.
questions.why: Dividing 61,000 by 88,000 gives about 69 percent, which is below the agreed 90 percent threshold, so a row-count check should fail the run.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find out why a Glue or EMR job ran to completion but produced far too few rows. Name one limit of the evidence you rely on and one check you would add so this is caught before a dashboard shows it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the run status, then the job's log in CloudWatch Logs, looking for the row count at each stage: rows read, rows after each filter, and rows written. If the count drops to near zero at one filter, I would compare the input column names against the catalog schema, because a renamed field makes a filter match nothing without raising an error. The limit is that a successful status and a clean log only prove the code ran, not that the data is right, and logs only show what the job chose to print. To catch this earlier, I would add a data quality rule that fails the run when output rows fall below a set share of input rows, and a schema check that alerts when source columns change. Then the problem stops at the pipeline, not on the dashboard.
rubricPoints: A success status only shows the job exited without error, not that the output is correct
Row counts at each stage, read in the job log, locate where data was lost
Schema or column mismatches between source and catalog can silently drop rows
A data quality rule comparing output to input volume, or a schema alert, would catch this before a dashboard

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a run that succeeded but produced wrong numbers, using logs and a quality rule, adds the most for this objective, and no listed mission covers Glue or EMR directly.

lessons.plain: When a program runs a data job, it can write short notes about what it is doing: when it started, how many records it read, and what went wrong. Amazon CloudWatch Logs is a service that collects those notes from many programs into one place, keeps them for a set time, and lets you search them later. Think of it as a shared logbook for your pipeline that stays readable after the machine that wrote it is gone. Logging well means the notes you write become useful evidence when a number looks wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job loads 1,000,000 rows and reports success, but the dashboard shows only 600,000. Without reading the job's code, what kind of note should the job have written during the run that would help you find where the other 400,000 rows went?
lessons.teach:
A log event is one timestamped note written by a program. A log group is a named container for related events, often one per pipeline. A log stream is the ordered sequence of events from one source, such as one run or one worker. Retention is how long events are kept before they are deleted. Structured logging means writing each event as named fields, usually JSON, so a tool can filter by field instead of a person reading free text.

It works because the service stores each event with its timestamp, outside the job itself. The evidence survives when the job ends, and you can search across many runs at once.

Worked example. Step 1: at the start, the job writes an event with a run ID, the source file name, and the expected row count of 1,000,000. Step 2: for each batch, it writes an event with the run ID, batch number, rows read, and rows rejected with a reason. Step 3: at the end, it writes totals: 600,000 loaded and 400,000 rejected, grouped by reason. Searching for that run ID now shows the rejection reason in minutes.

Common mistake: logging only 'job finished' or free text such as 'processed some rows'. Those notes cannot be counted or filtered, so the gap stays hidden. The opposite mistake is logging full customer records, which copies personal data into a store many people can read.

In a running system, a job that exits successfully with no count lines looks healthy to any check that only asks whether it ran. The wrong number then reaches people before anyone notices. The count check belongs inside the job, and the logs are where its evidence lives.

questions.prompt: A utility company loads smart-meter readings each night from four regional files. The loader's first event records the run ID and the expected meter count of 3,200. For each region, it writes an event with the run ID, region code, rows read, and rows dropped with a reason. The loader then writes nothing else and exits. The step that is missing is the closing event that should come after the regional events, once every file has been processed. Which closing event completes the design so that a bad night can be found from the logs alone?
choices: Write a closing event with the same run ID that gives the total rows loaded and states whether that total matches the expected meter count of 3,200
Delete the regional events once the run ends, so that the log group holds only one event per night
Set the retention of the log group to zero so that old nights do not take up space
Copy each meter's account number into the closing event so that support staff can trace any customer's readings
questions.why: The closing event with the run ID and totals lets a search compare loaded rows against the expected count, which is the evidence needed to catch a silent shortfall.

questions.prompt: A data team keeps every event from every nightly run of one pipeline in a single named container, and events from each individual worker in their own ordered sequence inside it. Which term names the container that holds the pipeline's related events?
choices: Log stream
Retention period
Log event
Log group
questions.why: A log group is the named container for related events, often one per pipeline, while a log stream is the ordered sequence from one source inside it.

questions.prompt: A nightly job ends by writing the line 'load complete, some rows skipped' as free text. An engineer says this is enough evidence. Which problem makes the note weak for catching wrong numbers?
choices: Free text cannot be counted or filtered, so nobody can compare rows loaded against the expected total
Log events are only kept for a fixed retention period, and this line would expire first
A log stream can only hold events written in JSON
The line is too short to be stored with its timestamp
questions.why: Free-text notes cannot be filtered by field or summed, so the gap between loaded and expected rows stays hidden, which is the failure the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A developer, trying to debug a failed import, logs each complete customer record that the job reads. Which risk does this create?
choices: It copies personal data into a log store that many people may be able to read
It stops the log stream from being ordered by time
It makes the timestamps on the events inaccurate
It causes the retention setting to delete the events sooner
questions.why: Writing full customer records into logs copies personal data into a store many people can read, which is a privacy problem separate from whether the logs are useful.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a data pipeline run should write to CloudWatch Logs and what it should never write, then name one limit or tradeoff of sending everything to a central log service.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each run should log a run ID, the source and its expected row count, per-batch counts of rows read, loaded and rejected with reasons, and final totals. Those fields let you filter and count across runs instead of reading text by eye. It should never log raw personal data, secrets, or full records, because the log store is readable by many people and copies sensitive values out of their protected place. The main tradeoff is cost and retention: logs cost money to ingest and store, so verbose logging at high volume adds up, and events are deleted once the retention period passes. If you need evidence beyond that window, you must decide what to keep and for how long before the logs expire. Also, a log only helps if someone or some check reads the counts, so logging alone does not stop a wrong number from reaching a dashboard.
rubricPoints: Names concrete fields to log, such as run ID, expected and actual row counts, and rejection reasons.
States that logs should not contain personal data, secrets, or full sensitive records.
Names a limit: cost of ingestion and storage, or retention that deletes old events.
Notes that logging alone does not catch errors unless a check reads the counts.

suggested.rationale: The core content is configuration terms and what to record, and no listed mission has the learner send logs to CloudWatch.

lessons.plain: When a pipeline runs without crashing but the numbers are wrong, the clues are in its logs, the written diary each program leaves behind. Analyzing logs means searching that diary for the moment things went off track. AWS offers several tools for this: one lets you ask SQL questions of log files stored as plain files, one runs large data processing jobs, one indexes text for fast search, and one searches logs that services send to a central log store. The skill is the same across all of them: choose a time window, filter for the warnings and counts that matter, and compare what happened in each run against what should have happened.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job reports a total that is 15 percent lower than yesterday, and it exited with a success status. Without any tools, what would you look for in its logs first, and why would a successful exit not prove that the numbers are right?
lessons.teach:
A log is a timestamped line a program writes about what it did. A pipeline is a chain of steps that moves and transforms data. Log analysis means querying many log lines at once to answer questions such as how many records each run read and how many it wrote.

Four AWS tools cover this objective. Amazon Athena runs SQL queries directly on files in object storage, so you can point it at exported logs without loading them into a database; you pay for the data it scans. Amazon EMR is a managed cluster for big data frameworks such as Spark, useful when log volumes are large or the analysis needs custom code. Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed search and analytics engine that indexes text so you can search and chart logs quickly. CloudWatch Logs Insights is a query tool over log groups, which are collections of logs that services write into CloudWatch, the central log store. All four rely on the same idea: filter by a time window, then group and count.

Worked example. A job writes one line per run: run id, records read, records written. Today's line for run 1042 shows read 1,000,000 and written 1,000,000, so the job reports success. Step one: filter the logs to run 1042 only. Step two: read the written count from that line. Step three: count the rows in the output table for that run. The table holds 700,000 rows. The gap sits between the logged write and the final table, so you check the steps after the write, any retries, and any overwrites.

Common mistake. Trusting that a job which exited successfully wrote correct data. Exit status only says the program finished, not that every record survived. Consequence: a dashboard fed by a silently short table shows a drop nobody can explain, which is why a count check comparing read, written, and final output should run before the data is published.

questions.prompt: A ride-share company runs a nightly fare job. Its log group in CloudWatch Logs Insights, which is the query tool over the log collections that services write into CloudWatch, holds one line per run with a run id, rows read, and rows written. Step one: the analyst filters the query to run 317 only. Step two: the analyst reads the rows-written value from that line, which is 480,000. Step three is missing. Step four: if the destination count and the logged count differ, the analyst checks retries and overwrites that happened after the write. Which completion fills step three?
choices: Count the rows in the destination fare table for run 317 only and compare that count with the logged 480,000.
Add up rows read across every run in the month to see whether the monthly total looks right.
Check that the job's exit code was zero, since a zero exit means every record was saved.
Re-run the dashboard query to confirm the chart looks normal before anyone questions it.
questions.why: The check compares the logged write count with the number of rows that actually landed in the destination for the same run, which is what reveals a gap.

questions.prompt: Which tool lets you run SQL directly on exported log files sitting in object storage, without loading them into a database, and charges you for the amount of data each query scans?
choices: Amazon EMR, a managed cluster for big data frameworks such as Spark.
Amazon OpenSearch Service, a managed search engine that indexes text for fast charts.
Amazon Athena, which queries files in object storage with SQL and bills by data scanned.
CloudWatch Logs Insights, a query tool over live log groups in CloudWatch.
questions.why: Athena is the option that runs SQL on files in object storage without a database load and charges for data scanned, while the other three work on different sources or are billed differently.

questions.prompt: A team has exported a week of pipeline logs as files in object storage. They want to list each run from that week whose rows written is lower than its rows read, grouped by run id. Which approach fits best?
choices: Build a managed Spark cluster in Amazon EMR and write custom code for a single count query.
Load the files into an OpenSearch index and build a dashboard panel for the mismatch.
