choices: Backups are only offered on self-managed services, so the managed catalog has none to review.
The provider's backups are encrypted with a key that the provider gives to all customers, so the catalog is already public.
Automatic backups make access reviews unnecessary only when the catalog is stored in a single Region.
Backups protect against losing data, but they do not decide who may read it, and access rules remain the team's responsibility.
questions.why: Durability features such as backups address loss of data, while access control is a separate governance duty that the managed model does not transfer to the provider.

questions.prompt: A three-person analytics team must choose between a managed reporting database and a self-installed database on virtual machines it rents. Which trade-off best describes what the managed option gives up and gains?
choices: It gives up some low-level control and version timing and often costs more per unit of capacity, in return for fewer operational duties such as patching and failover.
It gives up all responsibility for security and gains automatic compliance with every Region's rules.
It gives the team full control of every low-level setting and gains lower cost per unit of capacity.
It gives up responsibility for the data and gains the right to skip access reviews entirely.
questions.why: Managed services trade some control and often higher unit cost for less operational work, but the team still owns the data governance duties in both options.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that moving our data store to a managed service means we no longer have to think about security. Explain to them, in your own words, what a managed service takes off your team, what it leaves with your team, and one tradeoff of choosing it over running the software yourself.
lessons.modelAnswer: A managed service takes over much of the operational work: installing and patching the software, keeping the underlying servers running, and handling much of the failover and backup machinery. If we ran the same software ourselves, all of that would be our job. But managed does not mean hands-off. We still decide who can read and write the data, whether it is encrypted, where it is stored, and how we would prove those things to an auditor. Those are our configuration choices, and a wrong one exposes data just as much on a managed service. The tradeoff is control against effort. A managed service gives us less control over low-level settings and version timing, and often a higher price per unit of capacity, in exchange for fewer chores and fewer things that break at 3 a.m. So the useful question is not whether we are secure, but which security duties remain ours.
rubricPoints: Managed services move operational chores such as patching, hardware, and much failover to the provider.
Unmanaged means the team installs and runs the software and owns every operational duty.
Under the shared responsibility model, the team still owns access control, encryption choices, and data location.
A real tradeoff exists: managed gives less control and can cost more per unit, in exchange for less operational work.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the split of duties back in your own words is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine a large company where many teams share one building full of data. This objective is about the three levels used to organize that building in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, an AWS workspace for data and analytics work. The outermost level is a domain, the single container that holds the organization's users, shared data listings, and projects. Inside a domain, domain units form a tree of departments, so an administrator can manage their own branch without controlling the others. A project is a working room where a small team collaborates on its datasets, notebooks, and jobs, and decides who inside it can do what. Getting these three levels right keeps one team's work governed without exposing everything to everyone.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one analytics workspace serves three departments, each with several small teams, how would you arrange the levels so a department lead can manage only their own part, and a team can work on its own datasets without seeing unrelated ones?
lessons.teach:
A domain is the top-level container in SageMaker Unified Studio. It is the one place where an organization's users are connected, its catalog of shared data is kept, and its projects live. A domain unit is a named group inside a domain, arranged as a tree like departments in an organization chart. Its purpose is delegation: a domain unit can have its own owners and administrators who manage the units beneath it, and they cannot quietly change the branches they do not own. A project is a collaboration workspace inside a domain unit. It holds a team's members, its data connections, its notebooks and jobs, and the data assets the team publishes or subscribes to. Membership in a project decides who can work inside it.

Worked example. A company creates the domain Acme Analytics. Under it, the domain unit Retail is created, and under Retail sits Pricing. The Pricing team creates a project called Price-Tests and adds its five members. Pricing publishes a sales table to the catalog. A logistics analyst in a different unit searches the catalog, requests a subscription to that table, and the table owner approves it. Step by step: domain, then domain unit, then project, then publish, then request, then approve.

Common mistake: putting every team into one project, or assuming that because someone administers a domain unit they can read every project's data. Administration and data access are separate decisions, and a single shared project makes the whole company's data visible to its members.

Consequence: a wrong structure is hard to undo once teams have built pipelines in it, so the domain-unit tree should follow real ownership before projects are created.

A domain organizes the whole company, domain units delegate ownership inside it, and projects are where a team does its work and controls its members.

questions.prompt: A bank creates the domain Harbor Financial. Under it, the domain unit Lending is created, and inside Lending the team creates a project called Risk-Scoring and adds four analysts. An analyst in the Insurance domain unit then searches the catalog for the Risk-Scoring scores table, requests a subscription to it, and the table owner approves. One step is missing from this sequence, right before the subscription request: Harbor Financial, then Lending, then Risk-Scoring, then ______, then the search and request, then approval. Which step fills the blank?
choices: The four analysts are moved into one shared project with Insurance
Harbor Financial is deleted and rebuilt under a new name
The Risk-Scoring team publishes the scores table to the catalog
The Lending owner removes the Insurance unit from the domain tree
questions.why: An analyst can only search for and subscribe to a data asset that the owning project has published to the domain's catalog, so publishing must come before the request.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a domain unit in SageMaker Unified Studio?
choices: A single workspace where a team's notebooks, jobs, and data connections are stored
The top-level container that holds every user and the company-wide catalog
A named group in a tree inside a domain whose owners manage the units beneath it without changing branches they do not own
A list of members who are allowed to open one project
questions.why: The teaching text defines a domain unit as a named node in a tree that delegates ownership to its own administrators, who cannot quietly change branches they do not own.

questions.prompt: A company with twelve analytics teams puts all of them into one project so they can share notebooks. What is the main risk of this structure?
choices: Each team loses its ability to publish any table to the catalog
The domain will refuse to create any more domain units
The project will run out of storage for notebooks
Members of the shared project can see data across all twelve teams, which breaks the separation a project is meant to give
questions.why: A project decides who can work inside it, so placing every team in one project exposes the whole company's data to all its members, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: Maya administers the domain unit Ops-West, which contains a project called Fleet-Telemetry. Maya is not a member of Fleet-Telemetry and has no approved subscription to its published tables. Can Maya read the project's data?
choices: Yes, because administering a domain unit grants read access to every project beneath it
No, reading project data depends on administering the unit, so Maya must be promoted to project owner first
No, because administration and data access are separate decisions, and Maya has neither project membership nor an approved subscription
Yes, but only to tables the project published before Maya was made an administrator
questions.why: The teaching text states that administering a domain unit does not give data access, which depends on project membership and approved subscriptions to published assets.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a domain, a domain unit, and a project differ in SageMaker Unified Studio, and name one limit or tradeoff of organizing a company's data this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: A domain is the top container for the whole organization: it holds users, the shared catalog, and projects. Domain units sit inside it as a tree, so each department can have its own administrators who manage their branch. A project is the working space for one team, with its members, connections, notebooks, and published or subscribed data. The main tradeoff is that the tree is hard to reshape once teams have built work in it, so it should match real ownership before anything is created. A second limit is that administering a domain unit does not automatically mean being able to read every project's data. Access to the data itself is decided separately, through project membership and subscription approval, so a reviewer should check those controls rather than assume them from the org structure.
rubricPoints: A domain is the top-level container holding users, the shared catalog, and projects.
Domain units form a delegated tree so branches can be administered separately.
A project is a team workspace whose membership controls who works in it.
Administration of a unit is separate from access to a project's data.
The structure is costly to change later, so it should mirror real ownership.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product structure and console terminology, which a reference-style reading covers better than a hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: When a team needs a permission, AWS offers ready-made rule sets called managed policies. Sometimes none of them fits: they grant too much, or they miss the one thing you need. An IAM policy is a short document of rules that says who may do which actions on which things. Writing your own, called a customer managed or inline policy, means you describe exactly the allowed actions and the exact resources, and nothing more. The skill is keeping that document small and checking it, because a rule that is too wide quietly exposes data, and a rule that is too narrow breaks a pipeline at 3 a.m.
lessons.guessPrompt: A managed policy grants read access to every storage bucket in the account, but your reporting job should only read one folder in one bucket. Before any teaching, what would you expect to change in the policy you write, and what could go wrong if you simply attach the broad one?
lessons.teach:
An IAM policy is a JSON document made of statements. Each statement has an Effect (Allow or Deny), an Action (the API operation, such as reading an object), a Resource (the specific thing the rule applies to, named by an ARN, which is Amazon's unique name format for resources), and optionally a Condition that narrows when the rule applies. IAM denies by default: nothing is permitted unless some statement allows it. An explicit Deny in any attached policy overrides every Allow.

Why write your own? A managed policy is a reusable template, either maintained by AWS or created in your own account. It is built for a general case, so it often grants whole services or every bucket. A custom policy lists only the actions and resources your job needs. This is least privilege: the smallest set of permissions that still lets the work finish.

Worked example. A reporting role must read files under one prefix of the raw bucket and nothing else. Step 1: allow s3:GetObject on the object ARN raw-bucket/sales/*. Step 2: allow s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN arn:aws:s3:::raw-bucket, with a Condition that limits the listed prefix to sales/. Step 3: attach nothing else, because the default deny covers everything not listed.

Common mistake: putting ListBucket on the object path. Object actions need the path ending in /* , while listing needs the bucket ARN itself. The job then fails with AccessDenied even though the rule looks right.

Consequence: a grant that is too broad lets a reporting job read customer PII it never needed, and that exposure becomes an audit finding. Always test a custom policy with the real role before it reaches production.

questions.prompt: A vendor's ingestion role must upload files into the incoming/ folder of the bucket ingest-eu and must not read or list anything. The steps so far: Step 1 allows s3:PutObject on the object path arn:aws:s3:::ingest-eu/incoming/*. Step 2 is missing. Step 3 says to test the policy with the vendor's real role by uploading one file into incoming/ and attempting one upload to the bucket root, then attach nothing else.
choices: Add no further statement, because the vendor never lists or reads, and the default deny already blocks those actions
Add an explicit Deny on s3:GetObject, since an Allow for writing would otherwise let the vendor read
Add s3:ListBucket on the object path ingest-eu/incoming/* so the vendor can check what is already there
Add s3:PutObject on the bucket ARN arn:aws:s3:::ingest-eu so writes to any folder are covered
questions.why: The vendor only needs the single write grant, so Step 2 adds nothing: listing and reading were never allowed and the default deny already covers them, while the other choices either put an action on the wrong resource or add statements the job does not need.

questions.prompt: An audit role has a custom policy with one statement: Allow s3:ListBucket on the resource arn:aws:s3:::ledger-archive/2023/*. When the role lists the bucket, the job fails with AccessDenied. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The role needs s3:GetObject as well, because listing only works when the role can also read the files
The Effect should be Deny, because listing is a restricted action that must be explicitly blocked
The policy is missing a Condition, because without one every listing request is refused by default
The resource for listing should be the bucket ARN arn:aws:s3:::ledger-archive, because the path ending in /* does not match the bucket itself
questions.why: ListBucket is applied to the bucket ARN itself, and a path ending in /* names objects inside the bucket, so the statement does not match the listing request and default deny applies.

questions.prompt: An analytics role must list the bucket metrics-lake but only see keys that begin with 2024-06/, and it must read the objects under that prefix. Which pair of statements does this with the least access?
choices: Allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::metrics-lake and Allow s3:ListBucket on metrics-lake/2024-06/*
Allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::metrics-lake/2024-06/* and Allow s3:ListBucket on arn:aws:s3:::metrics-lake with a Condition limiting the prefix to 2024-06/
Allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::metrics-lake/* and Allow s3:ListBucket on arn:aws:s3:::metrics-lake/*
Allow s3:* on arn:aws:s3:::metrics-lake so the role has every action it could ever need
questions.why: Reading objects uses the object path ending in /*, listing uses the bucket ARN with a Condition that narrows the prefix, and nothing else is granted, which matches least privilege.

questions.prompt: A security reviewer approves a role because it uses an AWS-maintained managed policy and says that makes the access least privilege by default. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: Managed policies only apply to production accounts, so the reviewer should check the development account instead
A managed policy with an explicit Deny cannot be combined with an Allow from another policy
Managed policies are built for a general case and often grant whole services or every bucket, so a maintained policy can still be broader than the job needs
AWS-maintained policies cannot be restricted, so they are always the narrowest option available
questions.why: A managed policy is a reusable template written for a general case, so being maintained by AWS says nothing about whether it grants only what one job needs; a custom policy listing just the required actions and resources is what achieves least privilege.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should attach the broad managed read-only storage policy to the reporting role because it is faster than writing one. In your own words, explain when a custom IAM policy is worth writing, what it must contain, and the main limit or tradeoff of writing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would push back on that. A managed policy is fast, but it usually grants read access to every bucket in the account, so the reporting role could see PII it has no reason to touch. A custom policy is worth writing when the managed one is wider than the job or misses a specific need. It should name the exact actions, such as getting objects and listing a bucket, the exact resources as ARNs, and a condition where useful, such as a prefix. Remember that listing applies to the bucket ARN while reading applies to object paths. The tradeoff is effort and maintenance: someone must write it correctly, test it against the real role, and update it when the data layout changes. Still, a few minutes of careful writing is cheaper than an audit finding about exposed customer data.
rubricPoints: A custom policy is justified when a managed policy grants more than the job needs or misses a required permission.
The policy should name specific actions, resources as ARNs, and conditions such as a prefix.
Listing and reading use different resource ARNs, the bucket versus the object path.
The tradeoff is authoring, testing, and maintenance effort against a smaller blast radius.

suggested.rationale: A planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test allow and deny decisions against real policy documents, which is the core practice for this objective.

lessons.plain: Programs often need a password or API key to reach something else, such as a database. The safe way to handle that key is to keep it out of the code and the configuration files, store it in a locked service built for the job, and have the program ask for it by name when it starts. It works like keeping a house key in a secure box with a logged sign-out sheet, rather than taping it under the doormat. Anyone reading the code sees only where the key lives, never the key itself.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a service needs a database password to start, where should that password live so that the code can be shared with the whole company without exposing the database?
lessons.teach:
A credential is a secret value a program presents to prove who it is, such as a database password or an API key. The safe pattern is to keep that value out of source code and configuration files, store it in a dedicated service, and have the program request it by name at run time. Two AWS services do this job. AWS Secrets Manager is built for sensitive secrets and can rotate them automatically. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store is a general key-value store for configuration; its SecureString type encrypts the value with an AWS KMS key, which is a managed encryption key. Both services check every read against IAM (identity and access management) policies attached to the caller, so the real question is which identity may read this one name.

Why it works: the name reveals nothing, so the file that contains it can be reviewed and committed safely. The value lives in one place, can be changed without a code release, and each read can be audited.

Worked example. An order service must log in to a database. First, an engineer creates a secret named orders/prod/db holding the username and password. Second, the service's IAM role is granted read access to that one secret only. Third, at startup the service calls the get-secret operation with that name. Fourth, the service receives the value in memory and uses it to connect. The repository contains only the name.

Common mistake: printing the retrieved value in a startup log, or pasting it into a deploy script as a plain environment variable, which copies it into build logs and shell history.

Consequence: once a password reaches version control or a log, anyone who can read that history can use it, and the only real fix is to change the password.

questions.prompt: A courier company runs a nightly job that uploads route summaries to a partner's file server. The partner's login password is stored as a Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString named /courier/prod/sftp/password, so the value is encrypted with a KMS key (a managed encryption key). The job's IAM role has been set up to be allowed to read that name. The steps are: (1) an engineer creates the SecureString parameter holding the password; (2) ____; (3) when the job starts, it calls get-parameter with decryption requested for that name; (4) it receives the password in memory and uses it to open the connection. The repository holds only the parameter name. Which choice correctly fills step 2?
choices: The parameter is made readable by every role in the account so that future jobs do not need a new grant.
The retrieved password is written to the job's stdout so operators can confirm the login succeeded.
The password is pasted into the job's config file so the job still works if Parameter Store is unreachable.
The job's role is granted read access to that one parameter name and nothing broader.
questions.why: Each read is checked against the IAM policy of the calling identity, so the role must be granted read access to that specific name, which is the step that keeps the value limited to the one job that needs it.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, why is it safe to commit a configuration file that contains only the name of a credential rather than its value?
choices: Because the name is encrypted automatically by the source control system whenever it is committed.
Because a committed name is ignored by the program until someone manually replaces it with the value.
Because the file is marked read-only, so no developer can change it after the commit.
Because the name reveals nothing about the secret, and the value is kept in a dedicated store and requested at run time.
questions.why: The teaching text explains that the name reveals nothing, so the file can be reviewed and committed, while the value stays in the dedicated store and is fetched by name when the program runs.

questions.prompt: A developer at a bakery chain's loyalty app adds a line that prints a retrieved database password to the application log, to check a login problem, and the change is merged and deployed. What is the most direct consequence?
choices: The password has reached a place anyone with log access can read, so the password itself must be changed to make it safe again.
The app stops working until the developer removes the line, because the store locks any value that has been printed.
Nothing, because log output is encrypted by default and only the app can read it.
The password is rotated automatically by the secret service the next time the app restarts.
questions.why: Once a credential reaches a log or version control, anyone who can read that history can use it, and the only real fix is to change the password.

questions.prompt: A hospital's scheduling tool connects to a reporting database, and the security team requires that the database password be changed automatically every 30 days without a code release. Which service fits this requirement best, and why?
choices: Systems Manager Parameter Store, because any key-value store can rotate values on a timer.
A plain environment variable set in the deploy script, because deploy scripts run on a schedule.
AWS Secrets Manager, because it is built for sensitive secrets and can rotate them automatically.
A file on the application server, because files are easier to update than stored values.
questions.why: The teaching text states that Secrets Manager is built for sensitive secrets and can rotate them automatically, which is the requirement described, while Parameter Store is described as a general configuration store.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would store a value in AWS Secrets Manager versus AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, and name one limit or tradeoff of keeping credentials out of code.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use Secrets Manager for real credentials such as database passwords, because it is built for sensitive secrets and can rotate them automatically. I would use Parameter Store for ordinary configuration, and for secrets only with the SecureString type, where the value is encrypted with a KMS key. In both cases the application gets only the name in its code or config, and its IAM role decides which names it may read. The tradeoff is that the app now depends on the secret service being reachable at startup, and a wrong name or missing permission fails at run time, so the error path must be tested. Also, the value still exists in memory and must never be logged.
rubricPoints: Names the difference: Secrets Manager for sensitive secrets with rotation, Parameter Store for configuration with optional encrypted SecureString values
Explains that code and config hold only the name, and IAM controls which identity may read it
Names a real limit, such as a runtime dependency on the service or the need to keep values out of logs
Notes that the value must not be printed or committed

suggested.rationale: That mission has you fix how a deploy gets its secret without leaking the value, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Think of a shared office building. Each person has a badge, a team is a group of people who share the same door permissions, and a role is a set of permissions someone can take on for a while, like a visitor badge. In a database that holds shared data, you decide who may look at which tables, who may change them, and who may pass that power on. Managing this with groups and roles means you set the rule once for a team instead of one person at a time, so when someone joins or leaves the team, their access follows the membership. Getting this wrong either locks analysts out of their reports or quietly lets everyone edit the finance numbers.
lessons.guessPrompt: Five analysts all need to read the same reporting tables, and two of them will move to a different team next month. Would you rather grant read access to each person separately, or to one shared group? Give one reason for your choice.
lessons.teach:
A database user is a named identity that can log in to the database. A group is a named collection of users. A role is a named bundle of privileges that can be granted to users or to other roles. A privilege is one permission on one kind of object, such as reading rows from a table, inserting rows, using a schema (the named container that holds tables), or changing a table's structure. A grant attaches a privilege to a user, group, or role, and a revoke removes it. This is how Amazon Redshift, a managed data warehouse, controls access, and the same ideas apply to most shared databases.

Why it works: you grant privileges to a group or role once, and every current and future member inherits them. Permissions then follow the job rather than the person. This also makes access reviewable, because an auditor can ask which group can read the customer schema and get a single answer.

Worked example. A group called analysts should read the sales schema. Step 1: the analysts group receives usage on the sales schema, because without it a member cannot reach the tables inside. Step 2: the analysts group receives read privilege on the sales tables. Step 3: user Dana is added to analysts. Step 4: Dana can now select rows from the sales tables, but an insert fails because nobody granted write privilege. Step 5: Dana changes teams and is removed from the group, and her access ends without anyone touching each table.

Common mistake: granting read privilege on a table but forgetting schema usage. The user then sees a permission error that looks as if the table does not exist. Another frequent mistake is granting privileges to individual users, which turns every team change into a hunt across many objects.

Consequence in a running system: removing a user who owns tables can leave those tables without a clear owner, so ownership should sit with a group or role. Access granted through a group is only as sound as its membership list, so that list needs regular review.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy chain keeps its loyalty data in a schema named loyalty. A role named points_reader should let its holder read the table loyalty.members and nothing else. User Owen must get this access. The steps are: (1) create the role points_reader; (2) grant usage on schema loyalty to points_reader; (3) this step is missing; (4) grant the role points_reader to user Owen. Which statement fills step 3 so that Owen can read the members table without gaining write access?
choices: Grant select on loyalty.members directly to user Owen
Revoke usage on schema loyalty from points_reader
Grant select on loyalty.members to points_reader
Grant insert on loyalty.members to points_reader
questions.why: The read privilege belongs on the table and is attached to the role, and then the role passed to Owen in step 4 carries that read access down to him without any write privilege.

questions.prompt: In the terms of this unit, what is a privilege?
choices: A named collection of users that is kept in the warehouse's account list
One permission on one kind of object, such as reading rows from a table or using a schema
A named login identity that can connect to the database
A bundle of other roles that is assigned to a single database user
questions.why: A privilege is defined as a single permission on a single kind of object, while the other choices describe a user, a group, and a role respectively.

questions.prompt: A logistics company grants select on its logistics schema to a group named vendor_readers. A new contractor is added to that group on Monday. What does the contractor get, and what does the team need to do?
choices: The contractor gets write access automatically because group members always share the group's full rights
Nothing is inherited, so each logistics table must be granted to the contractor one by one
Only the schema is visible, and read access to tables must be requested from the group owner
Read access to the tables comes through group membership, so no per-table grant is needed for the contractor
questions.why: Privileges granted to a group are inherited by every current and future member, so adding the contractor to the group is enough for read access and no per-table grants are required.

questions.prompt: An analyst gets a permission error saying the table reports.daily_totals does not exist, yet the table is present and the analyst holds select on it. Which cause is most consistent with the teaching text?
choices: The analyst is missing usage on the reports schema, which makes the table look absent from their point of view
The analyst's login password has expired, which blocks access to every object in the database
The select privilege was granted to a role instead of to the analyst, which always produces a missing-table error
The table was dropped and recreated, so the earlier select grant no longer exists in any form
questions.why: Without usage on the schema that holds a table, a user cannot reach the table inside it, and the resulting error can look as if the table does not exist, as the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we grant read access to the analysts group rather than to each analyst directly, and name one limit or tradeoff of the group approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: We grant the privilege to the analysts group because access should follow the job, not the person. When someone joins the team, adding them to the group gives them the same read access at once, and when they leave, removing them ends it without editing each table. It also makes audits simpler, since one group membership list answers who can read the data. The tradeoff is that a group is only as accurate as its membership. If someone stays in the group after changing roles, they keep access they no longer need, so membership needs regular review. Also, a group gives everyone in it the same privileges, so if two people need different levels of access, you need a separate group or a role for that difference. Groups reduce repetitive work, but they do not remove the need to think about who belongs where.
rubricPoints: Access attached to a group or role is inherited by every member, so changes are made once.
Removing someone from the group ends their access without per-object edits.
Group membership must be reviewed, because stale members keep access.
Groups give identical privileges to all members, so differing needs require separate groups or roles.

suggested.rationale: A planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner trace whether a given user, group, or role is allowed a specific action, which is the reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Picture a shared storage room where several teams keep their files, with a front desk that decides who may open which drawer and which labels they can read. In AWS, many company datasets sit in raw storage buckets, and Lake Formation acts as that front desk for the tables that describe them. You write rules such as this team may read this table but not the salary column. The query engines the teams use must ask the front desk before handing over any data. Lake Formation is a managed AWS service, so AWS runs the desk for you. Your job is to know who it lets in and what could let someone walk around it.
lessons.guessPrompt: An analyst can already read every raw file in a shared storage bucket. If you then grant that analyst access to only some columns of a table through a permissions layer, what do you think happens when the analyst reads the raw files directly, and why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A data lake is a set of files, usually in Amazon S3 object storage, that many teams read. A catalog is a registry of tables that records where each dataset lives and what its columns are; on AWS this is the AWS Glue Data Catalog. A principal is whoever asks for access, such as a user or a role that a person or service assumes. Lake Formation is a permissions layer over the catalog. Instead of granting access to raw files, you grant permissions on catalog objects: a database, a table, specific columns, or rows selected by a data filter. Engines such as Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, and Amazon EMR ask Lake Formation whether a principal may read, and it returns only the permitted view.

Why it works: one set of rules is enforced in every engine that goes through it, so a hidden column stays hidden whether the analyst queries with SQL or a Spark job.

Worked example. A table called customers has the columns name, city, and email. Step 1: the analyst role is granted SELECT on customers with email left out. Step 2: the analyst runs SELECT name, city FROM customers in Athena. Lake Formation returns those two columns and the query succeeds. Step 3: the analyst runs SELECT email FROM customers. The request is refused because email was never granted to them.

Common mistake: the raw S3 files stay readable through an IAM policy the analyst also holds, or the catalog keeps a default setting that lets IAM-based access continue alongside Lake Formation. The analyst then reads email straight from the files and the column grant does nothing. You must turn that default off for the governed tables and remove direct S3 read from analysts, so Lake Formation is the only path in.

Consequence: in a running system a grant that looks correct on screen can be silently bypassed, and an auditor who checks the raw files will find the personal data exposed.

questions.prompt: A clinic network keeps a table called visits in the database clinic_db. Its columns are visit_date, clinic_id, diagnosis_code, and patient_phone. Step 1: the reporting role is granted SELECT on visits with patient_phone left out. Step 2: the reporting role runs a Spark job on Amazon EMR, a managed cluster service for large data processing, that selects clinic_id and diagnosis_code, and it succeeds. Step 3 is missing from this record. Step 4: the reporting role runs SELECT patient_phone FROM visits in Athena and the request is refused. What must Step 3 be so that patient_phone stays protected even though the reporting role also holds an IAM policy that reads the raw S3 files?
choices: Grant the reporting role SELECT on patient_phone too, so the Spark job and Athena can both read it consistently.
Remove the reporting role's direct S3 read permission and turn off the catalog default that lets IAM-based access run alongside Lake Formation for visits.
Enable server-side encryption on the S3 bucket holding the visits files, which blocks any reader who lacks a key.
Copy visits into a second table in a new database so the reporting role queries only the copy.
questions.why: Lake Formation only controls reads that go through it, so the direct S3 read and the default that allows IAM access alongside it must be removed or the column grant can be bypassed.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does Lake Formation control on an AWS data lake?
choices: The compute size of the Athena and EMR clusters that run queries, so that heavy jobs get more capacity.
Who may read catalog objects such as databases, tables, columns, and filtered rows, for every engine that asks it.
The encryption keys used to write new files into S3 buckets across every account in the organisation.
The physical Region and storage class of the S3 files, moved automatically whenever the data owner changes a setting in the console.
questions.why: Lake Formation is a permissions layer over the catalog, deciding which catalog objects a principal may read, and engines like Athena, Redshift, and EMR ask it for that decision.

questions.prompt: A bank stores a transactions table in the catalog with a region column. Only the EU analysts role should see rows where region is EU, while still being able to query the table through Lake Formation. Which grant does this?
choices: A column-level grant on transactions that hides the region column from every other team.
A SELECT grant on the whole transactions database, with the EU analysts told to add a WHERE clause themselves.
A data filter on the transactions table selecting rows where region equals EU, granted to the EU analysts role.
A bucket policy on the S3 prefix that holds the EU rows, so the analysts can list only that folder.
questions.why: A data filter is the Lake Formation object that restricts which rows a principal sees, whereas a column grant hides columns and a bucket policy bypasses the catalog entirely.

questions.prompt: A team hides the ssn column from the analyst role using Lake Formation. Later an auditor finds the analyst reading ssn from the raw Parquet files in S3, using a policy the analyst also holds. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The analyst's Athena workgroup has a result location set to a bucket that is not encrypted with a customer key.
Lake Formation cannot hide columns in Parquet format, so the column grant never worked from the start.
The grant was made on the database instead of the table, which always exposes every column to the principal.
Direct S3 read still works through IAM, so the analyst reaches the files around Lake Formation's column grant.
questions.why: When IAM still permits direct S3 reads and the catalog keeps the default that allows IAM access alongside Lake Formation, the column grant is bypassed because the files are reachable by another path.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Lake Formation controls access to a shared data lake across Athena, Redshift, and EMR, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Lake Formation puts a permissions layer over the catalog tables that describe our data in S3. We grant a role SELECT on a table, optionally leaving out sensitive columns or limiting rows with a data filter. Each engine, whether Athena, Redshift, or EMR, asks Lake Formation before returning data, so the same rule holds everywhere. The main limit is that it only protects paths that go through it. If someone still holds direct S3 read permission, or the old default that lets IAM-based access keep working is left on, they can read the raw files and skip the column restriction. So before trusting it, we turn that default off for governed tables, remove direct file access from analysts, and check the audit log to confirm who read what. It also adds upkeep: every new table needs its grants set, or the team that expects access will be blocked until someone adds them.
rubricPoints: Lake Formation grants permissions on catalog objects such as databases, tables, columns, and rows, not on raw files.
The same grant is enforced by Athena, Redshift, and EMR because each engine asks Lake Formation first.
A limit: direct S3 read or the old IAM default lets someone bypass the column or row restriction.
Governed tables need the default turned off and direct file access removed for analysts to be effective.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a who-can-read-what scenario with a hidden column and a direct-file path adds the most here.

lessons.plain: Authorization is the question of what a person or program is allowed to do with a piece of data, once we already know who they are. There are three common ways to answer it. Role-based control grants access to a job function, such as analyst, so everyone holding that role gets the same rights. Tag-based control uses labels attached to the data, such as marking a table as containing personal information, so the rule follows the label and protects new data automatically. Attribute-based control makes the decision from facts about the person and the data together, such as whether the person's department matches the data's owning department, so one rule can cover many cases without a new grant each time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shared data lake holds a table of customer phone numbers. Next month, ten analysts join and a new table of contact details is created every week. Would you rather grant each analyst access one table at a time, or write one rule saying members of the support team may read any table labelled as customer contact data? Explain which option you would pick and why.
lessons.teach: A principal is the person or program asking for access. An action is what they want to do, such as read or write. A resource is the thing being touched, such as a table or a folder in the lake. A policy is a written rule that says allow or deny a set of actions on a set of resources, optionally with conditions. Authorization systems usually start from deny: if no allow rule matches a request, the request fails. Role-based control attaches permissions to a role, a named bundle of rights that people or services take on, so you manage a small set of roles instead of thousands of individual grants. Tag-based control uses tags, which are key-value labels attached to resources, such as classification equals pii. A rule can allow reads only on resources whose tag has a particular value. Attribute-based control generalises this: a condition compares attributes of the principal, the resource and the request, such as principal team equals resource owner, so one rule covers many datasets. Worked example. Priya is an analyst whose team tag is analytics. The table orders_daily has an owner tag of analytics and a classification tag of internal. Step 1: the request is Priya reads orders_daily. Step 2: the policy allows read where the principal team equals the resource owner and the resource classification is not pii. Step 3: the team matches and the classification is internal, so the rule matches and access is allowed. Now the table customers carries classification pii. The classification check fails, no other allow rule matches, and the request is denied. Common mistake: letting the people being controlled edit the tags. If an analyst can change classification from pii to internal, one edit defeats the rule, so tag editing needs its own tightly held permission. Consequence: in a running pipeline, a job that writes new output without the correct tags creates data that the rules either hide from people who need it or expose to people who should not see it. Tags have to be set when data is created, not added later by hand.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental Group keeps a shared data lake. The table recall_letters has an owner tag of billing and a classification tag of internal. The policy allows read where the principal team equals the resource owner and the resource classification is not pii. Step 1: Dana, whose team tag is clinical, requests a read of recall_letters. Step 2: the read rule is checked against the request. Step 3: [MISSING STEP: the team and owner comparison is made and its result is applied to the rule]. Step 4: the rule outcome is recorded as the final decision.
choices: Because no deny rule matches, the default outcome is allow, so the read succeeds.
Classification is internal, which satisfies the rule on its own, so the read is allowed even though the teams differ.
Clinical is compared with the classification tag internal, the match succeeds, and the read is allowed.
Teams differ (clinical versus billing), the condition fails, no other allow rule matches, so the request is denied.
questions.why: The team condition is one part of an allow rule that must fully match, and since clinical does not equal billing, no allow rule matches and the default deny applies.

questions.prompt: A storage team labels every table with a key-value tag, sensitivity equals restricted, and writes one rule that allows reads only where that tag is not restricted. Which control model is being used?
choices: Deny-by-default, because a missing allow rule means refusal.
Attribute-based control, because it reads a badge number from the principal.
Role-based control, because the rule is attached to a named bundle of rights.
Tag-based control, because the rule decides using a key-value label on each resource.
questions.why: The rule depends on a key-value label attached to the resource, which is the defining feature of tag-based control.

questions.prompt: A pipeline job writes new output tables but never sets the classification tag on them. Later, an analyst on the marketing team reads one of those tables. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Classification-based rules have nothing to match, so the table is either hidden from people who need it or shown to people who should not see sensitive data.
The analyst's role is revoked automatically because a write happened without the correct tags.
Nothing changes, because tags only matter for audit reports and never affect access decisions.
The platform automatically assigns pii to every untagged table, so the analyst is blocked from reading it and the job fails.
questions.why: Rules that test tags cannot evaluate a table with no correct tag, so the output lands on the wrong side of the rule, which is the risk the teaching text describes for jobs that skip tagging.

questions.prompt: A lake has two designs. Design X gives a role named ingest-writer the right to write to many tables. Design Y uses one condition: the principal's project attribute equals the resource's project attribute. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Design X is attribute-based because roles are attributes of the principal.
Design Y is attribute-based, comparing attributes of the principal and resource, and one rule covers many datasets; Design X is role-based.
Design Y is role-based because it names a project.
Both designs are tag-based, because both need labels on the resources.
questions.why: Design Y compares attributes of the principal and the resource in a single condition, which is attribute-based control, while Design X attaches rights to a named role, which is role-based control.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between role-based, tag-based and attribute-based access control on a shared data lake, and name one limit or tradeoff of tag-based control.
lessons.modelAnswer: Role-based access grants rights to a job function, so an analyst role can read the sales datasets, and the number of roles stays small even as people join. Tag-based access attaches labels to data, such as classification pii or owner analytics, and writes rules that follow those labels, so a new dataset is protected as soon as it is tagged correctly. Attribute-based access compares attributes of the person, the data and the request in one condition, such as the requester's team matching the dataset's owner, which handles many cases with one rule. The main limit of tag-based control is that it is only as reliable as the tags. If tags are missing, wrong, or editable by the people being restricted, the rules quietly stop protecting the data. So tag values must be set at creation by the pipeline or a trusted process, and changing them must be a separate, audited permission.
rubricPoints: Role-based control grants rights to a job function or role rather than to individuals
Tag-based control makes rules follow labels on the data, so new data is covered when tagged
Attribute-based control compares attributes of the principal, resource and request in one condition
Tag-based control depends on accurate tags; restrict who can edit them and set them at creation

suggested.rationale: The planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test role, tag and attribute conditions against requests and see the allow or deny result directly.

lessons.plain: Least privilege means giving a person or program only the permissions it needs for its job, and nothing more. A custom policy is a written rule you create yourself that states which actions are allowed on which things, instead of borrowing a broad ready-made rule. Think of a key cut for one door rather than a master key for the whole building. Writing these rules well means naming exact actions, exact resources, and sometimes conditions such as a required folder or network location, so that a mistake or a stolen credential can do less damage.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job only needs to read files from one folder in a shared storage bucket and write its summary to a second folder. Would you give it full control of the whole bucket, or something narrower? Name the permissions you would grant and explain what could go wrong if you were too generous.
lessons.teach: A policy is a document made of statements. Each statement names an effect (Allow or Deny), one or more actions (the operations, such as reading an object or writing one), one or more resources (the specific things those actions apply to), and optionally conditions (extra tests, such as a required folder prefix or a source network). Least privilege means every Allow names only the actions and resources the job truly uses. Why it works: access is denied by default, so a request succeeds only if some Allow matches it and no Deny blocks it. Narrow lists mean fewer ways to succeed by accident. Worked example: a nightly sales job reads raw files under the raw/sales/ prefix of a shared bucket and writes results under curated/sales/. Step 1: the first statement allows only the read action, on resources matching raw/sales/. Step 2: the second statement allows only the write action, on curated/sales/. Step 3: the job lists the bucket to find its files, so a third statement allows the list action on the bucket itself, with a condition limiting listings to the raw/sales/ prefix. Step 4: a request to read raw/finance/ matches no Allow, so it is denied. Common mistake: when a job fails with access denied, engineers set the action and resource to wildcards so the error disappears. That fixes the symptom by granting everything, including other teams' personal data. Consequence in a running system: a bug or a stolen credential can then delete the raw archive or read PII the job never needed, and the audit log will point to the broad grant as the cause. A least-privilege policy keeps that blast radius to the one folder the job actually uses.

questions.prompt: A shipping team's job reads daily manifest files under the manifests/daily/ prefix of the bucket ship-lake and writes parsed results under parsed/daily/. Statement 1 allows only the read action on manifests/daily/*. Statement 2 allows only the write action on parsed/daily/*. The job also needs to list ship-lake to discover new manifests, but that third statement has not been written yet. Then a request to read manifests/archive/2023-06.csv is made, and it matches no Allow, so it is denied. Which third statement completes the policy correctly?
choices: Allow every action on the bucket ship-lake so that the listing works
Allow the list action on the bucket ship-lake, with a condition limiting listings to the manifests/daily/ prefix
Allow the list action on objects matching manifests/daily/* so the job can see its files
Allow the list action on all buckets in the account so the job never hits a gap
questions.why: Listing acts on the bucket itself, not on individual objects, so the list action is allowed on the bucket and a prefix condition keeps the listing to the one folder the job uses.

questions.prompt: In a policy statement, which element names the operations a principal may perform, such as reading or writing an object?
choices: The action
The effect
The condition
The resource
questions.why: Actions are the operations, such as reading or writing, while resources name what those operations apply to and conditions are extra tests.

questions.prompt: A reporting job needs to read files only from the analytics/2024/ prefix of the bucket finance-archive. Which statement follows least privilege?
choices: Allow the read action on every object in finance-archive so future folders are covered
Allow every action on every resource in the account
Allow the write action on the analytics/2024/ prefix
Allow the read action on objects under the analytics/2024/ prefix only
questions.why: Least privilege means the Allow names only the action the job uses (read) and only the resources it touches (that one prefix), so option 3 is the only fit.

questions.prompt: A job fails with access denied when it writes to a folder in a shared bucket. Which response keeps the policy least-privileged?
choices: Grant all actions on the whole bucket so the error cannot come back
Remove the conditions from every existing statement so nothing blocks the job
Add a Deny statement covering the whole bucket to stop the errors
Check the audit log for the denied action and resource, then add only that action on that prefix
questions.why: Reading the denial details shows the exact missing action and resource, so adding only that narrow grant fixes the failure without widening access to other teams' data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tighten a policy that gives a data pipeline role full access to a shared data lake. Name one limit or tradeoff of making the policy very narrow.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would replace the wildcard actions and resources with the specific operations the pipeline performs, such as reading from its raw input prefix and writing to its curated output prefix, and I would add a condition so listing the bucket only returns that prefix. Then I would test the policy against real requests, including one to a finance prefix that should be denied, and check the audit log for denied calls to see what is still missing. The tradeoff is maintenance: a very narrow policy breaks whenever the pipeline gains a new input or output path, so each change needs a policy review and a deliberate update rather than a quiet widening. Engineers sometimes resist that friction, but it is what keeps a failed or compromised job from reaching data it was never meant to touch.
rubricPoints: Least privilege means naming specific actions and resources instead of wildcards
Access is denied by default, so each Allow must match a real need
Conditions such as prefixes can narrow a grant further
Narrow policies break when needs change, so changes should be reviewed deliberately
Denied requests in logs reveal what a policy still lacks

suggested.rationale: The planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner write statements and see which requests are allowed or denied, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Data masking means hiding or altering sensitive values in a dataset so that people or systems who do not need the real value never see it. Anonymization goes further: it removes the link between the data and any real person, so the data can no longer be traced back. Companies and privacy laws often require this before data is shared with analysts, testers, or outside partners. Picture a shared spreadsheet where customer names are replaced with codes and card numbers show only the last four digits. The useful shape of the data stays, while the risky details are gone.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support analyst needs to count orders per city but must not see customer email addresses. Would replacing each email with a random number be enough to protect the customers? Explain your reasoning.
lessons.teach:
Masking is changing a sensitive value so it no longer reveals the original, while keeping enough form for the work to continue. Common techniques include redaction (removing the value or replacing it with a fixed placeholder), partial masking (showing only some characters, such as the last four digits of a card number), tokenization (swapping the value for a stand-in and keeping the real value in a separate, locked store), and generalization (replacing an exact value with a range, such as an age band instead of an exact age). A direct identifier names a person outright, such as an email address. A quasi-identifier is a field like postcode, birth year, or job title that is harmless alone but can single out one person when combined with others. Pseudonymization replaces identifiers with consistent stand-ins so records can still be linked, but the data stays personal because someone holding the key can reverse it. Anonymization aims for re-identification to be not reasonably possible, which is a stronger and harder claim.

It works because analysis usually needs the shape of the data, such as counts, groups, and order over time, rather than the identity behind each row. Masking keeps the shape and removes the identity.

Worked example: an orders table has email, city, and total. Step 1: email is a direct identifier, so the analyst does not need it. Step 2: drop the email column. Step 3: city and total remain, and counting per city works unchanged. Step 4: check that no city with very few customers combined with an exact total could point to one person.

Common mistake: replacing names with random numbers but keeping quasi-identifiers such as postcode, birth year, and gender together. Those combined can single out one person, so the dataset is still personal data.

Consequence: a dataset released as anonymous that can be re-identified breaks the compliance rule. The access log then becomes the evidence an auditor uses to trace who released what, and when.

questions.prompt: A clinic exports visit records for a research team. Each row has patient_name, phone_number, postal_code, date_of_birth, and visit_reason. Step 1: patient_name and phone_number are direct identifiers, so both are dropped. Step 2: date_of_birth is replaced with an age band such as 40 to 49, which is generalization. Step 3: this step is missing. Step 4: counts of visit_reason per age band still work unchanged, so the research goal survives. Which step 3 completes the process?
choices: Replace patient_name with a random number and label the table anonymous
Store phone_number in a separate locked table, which by itself makes the remaining rows anonymous
Check that no postal_code and age band combination is so rare it could point to one patient, and generalize postal_code further if it is
Keep postal_code and the exact birth date, since a postal code is harmless on its own
questions.why: A quasi-identifier such as postal code can single out one person when combined with an age band, so the missing step must test for rare combinations and generalize further if needed.

questions.prompt: A retailer replaces each customer ID with a consistent hashed token so that loyalty records can still be linked across months. The mapping from token to customer ID is kept by the marketing team. Which description is correct?
choices: The dataset is anonymized, because no customer name appears in it
The dataset is anonymized, because hashing is irreversible by definition
The dataset is pseudonymized and still personal data, because whoever holds the mapping can reverse the tokens
The dataset is redacted, because the customer IDs were removed
questions.why: Pseudonymization keeps records linkable through stand-ins, and because the key holder can reverse them the data remains personal, so it is not anonymous.

questions.prompt: A hospital researcher shares an extract with names removed. The extract still contains ZIP code, birth year, and sex for each patient. What is the main problem?
choices: Birth year is a direct identifier because it names a person outright
Dropping names makes the extract anonymous regardless of the other columns
ZIP code, birth year, and sex together can single out one person, so the extract is still personal data
Only the sex column needs masking, since the other fields are harmless
questions.why: Quasi-identifiers that are harmless alone can single out one person when combined, so removing names alone does not make the extract anonymous.

questions.prompt: A telecom support screen must show agents enough of a customer's phone number to confirm identity, but not the full number. The screen shows only the final four digits. Which masking technique is this?
choices: Generalization, because the number is replaced with a range
Redaction, because the number is replaced with a fixed placeholder
Partial masking, because only some characters are shown while the rest are hidden
Tokenization, because the number is swapped for a stand-in stored elsewhere
questions.why: Partial masking shows only some characters of a value, which keeps enough form for the agent's task while hiding the rest.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between masking, pseudonymization, and anonymization, and name one limit or tradeoff of anonymizing a dataset before sharing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Masking is any change that hides a sensitive value, such as dropping a column or showing only the last four digits of a card number. Pseudonymization swaps identifiers for consistent stand-ins, so rows can still be joined, but anyone who holds the mapping or key can reverse it, so the data is still personal under most privacy rules. Anonymization means the data cannot reasonably be traced back to a person, which is a higher bar. The main tradeoff is that stronger anonymization costs detail. Generalizing ages into bands or rounding locations makes the data less precise, so some analysis becomes less accurate. Also, removing names is not enough, because quasi-identifiers such as postcode, birth year, and job title can still single someone out, so the combination has to be checked before release.
rubricPoints: Defines masking as hiding or changing sensitive values, with an example technique
Distinguishes pseudonymization (reversible, still personal data) from anonymization (not reasonably re-identifiable)
Names the tradeoff of lost detail or accuracy after generalization or redaction
Warns that removing direct identifiers alone does not stop re-identification through quasi-identifiers

suggested.rationale: Choosing between masking, tokenization, and anonymization for a specific sharing requirement is an exam-style reasoning task that no current mission or planned engine covers directly.

lessons.plain: AWS KMS is a managed service that holds encryption keys for you, so you never have to store the raw secret yourself. A key is a secret value that scrambles data so that only someone holding the right key can unscramble it. Using KMS means asking the service to protect a key on your behalf and to perform encryption or decryption with it. In practice, most data is encrypted with a separate, short-lived data key, and KMS only protects that data key. This lets a data lake store large files safely while the master key stays inside the service.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you encrypt a 5 GB file using a key that lives inside a managed service, do you expect the whole file to be sent to that service and back, or something much smaller? Why?
lessons.teach:
A KMS key (short for AWS Key Management Service key) is a logical key object. It has an identifier, a policy that says who may use it, and settings such as whether it is symmetric or asymmetric. The secret material itself stays inside the service's tamper-resistant hardware, and you never download it. Instead you ask the service to perform cryptographic operations, and it checks your permission before doing so.

Symmetric keys use one key for both encrypting and decrypting, and they are the default and the usual choice for data at rest. Asymmetric keys come as a public and private pair and suit signing or cases where the encrypting party should not be able to decrypt.

Why envelope encryption works: a KMS key can only directly encrypt a few kilobytes, so services use envelope encryption. You ask KMS to generate a data key. KMS returns it twice: once in plain text, which you use to encrypt your data and then discard from memory, and once encrypted under the KMS key, which you store next to the ciphertext. To read the data later, you send the encrypted copy back to KMS to decrypt, receive the plain data key, and decrypt the file.

Worked example: a team writes a 2 GB Parquet file. Step 1: the writer requests a data key under the key alias orders-prod. Step 2: KMS returns plaintext key P and wrapped key W. Step 3: the writer encrypts the file with P, erases P from memory, and stores W in the file's metadata. Step 4: a reader fetches W, asks KMS to decrypt it, gets P back, and reads the file. If the reader lacks decrypt permission, step 4 fails and the file stays unreadable.

Common mistake: storing the plaintext data key beside the data, which defeats the whole design, or assuming one permission is enough. The key policy must allow the account to delegate to IAM, and the caller's identity policy must also allow the action.

Consequence in a running system: if the KMS key is disabled or scheduled for deletion, every wrapped data key becomes unusable, so the lake goes dark even though the files are intact. Treat the KMS key as a critical dependency, because losing access to it means losing the data it protects.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's backup tool encrypts a 6 GB database dump using envelope encryption, which means a fast data key encrypts the bulk data and a KMS key (AWS Key Management Service key, a protected key object that performs cryptographic operations without revealing its secret material) protects that data key. The tool works through these steps. Step 1: it asks KMS to generate a data key under the alias backups-eu. Step 2: KMS returns a plaintext data key P and a wrapped copy W, which is the data key encrypted under the KMS key. Step 3: the tool encrypts the dump with P. Step 4 is missing. Which action completes the design correctly?
choices: Write P into the backup manifest so a restore job can read it without calling KMS.
Store W inside the KMS key policy document so every account can find it.
Erase P from memory and store W alongside the encrypted dump.
Upload P to a separate bucket encrypted with the same alias so it can be recovered later.
questions.why: The plaintext data key must be discarded from memory after use, and the wrapped copy is stored next to the ciphertext so it can later be sent to KMS for decryption.

questions.prompt: A team needs one key that the same service uses both to encrypt and to decrypt large files at rest. Which kind of KMS key fits, and why?
choices: A symmetric key, because one key performs both operations and it is the usual default for data at rest.
A signing key, because signing keys are the only kind that can encrypt bulk data.
Any key works, because the choice between symmetric and asymmetric only affects cost.
An asymmetric key pair, because the public half encrypts and the private half decrypts.
questions.why: Symmetric keys use one key for both encrypting and decrypting and are the default for data at rest, while asymmetric pairs suit signing or cases where the encrypter should not be able to decrypt.

questions.prompt: An engineer disables a KMS key that protects an archive of old sensor readings, believing the files themselves are unaffected. What is the consequence for the running system?
choices: The archive files are corrupted and must be restored from a second copy.
KMS automatically re-encrypts every file under a new key within minutes.
The wrapped data keys become unusable, so the archive cannot be decrypted until the key is re-enabled, even though the files are intact.
Nothing changes, because the files hold their own keys and never call KMS.
questions.why: Each file's wrapped data key must be sent to KMS to be decrypted, so a disabled or scheduled-for-deletion KMS key makes the data unreadable while leaving the stored files unchanged.

questions.prompt: A reader role has permission to decrypt with a KMS key in its own identity policy, but the key's policy does not allow the account to delegate permissions to IAM. The reader requests a decryption. What happens?
choices: The request succeeds only after the key is rotated.
The request succeeds, because the identity policy alone is always enough.
The request succeeds but returns the wrapped key instead of the plaintext data key.
The request fails, because the key policy and the caller's identity policy must both allow the action.
questions.why: Access to a KMS key requires the key policy to allow the account to delegate to IAM and the caller's identity policy to allow the action, so a gap in either blocks the operation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why each file in a data lake is encrypted with its own data key rather than encrypting everything directly with the KMS key. Name one limit or risk of depending on KMS for decryption.
lessons.modelAnswer: A KMS key can only directly handle a small amount of data, a few kilobytes at most, and sending gigabytes through the service would be slow and costly. So KMS generates a separate data key for each file. The plaintext copy of that data key encrypts the file and is then discarded, while the encrypted copy is stored with the file. Only callers allowed to decrypt with the KMS key can recover the data key and read the file. The tradeoff is dependency: if the KMS key is disabled, scheduled for deletion, or its permissions are wrongly removed, the files become unreadable even though they are intact. So access to the key must be monitored and changed carefully.
rubricPoints: KMS keys handle only small amounts of data directly, so large files use a separate data key
The plaintext data key encrypts the file and is discarded; the wrapped copy is stored with the file
Decryption requires permission on the KMS key, so access control gates every read
Disabling or deleting the KMS key makes all dependent files unreadable, a real operational risk

suggested.rationale: The planned envelope encryption lab would make the learner generate, wrap, and unwrap data keys hands-on, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles data so that only holders of the right key can read it. When one AWS account owns the data and another account needs to read it, the key often lives in the owner's account, and that key's owner decides who may use it. Configuring this across account boundaries means opening two gates at once: the key owner must allow the outside account in, and that account's own identities must be allowed to use the key. If only one gate is open, access still fails, often with an error that looks like an ordinary permission problem. The skill is knowing which gate is which, and which kind of key can be shared at all.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bucket in account A is encrypted with a key that lives in account B. An administrator in account A adds a policy to their own user that allows using that key, but reads still fail. Before any teaching, what do you think is missing?
lessons.teach:
A KMS key is a key held in AWS Key Management Service. It performs encrypt and decrypt operations without revealing its raw material. A key policy is the resource policy attached to the key itself, and it lives in the account that owns the key. An IAM policy is attached to a user or role in the calling account. Cross-account means the caller and the key sit in different accounts. An AWS managed key is created and controlled by AWS for a service, such as the default key for S3. A customer managed key is created and controlled by you. Envelope encryption means the data is encrypted with a data key, and the data key is itself encrypted by the KMS key.

Why it works: a key use succeeds only when the key policy allows the principal and the caller's IAM policy allows the same action. Both must agree.

Worked example. Account A owns a bucket. Account B owns key K. Step 1: K's key policy names a role R in account A as allowed to call Decrypt and GenerateDataKey. Step 2: role R has an IAM policy allowing Decrypt on K's ARN. Step 3: a reader assuming R requests an object. S3 asks KMS to decrypt the data key. KMS checks the key policy, finds it allowed, and checks R's IAM policy, which also allows it. The decrypt succeeds. Remove step 1 and the same request is denied.

Common mistake: encrypting the bucket with the AWS managed S3 key. That key cannot be shared with other accounts, so no policy you write will make cross-account use work. Use a customer managed key instead.

Consequence: in a running pipeline, a job in another account that reads encrypted data fails with an access denied error from KMS. The job stops, and the error often looks like a storage problem.

A cross-account read of encrypted data needs the key owner's policy and the caller's own policy to both allow the action, using a customer managed key.

questions.prompt: Lumen Retail (account 5530) owns a customer managed KMS key, K-7. Its key policy allows the role VendorWriter in vendor account 7721 to call kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Encrypt on K-7. The vendor's nightly job assumes VendorWriter and writes files into a Lumen bucket that is set to encrypt with K-7. Lumen's key policy is already correct. The job fails with an access denied error from KMS. The one step still missing is on the vendor side: an IAM policy, attached to VendorWriter, that grants the same actions on K-7's ARN. Which fix completes the setup?
choices: Lumen switches the bucket to the AWS managed S3 key so the vendor's job no longer needs K-7
The vendor copies K-7's key material into account 7721 so the job can encrypt locally
Lumen adds a bucket policy that lets account 7721 read the bucket, and leaves the key settings unchanged
The vendor adds an IAM policy to VendorWriter in account 7721 allowing kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Encrypt on K-7's ARN
questions.why: A cross-account KMS call succeeds only when the key owner's key policy and the caller's own IAM policy both allow the action, so the missing piece is the vendor's IAM policy on VendorWriter.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, where does a key policy live, and what does it control?
choices: It lives on the key in the account that owns the key, and it says which principals may use that key
It lives in the S3 bucket, and it decides which KMS key encrypts each new object
It lives in AWS Organizations, and it sets the default encryption for every account under it
It lives on the user or role in the calling account, and it lists the buckets that user may open
questions.why: A key policy is the resource policy attached to the KMS key itself and sits in the key owner's account, controlling which principals may use the key.

questions.prompt: Analysts in account 3305 get access denied when they read files encrypted with a customer managed key owned by account 8810. The key policy in 8810 names the analysts' role, AnalystRead, as allowed to call Decrypt. AnalystRead has an IAM policy that allows s3:GetObject on the bucket but says nothing about KMS. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The bucket is in a different Region from the analysts, so KMS refuses the call on Region grounds alone
AnalystRead's own IAM policy does not allow kms:Decrypt, so the caller side of the agreement is missing
The key policy must also list the bucket's ARN, which is missing
The key is an AWS managed key, which can never be decrypted by any role
questions.why: A key use needs both the key policy and the caller's IAM policy to allow the action, and here the key policy allows Decrypt but the role's IAM policy never grants it.

questions.prompt: A team in account 6642 wants a role in account 1190 to read objects in a bucket owned by 6642. The bucket uses the AWS managed S3 key for encryption. Which statement is correct?
choices: Adding a bucket policy that names account 1190 is enough, because the bucket policy controls the key too
Cross-account reads will not work with that key, because an AWS managed key cannot be shared with other accounts, so the team should move to a customer managed key
Cross-account reads work as long as account 1190 has an IAM policy with s3:GetObject, regardless of the key
The AWS managed key can be shared by editing its key policy in the console, which is the simplest fix
questions.why: An AWS managed key is controlled by AWS and cannot be shared across accounts, so a customer managed key whose key policy you control is required for cross-account decryption.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a cross-account read of an encrypted object can fail even when the reader's IAM policy looks correct, and name one tradeoff of the fix you would choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: The reader's IAM policy only covers one side of the check. KMS also reads the key's own policy, which lives in the account that owns the key.
