Lambda has a short time and memory limit, so it is a poor match for a large nightly file; EMR works but needs more cluster management than the job justifies; Redshift is a data warehouse, not a file converter. For safe reruns, write output to a new prefix or partition for the run date, write to a temporary location first, and only publish when the job completes. Then a rerun overwrites the same date's output cleanly instead of appending duplicates or leaving half-written files visible to queries. Using Glue job bookmarks or a checkpoint of processed input files lets a rerun skip work already finished.

The nightly CSV job is best triggered by an S3 event notification on object creation, so it starts when the file actually arrives rather than at a fixed time that may be before the file is ready. The scanner pipeline needs no scheduled trigger because the stream itself pushes events to Lambda. For a late file, add an EventBridge scheduled rule that runs a check at a set time, such as 03:00, and looks for the expected file. If it is missing, the check sends an alert through Amazon SNS (a publish and subscribe notification service) to the operations team, and the job stays ready to run when the file lands, so a late file does not cause silent data gaps.

scenarios.title: Parcel status lookups and aging scan files at Harbor Peak Logistics
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Peak Logistics is a fictional courier company that records one row every time a parcel is scanned. Each scan is written as a small file to Amazon S3, which is object storage: you save files under names called keys, such as scans/2024/05/12/part-0001.json. A data catalog is a directory that records which datasets exist, where they live, and what columns they contain. The AWS Glue Data Catalog is AWS's version of that directory. A crawler is a job that reads files, guesses their structure (the schema), and registers the result in the catalog. A partition is a sub-folder that groups rows by a value such as date, so a query can skip folders it does not need. Two needs have come up. First, the customer app must show the latest status of one parcel, found by its tracking ID, in under 10 milliseconds. This is a key-value lookup, and Amazon DynamoDB is a managed table service built for that. Each item has a primary key, and a time to live (TTL) setting tells DynamoDB to delete items after a stored timestamp. Second, the analytics team queries scans by day. Raw scan files must stay in the standard storage tier for 30 days, move to a cheaper archive tier after 90 days, and be deleted after 7 years to meet a legal retention rule. Your team lead asks you to answer three things:
1. Choose the store for the tracking-ID lookup, name the primary key you would use, and explain how you would set TTL so status expires 90 days after the last scan.
2. Explain how a crawler and partition updates keep the catalog accurate when a new day folder appears every night, and what goes wrong if you skip this step.
3. Write the S3 Lifecycle rules for the archive move and the 7-year deletion, and explain what changes if versioning is turned on for the bucket.
subParts: Store and key choice with TTL
modelAnswer: Use Amazon DynamoDB, because it is a managed key-value table that returns one item by its key in single-digit milliseconds, unlike a data warehouse or a file store that scans many rows. Use tracking_id as the partition key (the partition key decides which internal storage node holds the item, which is a different meaning of partition from the date folders in S3). No sort key is needed if each parcel has one current status row. Add a numeric attribute such as expires_at that holds the epoch time of the last scan plus 90 days, then enable TTL on that attribute. Each new scan rewrites expires_at, so the clock restarts. Common mistake: assuming an item disappears the instant its timestamp passes. DynamoDB deletes expired items in the background, usually within a few days, so the app should also ignore items whose expires_at is already in the past if an exact cutoff matters.

A crawler reads the S3 prefix, infers the schema, and writes the table definition into the Glue Data Catalog. A new day folder such as scans/2024/05/13/ is a new partition, and the catalog does not know about it until you add it, either by running the crawler on a schedule or by calling a partition sync (for example adding the partition values in batch, or the Hive-style repair command in engines that support it). If you skip this, a query filtered on the new date finds no registered partition and returns zero rows with no error, so analysts see a silent gap. Schema drift works the same way: if a new column appears in tomorrow's files, the crawler can update the table definition, and older files that lack the column will read that field as null. Set a schedule and check the crawler's log each morning so new partitions and columns show up before reports run.

Create one Lifecycle rule scoped to the scans/ prefix with a transition action that moves current objects to an archive storage class after 90 days. Create a second rule on the same prefix with an expiration action after 2555 days, which is about 7 years, to meet the retention limit. Note that archive classes have a minimum storage duration and a retrieval delay, so archived files must be restored before a query can read them. If versioning is turned on, a delete does not remove data; it adds a delete marker and keeps older copies as noncurrent versions, which still cost money and still count as stored data. Add a rule that expires noncurrent versions after a set number of days, or the bucket keeps growing and the legal deletion goal is not met for the old copies.

scenarios.title: The green run with the wrong revenue
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Parcel Co. is a fictional courier company whose finance team reads a daily revenue report. A nightly pipeline is scheduled by Amazon MWAA, which is Amazon's managed version of Apache Airflow, an open-source scheduler that runs tasks in a defined order and records whether each task finished. The pipeline has three stages. First, an AWS Glue job (a managed service that runs Spark, a engine for processing large data sets, to transform data) reads raw order files from Amazon S3 (object storage that holds files in folders called prefixes) and writes cleaned Parquet files (a compressed column-based file format). Second, a second Glue job totals the orders per day. Third, an Amazon Athena query (a serverless SQL engine that reads files in S3 directly) feeds an Amazon QuickSight dashboard. Yesterday the whole run showed a green success status in MWAA. But finance noticed that yesterday's revenue was about 40 percent below the usual seven-day average, and nothing alerted anyone because no task failed. You are on call with three sources of evidence. The first is the CloudWatch Logs output of the first Glue job, where CloudWatch Logs is the service that stores the text a running job prints. The relevant line reads: Stage read complete, input_records=11904, rows_written=11904. The usual figure for this stage is about 48000 records per day. The second is the S3 listing for yesterday's prefix, orders/2024-06-13/, which contains 4 files where the usual count is 16. The third is a DataBrew profile of the cleaned table. DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool that can compute column statistics and run data quality rules, which are pass or fail tests on the data. The profile shows that the region column has one value, north, holding 97 percent of rows. Work through the following.

1. Using the log line and the usual volume, state which stage lost data, how large the loss was, and why the MWAA success status did not reveal it.

2. Describe an Athena query that counts rows per raw file for yesterday's date, and explain what its result would show about the missing files.

3. Name the data quality check that should have run before the dashboard refreshed, write its rule in plain words, and say what its failure would have done to the pipeline.
subParts: Locate the data loss in the logs
Confirm the gap with an Athena query
Name the check that should have caught it
modelAnswer: The first Glue job lost data. It read 11904 input records and wrote 11904 output records, against a usual figure of about 48000, so roughly three quarters of the day's orders never entered the pipeline. The loss happened at the read stage, before any transformation, because the input count itself was low. The MWAA success status only means each task ended without raising an error. It does not check whether the numbers are right, so a job that quietly reads fewer files still counts as a success.

Run a query such as SELECT "$path" AS source_file, COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM raw_orders WHERE dt = '2024-06-13' GROUP BY "$path". The $path is a built-in Athena column that names the file each row came from. The result would list only 4 source files, each with a normal-looking row count, instead of the usual 16. That shows the job did not see the missing files at all, which points to an upstream delivery or listing problem rather than a bug in the cleaning logic. Comparing this total with the seven-day average of the same query confirms the gap.

A row-count check should have caught it. The rule compares yesterday's row count for the cleaned table with the average of the previous seven days and fails the stage if the count falls below a threshold, such as 70 percent of that average. A failure stops the pipeline before the aggregation and dashboard steps, and it sends an alert through a notification channel. A skew check is a useful second rule here, because a single region value holding 97 percent of rows is a warning sign that partitions are missing or unbalanced. Either check run during processing would have blocked the bad numbers before anyone looked at the dashboard.

scenarios.title: Harrowgate Diagnostics shared data lake
scenarios.scenario: Harrowgate Diagnostics is a fictional medical-testing company. Its data lake is a set of files stored in Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service, an object store that keeps files as named objects in buckets). Three teams read from it: an internal analytics team, an external research partner, and a finance team that loads a Redshift data warehouse (a managed database built for large analytical queries). The customer table in the lake holds PII (personally identifiable information, any data that can identify a person), such as names and dates of birth. Harrowgate policy also says this data must stay in EU Regions (geographic areas of AWS data centres), so no copy may be written to a non-EU Region. Your manager needs three answers before next week's audit. 1. The analytics team may query customer rows but must never see the raw date-of-birth column, and the research partner may see only anonymized rows (rows where identifying details have been removed or replaced). Which access approach would you use in AWS Lake Formation (a service that grants permissions on data lake tables, columns and rows across engines such as Athena, Redshift and EMR), and why is an IAM policy alone not enough for these column and row rules? 2. The finance team's Redshift database password must be rotated every 30 days without an outage. Where should the password be stored, and what must the rotation process do so that running jobs keep working? 3. Auditors want proof that PII has been located and that no data has been copied to a non-EU Region. Name the tool that finds PII in S3, explain how you would prevent a non-EU copy and how you would detect one, and name the log that records who changed a bucket configuration and when.
subParts: Column and row access in Lake Formation
PII discovery, Region control and audit log
modelAnswer: Lake Formation is a managed permissions layer for a data lake. It grants access to catalogued tables and can go down to individual columns and, through data filters, to individual rows. IAM (Identity and Access Management) policies control who can call AWS APIs and reach resources such as an S3 bucket, but an IAM policy cannot see inside a table and hide one column. So you would grant the analytics role SELECT on the customer table with date_of_birth excluded, and create a data filter for the research partner that returns only anonymized rows. The common mistake is also giving those roles direct read access to the S3 files, because a direct read goes around the Lake Formation column and row rules and exposes the raw date of birth. The consequence is that the masking exists on paper only, and an auditor who finds the direct grant will treat the rule as failed.

Store the Redshift finance credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, a managed service that holds secrets such as passwords, encrypts them with a KMS key (a managed encryption key, which is a key that can encrypt and decrypt data without you handling the key material), and can rotate them on a schedule. The finance job fetches the password by secret name when it runs, so nothing is hard-coded in scripts. A rotation function creates a new password, sets it on the database user, tests the new credentials, and then marks the new version as current, so the job receives the working password on its next fetch. The common mistake is hard-coding the password in a script or configuration file, which means rotation silently breaks the job. The consequence is that the finance load fails on the first rotation until someone edits the file by hand, which is exactly the outage the rule is meant to prevent.

Amazon Macie is a managed service that scans S3 buckets and reports where sensitive data such as names and identification numbers sits. Macie finds PII but does not stop anything from being copied, so it is a discovery tool rather than a control. To prevent a non-EU copy you would use an AWS Organizations service control policy (a rule applied across accounts that can deny actions), which denies S3 replication and copy actions whose target Region is outside the EU. To detect any copy that slips through you would use AWS Config (a service that records resource configuration and evaluates it against rules), with a rule that flags non-EU replication destinations. The log that records who changed a bucket configuration and when is AWS CloudTrail (a service that records API calls with the caller, time, and source), and CloudTrail Lake can run SQL-style queries over those records for the auditor. The common mistake is treating the Macie report as proof of no copies, which proves only where PII was found. The consequence is an audit gap where the company can show where PII is but cannot show it never left the EU.
